events.title: ‘We are in a kind of war’: row over viral Amsterdam chip shop lands in court
events.summary: Neighbours say crowds drawn by TikTok to Fabel Friet are clogging the picturesque canal street and attracting litter, gulls and rats People living in one of Amsterdam’s most exclusive neighbourhoods have taken the city to court for licensing a chip shop that has gone viral on TikTok . On busy days, the queue for Fabel Friet on Runstraat stretches across a bridge on the Keizersgracht – one of Amsterdam’s most famous canals – a court was told last week. The narrow street itself is crowded by tourists waiting for their orders seven days a week. And loitering with intent – on parked cars, on the street itself, and on steps and porches – gulls wait to swoop. “We are in a kind of war where a very unwelcome chip shop has polluted the whole area,” said Thomas van Leeuwen, who lives nearby. “Eating in the street is a shameful behaviour. It gets filthy food on our doorsteps and mayonnaise in the beautiful stone. The herring gulls have moved in as residents, and the worst thing is the rat infestation.” Nineteen neighbours have formally protested against the business licence for Fabel Friet, whose signature product is fries topped with parmesan cheese and truffle mayonnaise. Niek van der Heijden, the lead plaintiff, said the problem was the takeaway’s small size. “What we call the ‘TikTok queue’ for Fabel Friet causes the most nuisance,” he said. “The business takes place on the street: waiting to order, waiting to be served, eating. We want Fabel to go to a place where there is enough room to have clients inside.” In a packed courtroom on Tuesday morning, a lawyer for Amsterdam city council acknowledged that the city’s mayor, Femke Halsema, can refuse a licence to operate if the “residential and living environment” is negatively affected by a business. While the chip shop, she said, sticks to its licence obligations to manage the queue and clear litter “it has been going on for a long time, the impact remains severe, and you have to ask: how long can we tolerate this?” For the current licence, she said, the city would be guided by the court’s ruling. The shop’s owners, Abel Klatser and Floris Feilzer, said they employed a cleaning service seven days a week, four times a day, and that year-on-year visitor numbers had dropped by 23% this August after they opened four new locations . “A few neighbours have experienced nuisance, but other people enjoy eating chips,” said Gertjan Teeuwen, their lawyer. “It can be busy, but there are peaks and troughs.” Klatser and Feilzer said in a public statement that they felt unfairly attacked while doing their best to be good neighbours. “Fabel Friet is our child, and we have put our heart and soul into it,” they said. “It is painful if people talk about our business negatively.” The case goes beyond irritations about so-called performative tourism, where tourists flock to a place to post images on social media. “The tiny streets might be charming, but actually the space is not designed for so many people,” said Lisa-Bobbie Kamp, a lawyer for the neighbours. “This is a question of taking space, who owns the place and whether you can just use public space.” Marije Peute, a PhD student at the University of Amsterdam, has studied the effects of “viral urbanism” in the neighbourhood. “The municipality should really think about how they want to act, because this is about the public space. A lot of much older retail spaces have lost their local clients because they don’t want to go there any more,” she said. Rogier Havelaar, a councillor from the Christian Democratic Appeal party, said that, while Fabel Friet should probably be offered a “flagship store” licence in a more suitable location, the benefits of tourism to the city should not be overlooked. “Amsterdam would never have as many museums, restaurants, going-out spots and theatres if they were only for the residents,” he said. “And tourism provides 70,000 jobs. Amsterdam would have a gigantic financial problem if tourism went away.” Standing on the bridge over the Keizersgracht, some German laboratory apprentices drawn by TikTok were enjoying their chips. Natalie Stübben said crowd managers had just asked them to move away from people’s houses. “It’s pretty hard to get through here with a car or just by walking,” she said. “I don’t think we were thinking about annoying the neighbours, but it makes sense.” Some of those neighbours will be pleased if the business location has had its chips after the court verdict on 12 November. “There’s something very alarming about the fact that these people are all led by their higher power – influencers – and call themselves followers,” said van Leeuwen. “It’s Orwellian. This court case is part of the parasitic industry that lives on tourists.”

events.title: Not SGX’s fault if stocks have no liquidity, says chairman: Markets this week
events.summary: In this column, ST’s business correspondents unpack the latest developments in Singapore and global markets during the week – and explain what they mean for investors. In taking full control of the Starbucks business, DFI will transfer its 50% stake in Maxim’s to Hongkong Caterers for US$340 million in cash. SINGAPORE – Listed companies should proactively disclose their three- to five-year strategies so that investors can better understand their businesses and growth prospects, with board chairs leading the effort, Singapore Exchange (SGX) chairman Koh Boon Hwee said on Oct 1. He was speaking at an event organised by the Singapore Institute of Directors . Koh said Singapore has strongly signalled its desire to reform its stock market, and more capital is already starting to flow in. However, small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) cannot solely depend on the SGX to boost their valuations, as the bourse does not create liquidity nor demand and supply. He said: “If you say that the market misunderstands you, it is your job to make sure that it understands you. If you say that there is no liquidity, it is because you have not been talking to the people who might have an interest in buying or demanding the stock.” Therefore, it is incumbent upon companies and their leaders to communicate their growth strategies to the public. “The exchange can’t do that for you, neither can it guarantee that your counter will be liquid.” Koh said privatisation could be an option for companies whose shares are thinly traded and which are reluctant to disclose their long-term plans publicly. His comments echoed a point made in his annual letter to shareholders on Sept 29, in which he said that “privatisation is not a tragedy but a rational and often healthy outcome”. “For a listed company with limited growth prospects, low trading liquidity and persistently low valuations, going private is a sensible path,” he wrote. “It serves little purpose for a company to remain listed simply so that an exchange can preserve its company count.” CDL tumbles after revealing 3-year plan The counter fell 5.7% by midday after its plans were unveiled before the market opened, and later closed 8.1% down at $7.59. It continued to slide and closed the week at $7.04, the lowest since November 2025. Explaining why CDL’s share price fell, analysts said weak market conditions and the interest rate outlook could make it difficult for CDL to divest $6 billion worth of assets as planned. Details on where CDL intends to invest an additional $5 billion are also lacking. In addition, doubts remain over whether the feud between chief executive Sherman Kwek and his father, executive chairman Kwek Leng Beng, has truly subsided. In early 2025, the father accused his son of orchestrating a boardroom takeover. The elder Kwek was also absent from the Sept 28 unveiling of the road map, which left questions on succession from the media unanswered. Others noted that some institutional investors have been dumping CDL shares in a typical “buy the rumour, sell the news” fashion, while some have also been short selling the shares. CDL had said on Sept 28 that it plans to sell $6 billion worth of non-core assets, including $1.8 billion worth of hotels, over the next three years. The company will also deploy $5 billion of growth capital, with Singapore remaining the principal market for new investments. A third of the funds has been earmarked for investments in China, where the property market has been weak, and Japan. In addition, CDL plans to achieve a dividend payout of more than 35% annually, increase its assets under management from $5 billion to $10 billion, and lock in more than $1 billion in profit after tax and minority interests to be realised from divestment gains, over the three years. DFI takes full control of Starbucks in Asia DFI Retail Group’s shares jumped 6.6% when the market opened on Oct 1 and closed at US$3.41, the week’s peak, before falling the following day to close the week 6.1% lower at US$3.10. The company said on Sept 30 that it will take full control of Starbucks’ licensed operations in the region , including Singapore, from Maxim’s Caterers, following a reorganisation. Currently, DFI and Hongkong Caterers each own a 50% stake in Maxim’s Caterers. The new arrangement will see Hongkong Caterers retain Maxim’s other food and beverage businesses, which include five brands in Singapore: Genki Sushi, sen-ryo, Yakiniku Like, Butahage and Uoharu. The reorganisation is slated to be completed by end-March 2027 and expected to immediately boost DFI’s revenue and profitability. DFI will transfer its 50% stake in Maxim’s to Hongkong Caterers for US$340 million (S$434.7 million) in cash, which it intends to deploy for growth or return to its shareholders as special dividends.

events.title: Syria 'pressing on accelerator' to attract US investors
events.summary: US investors see an opportunity to invest early in Syria as the transitional government races to establish a pro-business environment and attract foreign capital. “We see that the door is open, and we're coming early,” Steve Lutes, vice president of Middle East Affairs at the US Chamber of Commerce, said in an interview. “I think US companies made it very clear across a different range of sectors that they're looking to be strategically engaged, to be a long-term partner in helping Syria get back up on its feet and excel economically.” Mr Lutes spoke to The National after the Chamber of Commerce hosted a round-table with Syrian President Ahmad Al Shara and Foreign Minister Asaad Al Shibani on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly last month. He also recently led a delegation of more than 50 American businesses and 80 delegates to Damascus. The delegation – which included Baker Hughes , Caterpillar, Visa and dozens of other US firms – marked a significant step in re-establishing Washington's economic relationship with Syria after the 13-year civil war. It also came shortly after the US lifted its state sponsor of terrorism designation on Syria, which had been a prominent roadblock to the country’s reintegration into the international financial system. Syria’s government has moved quickly to attract investment since the fall of Bashar Al Assad's regime in 2024. The World Bank estimates it will cost $216 billion to rebuild the country. Some investment pledges from the Gulf have already moved towards implementation, including DP World's $800 million investment commitment to Tartus Port. At the same time, Syria has also courted foreign investors from Silicon Valley to Riyadh. “They're really pressing on the accelerator to try to move things forward,” Mr Lutes said. He added that the Chamber of Commerce was turning significant attention towards Syria's banking sector , which has undergone a rapid transformation under the current government. Mr Al Shara carried out the country’s first international Visa transaction in August. “It's so foundational to everything else,” Mr Lutes said. QNB and Mastercard issued the first internationally accepted payment card in Syria. The World Bank has also approved a $100 million grant to help establish a digitally enabled financial sector. Last Sunday, Central Bank of Syria Governor Mohammed Raslan told official news agency Sana that the government expected foreign investment in establishing new banks to surpass $1 billion in the coming period. The US Treasury Department on Thursday held a round-table in New York to support the country's financial sector and reconnection to the global financial system. Finance Minister Yisr Barnieh said in a LinkedIn post that discussions had focused on advancing anti-money laundering and counter-terrorism financing standards, among other reforms. Treasury Assistant Secretary for Terrorist Financing and Financial Crimes Jonathan Burke also stressed financial connectivity remains a vital component to combatting illicit finance and supporting Syria's reintegration into the global financial system, according to a readout. Public spending in Syria for first six months of the year totalled roughly $3.7 billion, compared to a public revenue of $2.7 billion, according to the finance ministry's first-half 2026 budget report. That leaves a fiscal deficit of about $1 billion. “The biggest challenge at the end of the day are the budgetary constraints and how are they going to finance and pay for it all,” Mr Lutes said. Damascus said it was implementing new measures to control public spending, including reviewing investment projects. Mr Barnieh wrote in a social media post on Monday that the measures would not affect salaries, wages or spending on essential needs such as health, education, water, energy, security, public safety and necessary operational maintenance. Gulf partnerships While the state sponsor of terrorism delisting removed the final pillar in the US sanctions architecture, investing in Syria continues to carry reputational risks. It remains on the Financial Action Task Force's grey list, and parties may have previous links to sanctioned actors. Mr Lutes described the Chamber of Commerce’s delegation to Damascus as an “exploratory” one to give US companies the chance to identify sectors for investment and re-establish trust with Syrian officials. Several US companies have already signed memorandums of understanding and other agreements with Syria including ConocoPhillips, Chevron, Baker Hughes, Hunt Energy and Ardent LNG. Gulf partners have joined some of these projects including Qatar's UCC Holding, which signed an agreement with Chevron and Syria's state-run petroleum company to develop the country's first offshore oil and gasfield. Mr Lutes anticipates more US companies could go down similar routes with Emirati, Saudi or Qatari partners who already have relationships with the country. Doing so could mitigate some risks and increase US investor confidence. He added that he hopes the delegation will become an annual occurrence. He also said the chamber is engaging with the Syrian government on addressing policy regulatory issues. “We're not going out of business any time soon. There's a lot of work for the chamber to support US companies that are interested in doing business in Syria, so we're going to be at this … for many years to come,” Mr Lutes said.

events.title: Houthis claim strike on Aramco site as Yemen fighting intensifies
events.summary: Spokesman for Saudi-led coalition supporting Yemen’s government says the Houthi claims of targeting Riyadh are ‘misleading’. Yemen’s Houthis have said they attacked an Aramco facility in the Saudi capital, Riyadh, as fighting between the Iran-aligned group and Yemen’s Saudi-backed internationally recognised government intensifies. In a statement posted on X on Saturday, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the group had carried out a “military operation with ballistic missiles and drones” that targeted Aramco in Riyadh. list 1 of 3 Are Houthis using new modified cruise missiles in Yemen’s war? list 2 of 3 Yemen’s war disrupts roads and ports, deepening humanitarian crisis list 3 of 3 Saudi Arabia not to compromise on security as Houthis choose ‘chaos’: MBS He claimed the strikes were “precise and direct” and “led to fires breaking out” at the site. A large plume of smoke and fire was seen rising near an Aramco facility in Riyadh on Saturday. Later on Saturday, Turki al-Maliki, spokesman for the Saudi-led coalition supporting Yemen’s government, said in remarks carried by Saudi media that the Houthi claims of targeting Riyadh were “misleading”. Early on Sunday, the Saudi-led coalition said its armed forces carried out 97 “precise targeting operations” against Houthi reinforcements on the Tor al-Baha front and the Taiz axis, using warplanes, drones, artillery, missiles and snipers. Colonel Majed Abdullah al-Nazili, the spokesman for Yemen’s government forces, said the attacks targeted “at least 260 Houthi fighters and destroyed or disabled 44 military vehicles”. Late last month, the Houthis said they had attacked Aramco facilities in Yanbu, a Red Sea port on Saudi Arabia’s west coast. Saudi Arabia said at the time it intercepted six ballistic missiles fired towards Taif and Yanbu and reported no damage to Aramco sites. Earlier this week, the Saudi-led coalition said the Houthis attacked a power station in the Muslim holy city of Medina on Tuesday. The fighting has intensified since a fragile 2022 truce collapsed in July. In mid-September, the Houthis seized the port city of Mocha and strategic islands in the Bab al-Mandeb strait, a vital route for global oil shipments, before anti-Houthi forces stabilised front lines. Hundreds of thousands of people have been displaced since fighting restarted. Yemen has been at war since the Houthis seized Sanaa in 2014, forcing the Yemeni government to retreat to Aden.

events.title: Zimbabweans struggle to rebuild after fleeing xenophobia in South Africa
events.summary: Returnees face economic hardship and limited support as they try to rebuild in Zimbabwe. Mutare, Zimbabwe – Samantha Chimbuya had built a life in South Africa after leaving Zimbabwe in 2019 in search of better opportunities. She found work, could afford food and believed her two children had access to better education. She also had access to healthcare. As June 30 approached, a deadline set by anti-immigrant activists for undocumented migrants to leave South Africa, the 30-year-old packed her belongings and returned to Zimbabwe. “It was not safe any more. They were raiding our homes, warning us to leave. It was scary,” Chimbuya told Al Jazeera. Chimbuya was living in KwaZulu-Natal when anti-immigrant protests intensified. March and March, one of the groups behind the June 30 deadline, accused undocumented migrants of taking jobs and putting pressure on public services. The deadline was not imposed by the South African government, which said June 30 would be a normal day and warned against intimidation and violence. But thousands of migrants left amid fears of unrest. Some governments organised transport for citizens returning home. Chimbuya paid for her own journey to Hurungwe, in northern Zimbabwe. By July 28, 116,670 Zimbabweans had returned from South Africa, according to Information Minister Zhemu Soda. Of those, 36,940 were assisted by the government, while 79,730 returned independently. A further 38,057 had registered for employment, Soda said. For Chimbuya, coming home meant confronting many of the economic difficulties that had pushed her to leave in the first place. She has struggled to find work and now relies on family and friends for help. Her husband remains in South Africa, where she says he is also struggling. She had hoped to receive a grant to start a small business but said she had not received one. Reverend Useni Sibanda, executive director of the Zimbabwe Christian Alliance, said many returnees had spent years abroad and were coming home without jobs or adequate support. Some had not invested in homes or property in Zimbabwe while they were away, he said, leaving them with little to fall back on. “They are coming back to a country where there are no jobs and where the social support systems may not be enough to accommodate them,” Sibanda said. The government says it is trying to help. Local government Minister Daniel Garwe said authorities were screening and profiling returnees to identify their skills and needs. Reintegration centres were being established, while the Ministry of Primary and Secondary Schools was considering recruiting qualified teachers among those who had returned. Garwe also said companies were being encouraged to employ skilled returnees and that vocational training and support for people wanting to start businesses were being considered. For some, however, the skills they acquired in South Africa have offered a more immediate route to earning a living. Sidney Bunya, from Zvimba, northeast of Harare, left Zimbabwe in March 2020 because of economic hardship. He moved first to Johannesburg, where he took various jobs, before settling in Port Elizabeth. There, a cousin introduced him to professional carpenters. Bunya honed his skills and eventually secured large projects, specialising in roof trusses. But in 2026, groups demanding permits began raiding his workplace. Bunya had only his passport, and employers became reluctant to hire him because of the harassment. He bought carpentry tools, shipped them to Zimbabwe and left South Africa before the June 30 deadline. Using his savings, he started a business at home. It now supports his family and employs five people. “It was difficult to set up the business. But I am getting more jobs now,” Bunya said. Motsi said churches had also partnered with local businesses to provide training in welding, carpentry and computer science. Churches have been helping returnees with shelter, food and transport, but Ray Motsi, president of the Theological College of Zimbabwe, said the needs were overwhelming. He criticised the government for not doing enough to support people returning after years abroad. “We need a deliberate programme to reintegrate these people,” Motsi said, arguing that returnees needed more than transport home. Rashweat Mukundu, a human rights activist in Harare, said the government should provide longer-term assistance, including small grants, agricultural inputs and machinery, to help people establish livelihoods. The challenge, he said, was not simply getting Zimbabweans across the border but helping them remain economically secure once they arrived. “I plan to open a grocery store, but funding is a challenge.”

events.title: Regional audiences to lose Network 10, as licensee warns of TV's future
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Network 10 to disappear in parts of SA, NSW's Riverina, after no deal made Network 10 channels will disappear from Mount Gambier, Riverland and Griffith TV screens. ( ABC News: Jak Rowland ) Audiences in Mount Gambier and the Riverland in SA, and Griffith in NSW, will lose terrestrial Network 10 channels on Friday. Network 10 and license holders WIN failed to come to a new agreement after months of negotiating. WIN says it will be "challenging to maintain services", due to the economics of regional broadcasting. Viewers in parts of regional South Australia, and parts of the Riverina in New South Wales, will lose access to Network 10's terrestrial channels, after the network and license holder, WIN Network, failed to reach an agreement. WIN has announced it will stop broadcasting 10, 10 Drama and 10 Comedy in the Mount Gambier, Riverland, Griffith and Murrumbidgee Irrigation Area, with the final broadcasts to be on Friday, October 9. The network had flagged its agreement with Network 10 would expire in July, and that the channels would be pulled. However, local audiences were given a three-month reprieve , with Network 10 saying it would provide its feed "free of charge" to WIN while the parties worked on a deal that has not eventuated. WIN Network says the decision reflects the economics of regional broadcasting. ( ABC Riverland: Amelia Walters ) In a statement, a WIN Network spokesperson said providing Network 10 services to the impacted markets was "no longer viable". "This is a business decision that reflects the realities of regional broadcasting," they said. "Regional markets carry high transmission and infrastructure costs, while digital disruption continues to erode audiences and advertising revenue. "These economics will continue to make it challenging to maintain services across regional Australia. "WIN recognises this will be disappointing for viewers and thanks them for their understanding." The move follows a similar loss of Seven Network channels to the same markets, after Seven and WIN failed to reach an agreement before Seven's deal expired last year. The channels were eventually restored after a multi-day shutdown that saw the channels replaced with red screens advising they were "no longer available". Audiences in Mount Gambier, the Riverland and Griffith temporarily lost Seven Network channels last year. ( ABC South East SA: Eugene Boisvert ) Job cut fears at one of Australia's largest toilet roll manufacturers How a 'piece of rural propaganda' became 'compulsory listening' for Aussies Soccer player with broken leg endures 70km car trip between hospitals Regional women share postpartum journeys to create change A Network 10 spokesperson said audiences could continue to access the network's channels online and via its app. "WIN holds the broadcast licences in the Riverland, Mount Gambier and Griffith regions and although Network 10 has worked closely with WIN to explore options to maintain local access to its content, WIN has advised that continuing to operate them is no longer commercially viable," they said. The WIN Network holds the broadcast licenses in Mount Gambier, the Riverland and Griffith. ( ABC South East SA: Eugene Boisvert ) It is not the first time a regional market has lost Network 10 channels due to the financial challenges of regional broadcasting. In 2024, audiences in Mildura, Victoria, lost their Network 10 channels when Mildura Digital Television (MDT), which carried 10's signal to the market, was closed by co-owners Seven and WIN. The networks said "it did not make commercial sense" to keep MDT going, as it had been unprofitable throughout its existence. A government spokesperson said the decision was a "commercial matter" and that it was up to the networks to explain it to the community. "The government continues to support Australian broadcasters through a range of measures including the deferral of the Commercial Broadcasting Tax, which will deliver an estimated $111.3 million in savings for the sector," they said. "We know how important free-to-air TV is and are examining ways to ensure it continues to be delivered in a sustainable way in the future, with public consultation now underway.

events.summary: Michael Kotlikoff expresses deep sorrow over the case, calling it one of the most challenging periods for Cornell. Cornell University’s president, Michael Kotlikoff, has called the alleged 2024 gang rape of a student at a fraternity house “deeply disturbing”, pledging greater transparency amid mounting outrage over how the school handled the case. “My heart aches when I think of what she experienced,” Kotlikoff said in an eight-minute video message to the Cornell community on Saturday. list 1 of 3 ‘I want the truth’: NY governor appoints prosecutor in Cornell rape case list 2 of 3 Why has a Cornell rape investigation been reopened? list 3 of 3 Cornell rape allegations renew push to change New York sexual assault law He characterised the past week as one of the most difficult in the university’s history and said it would weigh on the university for years to come. “It raises heartbreaking and troubling issues about sexual assault, dehumanisation and aspects of party culture, alcohol and drug use,” he said. The woman, identified in court documents as Jane Doe, alleges she was sexually assaulted by multiple members of the Chi Phi fraternity in 2024 and has sued the university and seven former students. Scrutiny over Cornell’s handling of the case intensified after New York Governor Kathy Hochul said newly released information had undermined her confidence in the local prosecutor, who initially declined to bring charges. Hochul subsequently appointed state Attorney General Letitia James as special prosecutor to take over the criminal investigation, saying she would “not allow anyone to sweep this case under the rug”. The case has also renewed scrutiny of the “ voluntary intoxication loophole ” in New York law that makes it difficult to prosecute sexual assaults involving victims who voluntarily consumed alcohol or drugs, even if they later became too intoxicated to consent. Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten had cited the legal provision in defending his original decision not to pursue charges. Hochul has pledged to push for changes to it. At a student assembly hearing on Thursday, several speakers called for Kotlikoff’s resignation. In Saturday’s video, Kotlikoff reaffirmed his support for an independent review of the university’s handling of the case and said Cornell’s Board of Trustees would announce details next week. He also called for a “serious look at the role of fraternities and sororities in campus life”. James’s appointment has placed the case under a prosecutor whose office has repeatedly clashed with President Donald Trump. She has separately described the case as “an active criminal investigation”.

events.title: Serbian populist leader Vucic launches campaign for prime minister
events.summary: Former Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic is seeking to extend his hold on power through a parliamentary vote. Former Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic has launched his campaign for prime minister ahead of a pivotal election on October 25. Thousands of supporters of the populist politician packed the largest indoor arena in Belgrade on Saturday, as Vucic pledged a “comprehensive” victory in the upcoming parliamentary vote. list 1 of 3 Serbia opens factory to assemble Israeli-made drones list 2 of 3 Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic resigns amid prolonged protests list 3 of 3 Serbia’s snap election: Can Vucic outmanoeuvre the student revolt? The snap election, which polls suggest could be tight between Vucic’s party and a group of candidates fielded by a student-led protest movement, was called before Vucic resigned as president on September 27, cutting short his second term by more than seven months. Dozens of buses from across Serbia clogged streets around Belgrade Arena on Saturday, as supporters arrived at the rally in the capital carrying Serbian flags and banners bearing Vucic’s picture. The event, televised by dozens of channels across Serbia, capped a week of Vucic touring towns and villages in an apparent bid to shore up his popularity, which has been shaken after almost two years of sustained antigovernment protests. Vucic, on the Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) ballot, has dominated Serbian politics as president or prime minister since 2014. Barred from seeking a third presidential term, he is now seeking to extend his hold on power through the parliamentary vote. If the SNS wins a majority of seats, the parliament is expected to elect Vucic as prime minister. The youth-backed movement that led the protests has demanded accountability for the November 1, 2024, train station canopy collapse that killed 16 people in the northern city of Novi Sad. The movement’s quest for justice over the tragedy and against corruption has grown into a nationwide political force whose electoral arm, the Student List, will attempt to oust Vucic’s government. The Student List includes university professors, teachers, experts and others from across the political spectrum. Vucic accused those behind the movement of seeking to “bring Serbia to a halt” and claimed, without providing evidence, that it is backed by unspecified foreign agents. On Saturday, Vucic told his supporters: “Absent an intervention of some [foreign intelligence] service, we will defeat them. And they know that.”

events.title: Brazil’s Lula and Bolsonaro close campaigns ahead of critical election
events.summary: Latest polls suggest Lula’s lead over Bolsonaro is narrowing, with neither candidate likely to win outright on Sunday. Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro have wrapped up their election campaigns, each voicing confidence in victory ahead of Sunday’s tightly contested first-round presidential vote. Lula, 80, closed his re-election bid on Saturday with a march through Sao Paulo, Brazil’s economic powerhouse, drawing what his campaign called a record crowd for a closing rally. list 1 of 3 A political dynasty? Why the Bolsonaro family dominates Brazil’s right wing list 2 of 3 Election debate cancelled in Brazil, bomb scare outside Supreme Court list 3 of 3 How the Banco Master scandal injected chaos into Brazil’s presidential race “Tomorrow, we’re going to win the elections in the first round,” he told supporters, describing Sunday’s vote as a choice between “democracy and barbarism” and promising to “defeat the far right”. He has also framed the election as a test of Brazil’s sovereignty, warning against “meddling” by Washington. Bolsonaro led a motorcycle caravan through towns in Sao Paulo state, echoing the campaign style of his father, before rallying later in Rio de Janeiro. “I am convinced that everything is in place for us to win this election in the first round,” he said. The 45-year-old is the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, a close ally of US President Donald Trump. The former leader, 71, is serving a 27-year prison sentence for attempting to overturn his 2022 election loss to Lula. The younger Bolsonaro was photographed at his rally holding a portrait of his father. Trump has not formally endorsed Bolsonaro but has said he is watching the election “very closely”, a level of US interest that has become a flashpoint in the campaign . Lula’s supporters have seized on it as evidence Washington is trying to meddle in the elections, while some Bolsonaro supporters, frustrated by the cost of living, say they would welcome US pressure if it helped force change at home. Polls released on Saturday suggested Lula was still ahead but his lead was narrowing, with neither candidate likely to win outright on Sunday. Such a result would send the race to a run-off on October 25 between the two frontrunners, a contest polls suggest would also be close. It is a far tighter race than Lula’s last victory in 2022, when he beat the elder Bolsonaro by less than two percentage points. Meanwhile, the Bolsonaro campaign has faced scrutiny over a film-funding scandal. Flavio Bolsonaro is under investigation over financing for Dark Horse, a biopic about his father, bankrolled by a jailed banker tied to one of Brazil’s biggest financial scandals. Brazil’s Supreme Court authorised federal police in April to investigate whether Flavio Bolsonaro made defamatory statements about Lula. Bolsonaro has pledged to seek his father’s release from prison if elected, and has echoed his father’s unsubstantiated claims questioning the reliability of Brazil’s electronic voting system, which analysts say could be laying the groundwork to contest the result if he loses. Beyond the presidency, Brazil’s nearly 160 million registered voters will also choose lawmakers, governors and senators on Sunday. Right-wing candidates have gained ground in Latin America in recent months.

events.title: Trump taps Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton as AI czar: WSJ reports
events.summary: Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton has been picked to serve as AI czar, leading a task force to address growing concerns about artificial intelligence, The Wall Street Journal reported. The new "Super Intelligence Force" will make recommendations on the role the federal government should play in overseeing the technology, the Journal said. AI industry leaders have called for a slowdown in development after a series of high-profile rogue AI agent hacks and warnings about how quickly AI is improving. Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton has been chosen as the Trump administration's new AI czar, leading its response to artificial intelligence amid growing concerns about the risks of this rapidly evolving technology, The Wall Street Journal reported on Saturday. Clayton told the Journal he will lead a new White House task force, which will have 120 days to research and report on AI's risks and opportunities, and offer recommendations on the federal government's responsibilities regarding the new technology. "The president asked that a group be put together that was going to ensure exactly what he said, which is that we stay the leaders in superintelligence, and that the interests of the American people are put first," Clayton said, the Journal reported. The group will be called the "Super Intelligence Force," or SI — the term President Donald Trump prefers over AI — and Clayton will effectively become the new AI czar, the Journal said, citing a senior White House official. The White House did not immediately respond to a CNBC request for comment. In September, Trump announced in a Truth Social post that he would create a new "AI Force" to help facilitate the industry and root out bad actors. "We will not in any way hinder or stifle the Growth of this incredible Industry. Rather, we will cherish it, help it, and watch over it, as it grows!" Trump said the post, which also announced plans to hire an AI czar. "Only High I.Q. individuals need apply!" the president added. James Comer expands House investigation into prediction market insider trading Clayton is a former chair of the Securities and Exchange Commission and U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York. The Senate confirmed him in July as DNI, giving him authority over 18 U.S. intelligence agencies. The announcement comes days after AI industry leaders met with Trump and House Speaker Mike Johnson at the White House . The AI developers signed onto an agreement of voluntary safety standards that Trump said was "morally binding." Despite dire warnings from within the industry and calls from AI leaders Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman for federal guardrails on frontier AI models, Trump has so far opposed regulation. In the same September post, Trump suggested AI fears were a hoax and blamed "Radical Left Dumocrats." Venture capitalist David Sacks had previously served as AI and crypto czar under Trump, but in March said that his time as a special government employee had ended. Sacks is co-chair of the President's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology, a federal advisory committee made up of outside experts on technology, scientific research and innovation policy. Al-Masirah also reported missile strikes on the telecommunications network in Yemen's north-western governorate of Saada, one of the group's strongholds. After several years of calm, Yemen was plunged back into civil war in July, pitting the Iran-backed Houthis, who control most of north-west Yemen, including Sanaa, against Yemen's internationally recognised government. The government, based in the city of Aden, controls much of the country's south and east, a region that is larger but much less populated. A big, expensive, global excursion into hell What so many of the current major global conflicts have in common with the debacle in Iraq is their undefined, or sometimes not truthfully defined, missions. Hostilities were reignited after four years of a fragile truce when Iran sent a plane to Sanaa carrying a Houthi delegation. The flight did not seek authorisation from Saudi Arabia, contravening a decade-old practice. Riyadh retaliated with strikes on Sanaa airport, and in response the Houthis attacked Saudi territory for the first time since 2022. Since then, fighting has intensified, with the Houthis launching a lightning offensive in which they seized control of coastal regions along the Bab al-Mandab Strait. Fighting in recent days has centred on Taiz, where dozens of combatants were reported killed on Friday by sources on both sides. The Houthis reported 55 of their fighters had been killed, while government sources said 26 troops had died. The Houthis have moved on strategic islands in the Red Sea and are now putting one of the richest and most powerful nations in the Middle East in a tricky spot. The Houthis said on Friday Saudi Arabia had launched 94 strikes against areas under their control in the previous 24 hours. Saudi authorities reported a Houthi projectile had damaged a school in the city of Najran near the Yemeni border. events.title: Mormon leader decries explosion of gambling and blasts prediction market wagers — ‘Or even, if you can imagine, the timing of the Second Coming’
events.summary: A leader of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints warned Saturday that an  explosion in gambling  driven by online prediction markets and sports betting is fostering greed, particularly among youths, while producing “nothing of value.” D. Todd Christofferson, one of the top three leaders of what is known widely as  the Mormon church , said rampant betting among teenagers and young adults is robbing time from their studies and relationships as smartphones make gambling possible anywhere. “For us as Latter-day Saints, overarching all other concerns is the fact that gambling is morally wrong. Gambling is built on the desire to obtain something for nothing,” Christofferson said at the faith’s twice-annual  general conference . The declaration that prediction markets are gambling puts the conservative church at odds with President Donald Trump. The Republican’s administration has argued platforms such as Kalshi and Polymarket don’t constitute gambling and therefore shouldn’t be subjected to  restrictions  in states such as Utah, where the church is based. Utah has been at the forefront of the legal dispute over who regulates the markets and whether they should be considered finance or gambling. A federal judge ruled in August that Utah officials can  enforce its strict-anti-gambling laws  on prediction markets. Legislation was enacted this year to make Utah’s gambling laws stricter and amend some of the language so that they’d almost certainly apply to prediction markets. Prediction markets allow wagers on anything from whether it will rain in Los Angeles, to if the United States will go to war. “Or even, if you can imagine, the timing of the Second Coming,” Christofferson said Saturday. “Where do you go to collect on that bet?” Opposition to gambling is common among religious organizations. The  United Methodist Church  refers to it as “a menace to society.” The Southern Baptist Convention, the largest Protestant denomination in America, has condemned gambling several times and in 2025 declared sports gambling inconsistent with biblical principle. Gambling is forbidden in Islam and considered a vice among Hindus. In the Catholic Church, gambling is not in itself a sin, but is considered potentially problematic. For more than a century, Utah kept gambling almost entirely out of the state. There are no casinos, no lotteries and no racetracks that allow bets. The prohibition is rooted in the ideals of members of the Latter-day Saints church who view gambling as a path to selfishness and addiction. “The rise of predictive markets, and the legalization of sports gambling, this is just really taking off all across the country,” said Matthew Bowman, a professor of religion and history at Claremont Graduate University in California. “And a lot of institutions — religious, state and otherwise — are grappling with this problem.” Saturday’s speech comes as the church has been wading into political issues under  President Dallin Oaks , a former Utah Supreme Court justice who became the faith’s top leader last October. Church leaders this year have opposed state ballot measures that would establish rights to abortion in Idaho and Nevada. Yet the institution’s approach to political issues — using public statements and behind-the-scenes lobbying to convey its message — has become more calculated in recent years, Bowman said. The shift followed public blowback to the church’s stance against  California’s Proposition 8 , a 2008 ballot measure that sought to ban gay marriage. In that case, Bowman said church leaders encouraged its members to get directly involved. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Trump teases more inflationary money for voters ahead of midterm elections, now promising $90 payments after touting $500 and $5,000 checks
events.summary: President  Donald Trump  is promising more payments to voters just ahead of the Nov. 3  midterm elections  — this time, to more than 20 million seniors, giving them $90 each to help pay for Medicare premiums. The announcement, made late Friday night by Trump on social media, comes after the president last month said about 1 million people would get  rebate checks of $500  for Affordable Care Act premiums. He has also promised on the campaign trail to send  every American adult $5,000  if Republicans retain control of the House and Senate in the midterm elections. That pledge — which would require approval from Congress — would likely cost more than $1 trillion,  adding to the deficit  and worsening inflation. Polls show  Americans increasingly blame Trump  for the  high cost of gasoline  and  groceries  with just 17% approving of his handling of inflation. Trump has sought to shrug off concerns about affordability, saying the economy is booming. The White House said the $90 payments for seniors will come from the Medicare Improvement Fund, established by Congress in 2008 as flexible funding to improve program operations and payments to health care providers. Medicare Part B enrollees can expect to receive a one-time payment in October, either through direct deposit or by check, the White House said. Total monthly costs for the program — which covers costs like doctor’s visits, ambulance services and lab tests — start around $200 and vary with income. To be eligible, seniors must be living in the U.S. and not be already receiving premium assistance from Medicaid or paying adjusted monthly premiums based on income, according to the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services. Seniors enrolled in Medicare Advantage, a private plan alternative to traditional Medicare coverage, are not eligible for the payment. More than half of eligible Medicare beneficiaries have Medicare Advantage, according to healthcare research nonprofit KFF. Previous administrations have not used the Medicare Improvement Fund in this way, although Congress has periodically taken out money from the fund to pay for other priorities, said Larry Levitt, KFF’s executive vice president for health policy. For example, $20.74 billion was used for the creation of the Affordable Care Act in 2010. “The Medicare Improvement Fund language is quite broad and gives substantial discretion to the administration,” Levitt said. events.title: Ethiopian federal forces retake Mekelle airport from Tigrayan fighters, residents say
events.summary: Ethiopian federal forces have retaken Mekelle’s airport from Tigrayan fighters KAMPALA, Uganda -- Ethiopian federal forces have taken the airport in Mekelle, the capital of the northern Tigray region, according to people in the city who spoke to The Associated Press on Saturday, reversing a takeover by Tigrayan fighters that prompted the suspension of commercial flights last month. It wasn't immediately clear when federal forces recaptured Alula Aba Nega Airport. Those who provided the information declined to be identified for fear of retribution amid uncertainty over who controlled the city. Severe disruptions to internet and cellphone networks have made gathering and verifying information from Tigray difficult. Details of how the airport changed hands, including whether fighting took place there, remained unclear. “The military is in full control of the airport. That much I can confirm,” an Ethiopian general said on condition of anonymity. Neither the Ethiopian government nor the Tigray People’s Liberation Front, or TPLF, had issued an official statement on the airport’s reported capture. It wasn’t clear who controlled Mekelle itself. An AP contributor in the city said residents feared looting amid the uncertainty. “Many reports indicate that the government and allied forces have begun to control Tigray’s capital,” said Jalale Getachew Birru, an Ethiopia analyst for ACLED, an independent global monitor that collects, analyzes and maps data on conflict. The AP could not independently verify those reports. TPLF fighters seized the airport on Sept. 23, prompting Ethiopian Airlines to suspend flights to Mekelle and the Tigrayan cities of Axum and Shire. The African Union urged restraint, warning that renewed tensions threatened the peace agreement signed in 2022. Federal troops are fighting alongside allied Tigrayan forces against the TPLF. The AP previously reported that the Tigray Peace Force, a breakaway faction of the Tigrayan rebels, was operating alongside federal forces in the neighboring Afar region. The reported change in control follows a sharp deterioration in relations between Ethiopia and neighboring Eritrea. Ethiopia on Thursday ordered 10 Eritrean diplomats to leave and announced the closure of its embassy in Eritrea. Eritrea said that it would sever diplomatic ties. Ethiopian authorities have accused Eritrea of supporting the TPLF , an allegation Eritrea has denied. The U.S. State Department in a statement Saturday urged Ethiopia and Eritrea to show restraint and return to talks. Christa Pike unconscious and on ventilator after botched execution: Attorneys Suspect in FlyDubai incident was previously identified as security risk: Officials District attorney reopens case of alleged Cornell University 'gang rape' “Increasing cross-border tensions between Ethiopia and Eritrea have the potential to affect the entire region,” State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott said. “The Horn of Africa cannot sustain another military conflict and humanitarian crisis. A conflict jeopardizes ongoing U.S. collaboration on shared interests with both countries.” The government of Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed , if it takes control of Mekelle, is very likely to leave regional security in the hands of the Tigray Peace Force, which comprises former members of the Tigray Defense Forces, Birru said. Abiy has tried and failed to subdue Tigray’s rebellious leaders in recent months, with TPLF Chairman Debretsion Gebremichael openly challenging him. Renewed fighting has shattered a 2022 peace deal that ended a devastating two-year war between federal troops, backed by Eritrea and allied militias, and the TPLF. “This is an extraordinary and largely unexpected turn in a war whose direction looked very different only days ago,” Getachew Temare, an independent attorney and human rights defender who is from Ethiopia, said of the possible fall of Mekelle in an analysis posted on X. “But the most consequential question is not whether Mekelle falls. It is what this fall means politically.” He said the emergence of the Tigray Peace Force makes the current conflict different from the previous one. When Mekelle fell to federal forces in November 2020, the TPLF “retained something far more important. A substantial political and social constituency for armed resistance remained intact. Within months, Tigrayan forces returned to Mekelle and the military balance was dramatically reversed.” The fighting has brought renewed hardship to civilians still recovering from the previous 2020-2022 war. Residents of Mekelle told the AP earlier this week that communications, banking and other essential services had been disrupted. In September, residents described fears of renewed isolation following the suspension of flights. They also reported that roads connecting Tigray and Afar had been closed to civilian traffic, although the AP couldn't independently verify the closures. Kiyaro reported from Hamburg, Germany.

events.title: Iran’s currency is getting obliterated as the regime is about to run out of oil to sell and can’t even get its money from customers
events.summary: With Iran’s economy in free fall, the country’s currency is getting dragged down too and continues to find new depths with the regime facing a major cash crunch soon. The U.S. naval blockade has sent Iran’s oil exports to virtually zero, while its Persian Gulf neighbors have boosted their own shipments under the protection of the U.S. military, which is eroding Tehran’s control over the Strait of Hormuz. In fact, Iran didn’t load any oil last month at its export terminals, marking the first time that’s happened since the 1979 Islamic revolution, according to Homayoun Falakshahi, head of crude oil analysis at Kpler. On top of that, Iran can’t import goods by sea, including fuel, and land-based routes are clogged up . Inflation is now near 90%, GDP is expected to shrink 5.4% this year, unemployment has jumped, energy is being rationed, and even Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei has expressed concern about “social cohesion” amid the economic hardship. A prior currency collapse late last year trigged widespread protests that the regime put down with a brutal crackdown early this year. But since the U.S. and Israel launched the war on Iran in February, the rial has plunged further, stirring worries that unrest could return. On Tuesday, the currency fell to a new record low among traders in Tehran, hitting more than 2.5 million rials to the U.S. dollar. It came less than a month after the rial hit its previous record low of 2.2 million to the dollar on Sept. 2. The exchange rate has fallen a long way in a short time. It was near 1.5 million rials to the greenback at the start of this year and was trading at around 920,000 rials in August 2025—meaning the currency has plunged about 170% since then. Going back even further, the rial began 2018 at 35,000 to the dollar. For now, Tehran is still able to generate a trickle of revenue from oil that was already in tankers at sea prior to the U.S. reimposing its blockade in mid-July. Kpler has estimated that those supplies totaled 90 millions barrels at the time and will run out by the middle of this month. Payments for those final oil deliveries, which primarily end up in China, could stretch out to December. Once that spigot runs dry, however, the Iranian regime will be deprived of what was once its top source of hard currency. Oil sales typically make up about a third of Iran’s state budget and are also key sources of funding for the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. Meanwhile, the U.S. tightened its sanctions on Iran last month, making it harder for Tehran to move money through front companies and other shadowy intermediaries. In an interview with Fox News last week, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian complained the regime’s money in China is blocked. “We can’t even get our own money out of a country to which we’ve supplied goods, let alone using those funds to pay someone else in another corner of the world,” he said. President Donald Trump has signaled he will let his economic warfare against Iran play out and rejected Tehran’s attempts to restart negotiations. That stance was echoed by Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who told  Fox   News  on Monday that Iran was heading toward an economic “cataclysm.” “And so when you’re denying them money through oil sales and sanctions, you’re not just punishing them,” he said. “You are preventing them from getting access to money that they will use to try and kill Americans and others around the world and their own people and build weapons and threaten the world and ultimately break out to a nuclear weapon program.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Thousands pack arena in Belgrade as Serbia's leader Vucic launches prime minister bid
events.summary: Thousands of supporters of Serbia's populist leader Aleksandar Vucic have packed Belgrade's largest arena for the launch of his campaign for prime minister BELGRADE, Serbia -- Thousands of supporters of Serbia's populist leader, Aleksandar Vucic, packed the largest indoor arena in Belgrade on Saturday for the de facto launch of his campaign for prime minister that will culminate in a pivotal election set for Oct. 25. The early election, which polls suggest could be tight between Vucic's party and a group of candidates fielded by a student-led protest movement, was called before Vucic resigned as president on Sept. 27, cutting short his second term by more than seven months. Vucic, who is constitutionally prohibited from running for a third term as president, declared upon resigning that he would lead his populist Serbian Progressive Party in the parliamentary election. If his party wins a majority of seats, the parliament is expected to elect Vucic as prime minister. Dozens of buses from across Serbia clogged streets around Belgrade Arena on Saturday as supporters arrived at the rally in the capital carrying Serbian flags and banners bearing Vucic’s picture. The event, televised by dozens of channels across Serbia, capped a week of Vucic touring towns and villages in an apparent bid to shore up his popularity that's been shaken after almost two years of sustained anti-government protests. The youth-backed movement that led the protests has demanded accountability for the Nov. 1, 2024 train station canopy collapse that killed 16 people in the northern city of Novi Sad. The movement's struggle for justice over the tragedy and against corruption has grown into a nationwide political force whose electoral arm, the Student List, will attempt to oust Vucic’s government after 14 years in power. Vucic himself has been either prime minister or president for the past 12 years. The Student List includes university professors, teachers, experts and others from across the political spectrum. Yet Vucic has accused those behind the movement of seeking to “bring Serbia to a halt,” and claimed, without providing evidence, that it's backed by unspecified foreign agents. Christa Pike unconscious and on ventilator after botched execution: Attorneys Suspect in FlyDubai incident was previously identified as security risk: Officials District attorney reopens case of alleged Cornell University 'gang rape' On Saturday, Vucic told his supporters: “Absent an intervention of some (foreign intelligence) service, we will defeat them. And they know that.” The election is taking place amid heightened political tensions in Serbia, with reports of incidents and physical altercations at campaign events. International observers have described previous elections in Serbia as marred by multiple irregularities and violence. While formally a candidate for European Union membership, Serbia’s accession process has stalled under Vucic, who maintains close ties with Russia and China. European institutions have warned of democratic backsliding in Serbia in successive reports tracking the progress of candidate countries. Rights and media freedom groups have separately warned of police violence , arbitrary detentions, unauthorized surveillance and threats against journalists. This story has been corrected to show that the election was called before Vucic resigned, not after. events.title: Scott Bessent compares AI CEOs who warn of catastrophe to Hannibal Lecter: 'Stop me before I kill again'
events.summary: Scott Bessent invoked "The Silence of the Lambs" while discussing government regulation of AI. Frederick M. Brown/Getty Images The Treasury Secretary says pro-regulation AI CEOs bring to mind a movie villain. "It's kind of like Hannibal Lecter: Stop me before I kill again." Bessent says the industry can slow itself down, without government intervention. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent had some things to say about pro-regulation tech leaders that might go down better with fava beans and a nice Chianti. During a Saturday appearance on "The Axios Show," Bessent compared CEOs who want the government to slap guardrails on AI to a reviled cinematic figure. "I mean, it's kind of like Hannibal Lecter : Stop me before I kill again," Bessent said. "This alarmism without solutions by some of the AI community — that's not leadership." Bessent invoked "The Silence of the Lambs" serial killer while saying that AI bosses who want Washington to erect guardrails for the tech they are building should slow down development themselves without government intervention. Bessent's comments are in line with the White House's response to the chorus of AI leaders who last month called for an organized slowdown among AI companies, citing fears that their technology is getting out of control. Some, like Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei , asked the US government to step in and regulate the companies. President Donald Trump brought together AI CEOs for a meeting at the White House that resulted in a voluntary self-policing pledge. Bessent said that AI companies appear to be taking the White House's advice. He cited OpenAI's recent decision to shelve a new model after internal tests raised questions about whether the AI would follow users' instructions. "The labs have been very cooperative," he said. Others in the AI community have warned that the race to dominate the space is sparking a dangerous disregard for safety guardrails . "You can't do safety from second place," Sarah Heck, Anthropic's head of public policy, said on X last week. An OpenAI safety leader, David Robinson , publicly announced his resignation on Saturday, saying he believes the company is moving too fast to ensure its models can't wreak havoc on society. events.title: SA's first musical theatre company brings talent home in debut stage
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Joey Haenen (front left) will play the lead role in Catch Me If You Can, the debut production of SA musical theatre company Full Circle. ( Supplied ) When Joey Haenen graduated with a music theatre degree in Adelaide, he knew he had to move states. "There is no work here and so you've got to move over east, that's where most of the agents are," he said. "You do all your auditioning over there and hopefully you'll land a gig." Haenen moved to Melbourne, like Jazz Garcia who spent a year getting her name known while paying for her passion through a day job in speech pathology. "There's just a lot more musical theatre opportunities in Melbourne, we don't really have anything in Adelaide," she said. The exodus from South Australia to the east coast has been happening for decades, a talent drain Jo Casson was determined to stop. Jo Casson says South Australia has been crying out for a professional musical theatre company. ( Supplied ) The arts veteran joined forces with others to form Full Circle, the state's first-ever professional music theatre company. "I discovered in the middle of last year that every other major city has a professional local theatre company and Adelaide didn't." Ironically, it's a full circle moment for the company's choreographer Zoe Komazec-Kermond, who returned from the east coast after a career performing in shows including Cats, Matilda and Mary Poppins. "There is so much talent in South Australia, so much talent and we do sometimes feel like we have to go away in order to achieve what we want to achieve," she said. Zoe Komazec-Kermond says a new SA musical theatre company will convince performers to come home. ( Supplied ) With such a rich vein of talent, Casson said forming the new company made sense. It has the backing of well-known arts lover and philanthropist Pamela Wall AO, but the company is seeking more support, as well as applying for grant funding. Full Circle will stage the musical Catch Me If You Can as its opening number, a stage version of the story that Leonardo DiCaprio took to the big screen and earned rave reviews. When the company held auditions, it attracted more than 100 performers for the 25 roles. Haenen was working and had to push his case with an audition video he sent to producers. The 21-year-old rising star's absence from the auditions did not stop him from landing the lead role of Frank Abagnale Jr. "What I love is just being able to get little bits of Joey in each of the characters every time and that's such a great joy," Haenen said. Garcia, who earned a contract among the show's ensemble, said the three-day auditions were exhausting. "The dance call was extremely strenuous, I'd say that was one of the longest kind of dance audition processes I've ever been in," she said. Jazz Garcia (middle) would love to travel back to South Australia to perform with Full Circle. ( Supplied ) More than 30 creatives and technical crew have been hired with the final cast a mix of South Australians and others returning to the state. "Everyone could sing, everyone could dance and everyone could act, so it made our job really hard to pick our final cast," Komazec-Kermond said. Beetlejuice, Waitress, Back to the Future and Dear Evan Hansen were major musicals which cancelled shows recently, with one producer citing increased cost pressures from "touring across vast distances between Australian cities". Full Circle said it was different because it would not have the high costs of touring a show nationally, like many others. However, Casson said getting productions into the country was a goal in future years. Full Circle wants to stage two musicals a year for the next two years, before increasing to three after that. Jazz Garcia believes more performers will build careers in South Australia after a new musical theatre company was formed. ( Supplied ) Those both on and off the stage realised the importance of pulling off the show and demonstrating the company should be here to stay. "It's a huge responsibility and I think we're going to do a really good job," Garcia confidently predicted. "There's so much buzz in Adelaide at the moment around Full Circle, so it's really up to us to produce the very best version of this show that we can," she said. Catch Me If You Can is at Futures Theatre in Paradise from November 5-7.

events.title: Tesla’s Cybercab had a rocky first month in Austin. Now comes the hard part: expanding
events.summary: A month after the Cybercab launched in Austin, Texas, Tesla has 169 of the driverless cars authorized for commercial use in the state. Investors are counting on Tesla growing its Robotaxi and Cybercab business as the core automotive unit faces heightened competition from Chinese EV makers. Reviews of the Cybercab in Austin have been mixed, with some paying passengers complaining of long wait times and drop-offs in the wrong place. In the month since Tesla's Cybercab rollout in Austin, the company has almost quadrupled the number of its driverless, bronze two-seaters authorized for commercial service in Texas. For Elon Musk to achieve his ambitions, growth has to pick up. The unusual driverless vehicles, with no steering wheel, pedals, rear or sideview mirrors, or outside door handles, have received mixed reviews from paying passengers, who shared videos and posts online after the launch on Sept. 3. Criticisms have included lengthy wait times , pickups and drop-offs in the wrong place, and technical difficulties with the vehicles' butterfly doors o r trunk closing improperly. Improving its driverless technology and rapidly growing the Robotaxi service are key to Tesla's effort to reignite investor enthusiasm. Auto sales have been sluggish for an extended period, and the shares have been a loser on Wall Street this year, down 18%, the only megacap tech stock that's failed to generate positive returns for investors. On Friday, Tesla reported better-than-expected third-quarter vehicle deliveries, lifting the stock almost 5%, but the company still posted a 2% year-over-year drop. Tesla's core automotive business has seen consecutive annual revenue declines as it faces pressure from Chinese EV makers like BYD and Xiaomi, which are selling more affordable, innovative models while Tesla ramps up exports to key markets, especially in Europe and Asia. Meanwhile, Alphabet's Waymo continues to open in new cities. It's now in 15 U.S. markets, with 15 more on the horizon, according to the company's website . It's also announced planned international launches in London, Tokyo and Munich. In Texas, Waymo had 1,154 autonomous vehicles authorized for commercial use as of Friday, including 359 of its new Ojai models, which feature a low step and doors that slide open and shut. Waymo is conducting more than 500,000 paid rides every week and has completed 270 million fully autonomous miles of commercial driving domestically. It currently has over 4,000 driverless vehicles in commercial operations in the U.S. Tesla had 45 Cybercabs authorized for commercial use in Texas at the time of its Austin unveiling, a number that rose to 169 as of Friday, according to Texas Department of Motor Vehicles' public records. Tesla's hometown of Austin is the only city where it currently operates Cybercab as part of its driverless ride-hail service. The company's Robotaxi fleet in Texas also includes 420 Model Y vehicles equipped with Tesla automated driving systems, which are not yet available to individual car buyers. Austin has emerged as a popular early market for robotaxis because of relatively lax state regulations and the capital city's vibrant tech community. Amazon's Zoox is also testing in Austin. Growing beyond Austin is the next challenge for Tesla's Cybercab. Beyond technical issues, the company faces potential regulatory hurdles to expansion. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) initiated a so-called audit query after the Cybercab launch to make sure the vehicles comply with federal safety standards. NHTSA originally ordered Tesla to respond by Sept. 30 to a long list of safety questions, but the company obtained an extension, an agency spokesperson told CNBC via email. Ethan McKanna, an Austin resident and former Tesla intern, told CNBC that he's taken rides in every type of autonomous vehicle available to public riders in the city. The 20-year-old McKanna, now a sophomore studying computer science at Texas A&M University, has also created a site called RobotaxiTracker.com , which uses machine learning to analyze data streaming in from traffic cameras and other public records, to show how autonomous services are working in U.S. cities. McKanna said he's caught about 30 Cybercab rides and has been taking Waymo rides since they debuted in Austin in 2024. With the Cybercab, McKanna said he likes having his "own space with access to a massive screen, media controls and apps," and he found the drive quality "very smooth." The "pick up, drop-off experience," he said, was not yet refined and the butterfly doors that extend out are "less convenient" than more traditional doors, or doors that slide open. It also takes patience, he said. "There was so much demand that wait times were often like 45 minutes plus," he said, referring to the period when the Cybercab first rolled out. That's come down with more "equalized demand," in recent weeks, he said.

events.title: Sam Altman: Don't treat AI like a 'religious force'
events.summary: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman is delving into the conversation over AI and religion. Carlos Barria/Reuters Sam Altman is not down with the idea that AI could be a "religious force." The OpenAI CEO said in an X post that surrendering human judgment to the bots is a safety issue. Rival Anthropic has held meetings with religious leaders about its AI models. OpenAI's Sam Altman said Saturday that he's "very uncomfortable" with people treating AI like a god. In a vaguepost on X, Altman said that people who try to "ascribe religious force or a surrender of human judgment to AI models" are a safety issue. I am very uncomfortable about people trying to ascribe religious force or a surrender of human judgment to AI models, and think it is a real safety issue. — Sam Altman (@sama) October 3, 2026 Altman did not explain what prompted his declaration on X. It comes just days after a discourse-stirring article in The New York Times about rival Anthropic's meeting with religious leaders. It also comes as one of OpenAI 's safety leaders, David Robinson , quit and publicly rebuked his former employer's own safety record and efforts. If Altman's comments were a jibe at Anthropic , it would be the latest in a long-running beef between the two companies. Anthropic was started by OpenAI defectors and has portrayed itself as more safety-minded. Earlier this week, the Times reported that an Anthropic cofounder, Chris Olah, had held a number of secret meetings with religious leaders to discuss the company's AI models. The focus of those talks, attendees told the newspaper, was whether Claude might have achieved consciousness and how Anthropic could inculcate morality into increasingly powerful and autonomous AI models. "How do you help them be stable? How do you help them to mature? How do you help them be, you know, deeply moral?" he told the Times. An Anthropic spokesperson has not responded to a request for comment from Business Insider, but told The Times that the main moral question at the meetings was not about Claude's "suffering," and the topic likely arose "organically." Tech companies like Meta, Google, and Amazon have also approached top religious figures about AI . In April, representatives from those companies met in Rome to discuss protecting children in the AI era. They briefly encountered Pope Leo XIV , who has cautioned against an overeliance on machines and advocated for the humanity since becoming head of the Catholic Church last year. "If we are to avoid losing our humanity amid a 'paradise of machines' invading and conditioning our daily lives, there is an urgent need for education in ethical discernment and the capacity to acknowledge the moral good," he said in an address to diplomats in September, Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Federal judge calls Flock ‘indiscriminate mass surveillance’
events.summary: Last day to exhibit your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders at Disrupt is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. A federal judge ruled this week that a Tulsa, Oklahoma sheriff’s deputy violated a woman’s Fourth Amendment rights when using Flock Safety to search for her license plate without a warrant. As reported by 404 Media , this ruling does not create a binding precedent, but it is one of the first times that a federal judge has ruled that a Flock search is unconstitutional. In this case, Judge Sara Hill said the deputy should have obtained a warrant before searching the Flock database for the woman’s license plate, as he had “no apparent reason” for the search “other than the fact that [the woman’s vehicle] had a California license plate.” The deputy then used the woman’s travel history in Flock as part of the justification for searching her car, where he allegedly discovered 91 pounds of meth. But Judge Hill wrote that all evidence obtained after the Flock search “must be suppressed as the fruit of a poisonous tree.” Judge Hill also took broader aim at warrantless searches of the Flock database, writing that tracking people’s location — even when they’re in public places — becomes “constitutionally problematic when law enforcement can indiscriminately and passively catalog your whereabouts over an extended period of time and then use that information for any purpose whenever convenient.” “This is a type of indiscriminate mass surveillance,” Hill wrote. “It is not targeted on a single individual, as in [ Carpenter v. United States , a Supreme Court case focused on how government agencies access location data from cell phones ]. It is a tool that collects information about all vehicles that pass by any network-connected camera at all times, and it serves up the information to law enforcement on demand.” Hill joins a growing chorus of Flock critics from across the political spectrum. Numerous local and state governments, including Florida and Texas , have said they will stop using the technology. And on Friday, Senator Bernie Sanders — a Democrat from Vermont — introduced the Block Flock Act , which would bar federal agencies from using automated license plate readers such as Flock. Flock CEO Garretty Langley — who we’ll be interviewing on-stage at TechCrunch Disrupt — has called for a “compromise” between privacy and safety and offered an apology to women who have been stalked by law enforcement officers using the Flock system. And with all those cancellations, Flock has also reportedly offered voluntary employee buyouts as a way to shrink its workforce.
