events.title: Zohran Mamdani says ‘you have to luck out in some big way’ to achieve the American Dream now—and many people see better odds of winning the lottery
events.summary: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said the American Dream should be a guarantee and not a vague hope, lamenting that it’s now viewed as being less attainable than winning a lottery jackpot. In an interview on Theo Von’s podcast This Past Weekend , Mamdani warned that if the American Dream is just an ideal that’s out of within reach, then people may start to give up. The democratic socialist compared it to legendary NYC Mayor Fiorello La Guardia’s observation during the rise of fascism in Europe, saying people turned away from democracy not because they were tired of liberty, but because they were tired of being hungry. “So if democracy doesn’t mean the better life that it has to, it’ll lose its worth. And the same thing with the American Dream: if it’s something you can only see when you turn on your TV or you hear about that one guy you grew up with who made it, that doesn’t mean enough,” Mamdani said. That’s why his administration has focused on making housing, child care, and groceries more affordable, he added, calling them the “basic aspects of a good, dignified life.” Smaller efforts also make a big difference, Mamdani explained, pointing to free child care for a night to give parents a chance to go out or providing free tickets to the opera. When asked later if he thinks the American Dream is still alive, he replied, “It feels like you have to luck out in some big way. In many ways, I feel like it’s why a lot of people play the lottery. For many, it feels like their only chance. People think that they have better odds playing the lottery than making it in their own life. What does that say about the country that we live in?” New York City has the added dimension of having plenty of wealth while many others grapple with wages that haven’t kept up with the soaring cost of living, Mamdani noted. That’s not due to a lack of opportunity. Instead, that opportunity is “being consolidated,” he argued. While Mamdani has sought to tap some of the city’s wealth with an annual surcharge on luxury, non-primary residential properties, it’s run into some legal setbacks . Last month, a judge threw out New York’s rollout of its pied-à-terre tax, ordering the city to cancel the notices it sent to property owners  and restart the process of deciding who owes the surcharge. Harnessing some of the city’s wealth is key to making New York more affordable, Mamdani insisted during the podcast interview. “Because right now it feels like the city is becoming a museum—something a middle-class family can afford to visit once a month, maybe on the weekends. We want people to live here, and there’s more than enough money for everyone to be able to,” he said. For his part, Mamdani has acknowledged that he is one of the lucky few. When asked on the Fourth of July if he was living the American Dream, he told CNN the “I’m living one of them.” “I think the beautiful thing about today is it’s a chance to celebrate that the promise of our nation is still true—that promise of opportunity, of freedom, of self determination,” he added. “And to be the mayor of our city today, it’s something more than i could ever ask for.” Mamdani’s comments come as the affordability crisis has threatened some of the key hallmarks of the American Dream, such as homeownership, a car or two, and kids. While U.S. households still, on average, believe it  can be achieved, their hopes are fading fast while some economists see a “ Great Postponement .” JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon has also warned the American Dream is in trouble , and has committed the New York-based banking giant to a sweeping multiyear effort to expand economic opportunity across the country. “The American Dream is alive, but it’s slipping out of reach for too many people—and for future generations,” he said in March. “This slows economic growth, hurts communities, and prevents many people from getting ahead.” More recently, Dimon has teamed up with Ford CEO Jim Farley, who said America’s skilled-trades shortfall has become too large and too varied by region and occupation. “Skilled trades are the backbone of our country and American manufacturing, and the backbone of the American Dream,” Farley said last month. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: OpenAI leader who quit says he can do more for safety from outside the company
events.summary: David Robinson resigned from OpenAI and said the company is being careless with the technology. World Economic Forum Just-department OpenAI staffer David Robinson published an essay about AI safeguards. Robinson said he intends to "strengthen the incentives" for AI to develop at a safe pace. His departure comes after OpenAI faced scrutiny over the Hugging Face hack. The OpenAI leader who just quit and issued a stark warning about safety says that, like other recent Big Tech defectors, he plans to help solve the problem from the outside. David Robinson worked at OpenAI for three and a half years and ran transparency for the safety team. In an essay published Saturday in The Atlantic , he said he oversaw the company's "preparedness framework" and the writing of a slew of safety reports. "Perhaps I should have stayed and fought for fundamental shifts in our staffing and culture, but in practice, my colleagues and I were so busy sprinting that we seldom had the chance to consider big changes, much less to actually make them," he wrote. "That's why I concluded that stronger incentives for safety — coming from outside the company — are a big part of getting this right." Robinson said he hired a PR firm, Spitfire Strategies, to help him with the public attention he'll receive following his departure. "But the decision to speak out is mine alone," he added. That might be aimed at claims from some that public resignations by workers from companies, including Anthropic and Google, are part of a coordinated effort to spread mistrust of AI and foment government regulation. Elon Musk, for instance, said that former Anthropic employee  Jacob Coxon 's resignation and subsequent public appearances seem "like a setup," which Coxon denied. In response to Robinson's essay, an OpenAI spokesperson said in a statement that the company is working to ensure AI models don't outpace the safety measures they've implemented. "As our models become more capable, we continue to strengthen our safety and security practices to address the risks we see today while building safety cases to anticipate the risks of future advances," the spokesperson said. "We're making sure our models don't become more capable than we can safely manage and secure, and we pause training or hold back models when we need to slow down." The spokesperson said OpenAI is taking steps to improve security for its AI models. "We're making significant changes to strengthen security in our research and testing environments, train models to not just complete tasks but do so responsibly, expand our work with third-party evaluators, and improve real-time monitoring so we can detect and respond to concerning behavior earlier in the training process," the spokesperson said. Robinson's departure comes two months after OpenAI agents escaped their system and hacked another AI company, Hugging Face , in July. OpenAI is not the only company struggling to balance the AI race with calls for guardrails. Last month, a small AI startup said it used Anthropic's Claude to hack into OpenAI's codebase , and The Wall Street Journal reported that Google's Gemini had hacked three companies this spring. More recently, Australia's Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said an OpenAI agent hacked a government website in June. Robinson's PR reps did not respond to an inquiry from Business Insider about his next steps. In The Atlantic, he suggested his game plan is in flux. "Now I plan to work on the outside, in the hope that I can help more people understand the risks I saw, and strengthen the incentives OpenAI and other firms have to be safer," he wrote. "Like other colleagues, I'm figuring out exactly what that means." Read the original article on Business Insider

Amazon Web Services CEO Matt Garman said the company has stopped using nondisclosure agreements (NDAs) in its dealings with government agencies as it seeks approval to build new data centers. Garman’s statement is just one sentence in a longer blog post in which he tried to push back against widespread suspicion of data centers, and to make the case that they’re actually good for communities. NDAs are a significant piece of the broader data center backlash. For example, environmental activist Erin Brockovich recently said that the number one complaint she’s heard about data centers is transparency , with these projects following a common pattern: “projects announced after permits are already secured, developers who don’t return calls, local officials who signed NDAs before their neighbors knew a project was being considered.” As a result of that backlash, New York announced a one-year moratorium on permits for large data centers , and according to Garman, there are more than 100 data center moratoriums currently being considered across the United States. “If these measures are enacted, the U.S. could be writing its own losing ticket to this race, and the consequences would last generations,” Garman claimed. “As a country, we can’t afford to find ourselves in that position.” Garman also attempted to puncture what he said are four big myths around data centers: that they consume too much water, that they increase electricity costs, that they emit an enormous amount of pollution, and that they don’t provide any benefits to their communities. Pointing to an Amazon report about its own water usage , Garman said that “direct data center water consumption” only accounts for 0.5% of all industrial water usage in the United States, “orders of magnitude less than golf courses, almond farming, and many other industries.” Nvidia recently said its new cooling system eliminates “pretty much all water usage” inside the data center , but those claims — like Amazon’s — seem to ignore the broader water usage involved in electricity generation and chip manufacturing. Scientists have also said they need to study data centers’ water and energy usage independently , since there are no federal or state requirements around how tech companies report this data. As for electricity rates, Garman said they’ve only gone up in some states with large numbers of data centers, while they’ve gone down or at least grown more slowly in others. And he argued, “In instances where energy rates are going up, it’s primarily because the grid is old and hasn’t been invested in and expanded before the demand arrived.” On the other hand, an independent watchdog said recently data centers were the main culprit behind a 76% year-over-year price increase on America’s largest electrical grid. When it comes to pollution — an issue that the NAACP is currently suing Elon Musk’s SpaceX/xAI over — Garman complained that critics focus on the maximum amount of pollution allowed under data center permits. For example, a planned Amazon data center in Texas is permitted to release 33 million tons of carbon dioxide per year, which is more than any other power plant in the United States. “The truth is data center generators almost never run,” Garman said. “They’re idle 99.9% of the time (they run roughly 10 hours per year, mostly for required maintenance testing).” As for the community benefits, this is where Garman wrote, “We no longer use nondisclosure agreements with the government agencies we work with on our projects.” Plus, he said, “Over the past three years, Amazon has contributed more than $1 billion to communities across the U.S. in which we have a meaningful data center presence.” Will this be enough to quell community suspicion? Perhaps not — Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei recently argued that the AI backlash is “fundamentally a crisis of trust, ” where people assume governments and tech companies are always “cooking up some new way to screw them over.” Similarly, writer Jasmine Sun noted that when data center opponents are presented with the tech companies’ arguments, their response is usually, “I don’t believe them.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . events.title: Can you really rely on your phone to save you in a bushfire?
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts When a bushfire comes, what happens if the phones go dead? Who warns you of disaster when your mobile fails? One community has a plan On January 8, 2026, Victorian authorities began warning a catastrophic fire rating had been declared for the following day. Conditions would be "the most dangerous experienced this summer", the Country Fire Authority (CFA) said. One brigade in central Victoria issued a clarion call on social media: "160 people died on Black Saturday in the district 12 response area" on a similarly risky day. Further west, in Castlemaine, Fiannuala Morgan was encouraging her parents to leave their property in the bone-dry, flinty hills outside of town. Fiannuala would be staying in Castlemaine, a town of about 7,000 people etched out of gold rush-era buildings and wide, sleepy streets. By 9 o'clock the following morning, it was 31 degrees. "I was aware of this catastrophic rating but did not have an integrated sense of what that actually meant," Fiannuala tells me. "Because when the fire started, it really went from zero to 100 in a matter of seconds." Everything seemed to happen at once. When a ferocious hot wind arrived, it was as if the door of a giant oven had burst open. The power went out. The emergency app on Fiannuala's phone lit up, showing multiple fires had started. "And then my phone stopped working, but not completely," she says. "The first thing that happened was my emergency app froze. And then I tried to call my mother, and I couldn't get through on the phone. I tried to send a text to either my mother or my father, and that didn't work either." A few kilometres away, a grass fire was racing through paddocks towards the nearby orchard town of Harcourt, known for its juicy apples. Fiannuala knew about the fire because she was able to call her brother in Melbourne, even though other calls were failing. "So then, he was updating me about what was happening on the VicEmergency app." At some point, Fiannuala left her house and walked up a nearby hill to try to get reception. From the hill she watched as a thick cloud of smoke turned the blue sky an ominous shade of orange. Her brother told her the wind was pushing the fire towards Castlemaine. "I had always thought that Castlemaine was a very safe place if there was a fire but suddenly you realise, oh gosh, there's actually nowhere in these conditions that is safe," she says. Back at home Fiannuala put her Persian cat in the bath because the air conditioning had dropped out along with the power. The blackout had also rendered the NBN useless . She didn't have a backup battery-powered radio, so she turned on her car radio to listen to the ABC's emergency broadcast. "But by that point," she says, "the broadcasting tower at Mount Alexander had burned". Alone, and with dwindling access to information, she decided to find her parents, who were now sheltering at a friend's house nearby. "It was not responsible of me to go," she says. "There were no traffic lights … people were driving erratically." Fiannuala found that her parents had patchy mobile phone signals and couldn't access the emergency apps either. "Sometimes you could use your phone and sometimes you couldn't," she says. As the afternoon progressed, emergency warnings "to shelter indoors now" were being issued for nearby Harcourt. The fast-moving grassfire would eventually destroy 66 dwellings. The only certainty was that there wasn't any. Some houses and business were mangled, blackened wrecks, others stood undamaged beside them. Lives were up-ended. But a wind change turned the flames away from the larger town of Castlemaine. For Fiannuala, a lecturer in publishing and communications at the University of Melbourne, the day brought a "completely new awareness of risk". She has channelled the experience into understanding why multiple forms of communication failed and what that means for regional communities in Australia facing increasingly severe natural disasters in an era of climate crisis. The communication networks that support essential services like bushfire warnings have "not been adequately strengthened", she has warned , and recent changes, like the rollout of the NBN, the retirement of copper-wire landlines (which were more reliable during power outages), and the shutdown of the 3G network, have left communities like Castlemaine dangerously unaware of the fragility of the communication systems they should be able to rely on in an emergency. There is every chance that the next time this happens, the outcome could be fatal.

events.title: High mortgage rates are trapping homeowners in place, and making renovations harder to afford
events.summary: To learn more about the CNBC CFO Council, visit cnbccouncils.com/cfo Homeowners locked into 2-3% mortgages are staying put rather than refinancing, but with HELOCs now too expensive to tap, many are stuck unable to afford the very upgrades that would make staying worthwhile. Big-ticket item purchases have fallen sharply at Lowe's and Home Depot. Mortgage rates hit their highest level in three years this week, above 7.5%, and according to home services platform Angi, many homeowners are staying in their current houses five years longer than they originally planned. With mortgage rates continuing to stay untenably high for most Americans, many are staying put. But that doesn't mean homes don't need improving and upkeep. And some homeowners figure that if they can't move into a new home, they'll make their old home "newer" — a new deck or perhaps a walk-in closet. Traditionally, a home equity loan or home equity line of credit would be the first tool to reach for. But even those are getting too expensive for homeowners. This leaves homeowners effectively trapped in aging homes with no easy way out, or way to improve them. And even when homeowners are tapping into home equity loans — homeowners did originate nearly 20% more second mortgages or HELOCs in the second quarter of this year compared with the first quarter — they likely aren't using the equity for improvements. Experts say they are using them to stay afloat. Untapped or expensive, Americans are sitting on a record amount of home equity . "As rates keep rising, tapping into home equity will become more and more expensive for homeowners. This will generally hold back consumer spending, but it will hit big-ticket items, like home renovations, particularly hard," said Tom Graff, chief investment officer of Facet, a financial planning and wealth management firm. This struggle is something built into the rate hikes, according to Graff. "The Fed is hiking interest rates in an attempt to control inflation. One of the ways that is supposed to work is by pushing down consumer spending. So the fact that consumers will struggle to finance large purchases is by design," he said. But the Fed policy also comes with risks for a consumer-driven economy. "Consumer spending is already lagging way behind as a driver of GDP growth," Graff said. And he added there is little cushion in the economy, given the soft jobs market , wage growth that has been declining , high gas — as well as diesel — prices, and net negative immigration. The biggest economic driver right now is data centers . "Spending on data centers is really driving GDP growth and holding the economy together. If that were to slow even mildly, the economy could easily fall into recession," Graff added. An unexpected five-year extended residence Angie Hicks, co-founder and chief customer officer of Angi, the home services marketplace that connects homeowners with contractors and other service professionals, says homeowners are holding back on big projects as HELOCs and equity loans get priced out of reach. Hicks says that people are going to hold on to that two to three percent mortgage rate as long as they can. "And it's never coming back, this six to seven percent is a more normal range," Hicks said. So that has owners wanting to turn their home "for right now" into a "forever home." "We are seeing people living in their houses about five years longer than they thought," Hicks said. "People are feeling a squeeze." Hicks says people are prioritizing maintenance, doing a furnace tune-up rather than a major kitchen remodel. "You don't want to wake up on the coldest morning of the year in the winter to a furnace that doesn't work, so people are spending for the tune-up," Hicks said. This is consumer behavior that is on par with other times of economic angst. "When inflation kicks in or there is a shock to the economy, people don't stop spending on their homes, they just reprioritize what they are spending on, for instance, a water heater instead of a new deck," Hicks said. And when it comes to home improvement, people tend to tap into savings or take on projects, like landscaping, that lend themselves to being done in phases. Angi data shows 60 percent of consumers are now putting off projects and switching to maintenance. Kitchens and bathrooms are the most popular projects, but there are lots of ways those spaces can be given a fresh look, according to Hicks, without the big-ticket upgrades. She says new cabinetry is the biggest cost of a kitchen remodel, so owners are looking at swapping out the handles or applying new coats of paint instead. "The data points to a consumer who is staying in their home but deferring major projects," said Philip Odelfelt, CEO of Datavations, a retail analytics firm that tracks point-of-sale data for home improvement manufacturers.

events.title: Elon Musk says Tesla is trying to prevent robotaxis from running over cats at night
events.summary: Elon Musk says gray cats on a dark road are vexing for robotaxis. Kaylee Greenlee/Reuters Tesla CEO Elon Musk said one problem for robotaxis at night has whiskers and a tail. "Literally trying to avoid grey kittens on grey tarmac in the dark," he said. A Waymo hit and killed a cat at night last year. There are many challenges to putting self-driving cars on the road. Elon Musk says one of them has nine lives. The Tesla CEO announced on Saturday that the company is expanding the operating hours of its robotaxis from 10 p.m. to 11 p.m. in Austin and said that his team has been trying to overcome a rather stealthy problem. "The main thing we're trying to solve is making sure that we don't run over pets when they're hard to see at night," Musk wrote in an X post . "Literally trying to avoid grey kittens on grey tarmac in the dark." After years of delays , Tesla's robotaxis were rolled out in Austin last year. Since then, the company has gradually expanded the availability there and in other Texas cities and in Florida. Cybercabs use "camera vision and sensors" to navigate, according to Tesla. In its vehicle manuals, Tesla says that low or limited light — including unlit or poorly lit roads at night — can limit a camera's ability to provide accurate visual information. Cats and dogs, which are prone to darting unpredictably into the street, could pose a higher risk than the relatively routine flow of traffic. In a reply to a comment on his X post on Saturday, Musk pointed to AI-assisted camera processing as a way to improve nighttime visibility. "Visual spectrum cameras can see very well in the dark when AI is doing the photon count analysis," he said. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration is investigating Telsa's camera system for full self-driving vehicles and whether it's good enough at spotting road hazards in less-than-ideal visibility conditions. The robotaxi industry leader, Waymo, uses a different system than Tesla — LiDAR , which uses laser beams to scan the environment. One late night last year, a Waymo struck and killed a 9-year-old tabby cat named KitKat — prompting an outpouring of tributes from residents in the neighborhood. In September 2025, a Tesla Model Y operating in its Austin robotaxi service struck a dog that ran into the street, the company reported. The report, which Tesla filed with the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, said the dog ran away from the car, apparently uninjured. Musk has owned cats , including one named Schrödinger, after a physicist's famous feline-based thought experiment. Musk once said he "tried liking" Schrödinger, but "the feeling wasn't reciprocated. Not even slightly." "One day she disappeared," he said. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: People say I don't look like a multimillionaire. Good — I'm not trying to.
events.summary: Tori Dunlap went into debt to buy her car at age 22, she's now a multimillionaire. Courtesy of Tori Dunlap Tori Dunlap became a millionaire at 27, about five years ago. She refuses to spend on signifiers of wealth that aren't meaningful to her. Her privacy has become more important as she builds wealth, she says. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Tori Dunlap , founder of Her First $100K and author of " Financial Feminist ." It has been edited for length and clarity . My parents were very good at teaching me about money , not just by what they said, but by what they did. They were middle-class — by no means rich — but they made very smart financial decisions and equipped me with a lot of financial skills. By college, I was the friend whom other friends came to ask about money. I set myself a very public goal of saving my first $100,000 when I was 25 — which I achieved. By 27, I was a millionaire, and now, at 32, I'm a multimillionaire . Yet I don't look or act the way many believe a multimillionaire should. Here's what I refuse to spend on — and what's become even more important to me as I build wealth . I don't spend on signifiers of wealth I'm often told online that I don't look like a multimillionaire should. My hair, for example. If I'm going to be on television, I'll get it blown out. But when I'm creating content for my community, it's often pulled back. Tori Dunlap gets her hair done every three months. Courtesy of Tori Dunlap I get my hair done about every three months, which is more than most people. Yet I'm not going to spend the money — or, more importantly to me these days, the time — to have it done constantly. It's just not a priority for me when I have a company to run. I drive a 12-year-old Toyota I still drive the same Toyota RAV4 that I went into debt to purchase when I was 22. It's a cute car, it's dependable, and it does everything I need it to. Maybe I'll change my mind and get a flashier car in the future. It's fine for people to change their minds about what's important to them. But I'm not going to buy a luxury car just to show my wealth. I rented until last year Until last year, I rented an apartment even though I was a multimillionaire. I could afford to buy, but I didn't have the time to search for a house. Then, my landlord decided to sell. That happened to me twice in a row, and made me realize I was willing to invest the time to find a house I love. As I've built wealth, time has become the currency that matters most to me. I don't think there are silly purchases — just ones we don't think about I'll never be the financial expert telling you that spending on lattes is stupid. I'm not saying that spending on hair, cars, or homes is silly either. What's stupid, to me, is spending on things that don't matter to you. If you're buying a certain bag, vehicle, or home just to keep up with the Joneses and look wealthy, you're not being intentional. In my book, "Financial Feminist," I say that we don't need to stop spending money. But we do need to stop spending on things that we don't care about. I indulge, but not always publicly I spend pretty unabashedly on travel. To me, it's one of the most important things. I'm also proud of the house I bought last year. It's newly renovated and has a beautiful view. Yet, I don't share it online because my privacy is more important to me than showcasing my home. I've been very intentional about keeping some things private, including my partner and house. My markers of success aren't material The vision we've been sold of financial success is sexy: it's designed bags, sleek blowouts, and marble columns. I'm out here showing a different version of success. For me, success means having enough financial security that I never have to be in a situation that doesn't respect me. I want to be able to donate to causes I believe in, and always pick up the check for friends and family without worrying about it. Women in my community have been able to leave abusive relationships or toxic workplaces because of their financial independence. They can improve their communities and families. For them — and me — those markers of success matter so, so much more than any material markers of wealth. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: I've been to Cancún countless times — but I prefer this quieter island about 30 minutes away
events.summary: Isla Mujeres offered gorgeous food, great views, and fewer crowds than Cancún. Kaila Yu I love visiting Cancún , but I've been on the hunt for a similar spot that has fewer crowds. Recently, I fell in love with Isla Mujeres, an island near Cancún that has great food and beaches. I think Isla Mujeres is a perfect spot for fans of Cancún who want a beach trip with less nightlife. I love Cancún's balmy, multi-blue-toned water, but I'm less fond of the crowds, nightlife, and traffic. These days, when I travel, I want as much peace and nature as possible, from calming ocean waves to the squeaky chatter of local birds. I've been to Cancún countless times, but recently visited the nearby Isla Mujeres for the first time — and found it to be the quiet, tropical escape that I needed. This island is just a 30-minute boat ride from Cancún, but it feels worlds away. It's also much smaller — the entire island of Isla Mujeres is 5 miles long, less than half of Cancún's Hotel Zone alone. The island is ideal for those who, like me, want to avoid the crowds and loud music of Cancún and Tulum. The island is just a quick ferry ride from Cancún I felt relaxed as soon as I arrived. Holly Hildreth/Getty Images Isla Mujeres is an easy day trip from Cancún, but there are plenty of hotels — from luxury options to budget picks — for those who wish to stay longer. On this trip, I picked an all-inclusive resort that provided a catamaran ride from Cancún, though there's also take a ferry for under $20 (one way). The vacation began the moment I boarded the catamaran: I found a prime, comfortable spot next to the captain and enjoyed the scenic boat ride . The crew told us it's not rare to see dolphins along the way (although we sadly didn't). One of the first things I did upon arriving was explore the island. It was fun to pass brightly colored homes painted in shades like banana yellow and aquamarine, and watch cute iguanas sunbathe. I also stopped at popular Instagrammable spots and monuments, such as the Mayan goddess Ixchel statue at Punta Sur, toward the southern tip of the island. Isla Mujeres is one of the best places in the world to swim with whale sharks On Isla Mujeres, you can swim with whale sharks. Brandi Mueller/Getty Images Every year, hundreds of whale sharks arrive on Isla Mujeres between summer and early fall for a bountiful plankton feast. I learned that this is widely considered one of the ethical places to swim with whale sharks because regulations are in place to protect the animals and their environment. I was lucky enough to visit during the prime season to see these gigantic, gentle creatures on a boat tour. I also got an unexpected bonus: There were at least a dozen surprise manta rays swirling around. Isla Mujeres is also a fantastic base for scuba diving . I didn't get a chance to dive on my trip, but next time I visit, I plan to explore the MUSA Underwater Museum, which has hundreds of life-sized underwater sculptures. There are several white-sand beaches , but my favorite was the popular Playa Norte, located on the northern tip. I highly recommend stretching out on the sand and grabbing a treat from one of the roving ice cream vendors. The food was incredible I'm still thinking about the food I ate on my trip. Kaila Yu Seafood is especially good here, and you'll find nearly every kind of Mexican food you'd expect on the mainland. I tried tikin xic for the first time; locals told me that it was one of the island's most famous dishes . It's usually served whole, marinated Mayan-style with peppery achiote paste and spices. I couldn't get enough of the tender, smoky, and slightly spicy fish. I didn't get to try these dishes while I was there, but I was told that cochinita pibil (marinated, slow-roasted pork) and marquesita (a fried, crepe-like wrap filled with cheese) were other local musts. Isla Mujeres is a perfect place for Cancún and Tulum fans who want turquoise water without the crowds I hate crowds and lines, and I loved feeling relaxed at every activity and restaurant. I found that I could also walk around town and feel comfortable and at ease, since the streets felt generally less populated with tourists. For those who are interested, there was some nightlife, with live music and bars downtown — but in my experience, the party scene seemed to wrap up on the earlier side, around midnight. This was a bonus for me, since I'm usually in bed by 9 p.m. and I don't drink alcohol. For a sober, early-bedtime girl like me, Isla Mujeres is the ideal alternative to Cancún. I already can't wait to go back. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: U.S. debt is increasingly at the mercy of the market as interest costs surge while elections add more risk to the debt ceiling, ratings agency warns
events.summary: The recent jump in Treasury yields has highlighted how vulnerable the U.S. debt outlook is to the bond market, which Scope Ratings flagged in a new report. On Friday, the Europe-based credit ratings agency maintained the U.S. sovereign score at AA- , three notches below the top rating and two steps below AA+ grades from rivals Moody’s, Fitch and S&P Global Ratings. Scope listed what the U.S. still has in its favor: a strong economy, the dollar as the world’s reserve currency, strong institutions like the Federal Reserve, as well as the deepest and most liquid capital markets. But while Scope kept the U.S. credit outlook at stable, it sees deficits worsening due to the persistence of “structural expenditure pressures” and limited political will for fiscal reform. At the same time, debt-servicing costs will drive further fiscal deterioration as U.S. primary deficits, or deficits excluding interest payments, will actually remain stable at around 3.5% of GDP, according to Scope. With the 10-year Treasury yield now at 5.27%, it has already blown past long-term forecasts from the Congressional Budget Office, which saw them at 4.3% from 2028 to 2031 and 4.4% from 2032 to 2036. The Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget has estimated that if yields stay roughly 1 percentage point above where CBO projected, about $3.5 trillion would be added to the debt over the next decade. Scope warned that the increasingly heavy interest costs limit the government’s ability to respond to future shocks. And without stronger economic growth or substantial fiscal adjustment, the general government debt burden will approach 160% of GDP by 2036, it added. “This trajectory points to an unsustainable medium-term fiscal path and leaves the sovereign increasingly exposed to shifts in market sentiment and financing conditions,” Scope said. In fact, the U.S. has been rebalancing its debt toward short-term maturities and away from long-term bonds that carry higher rates. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent continued this strategy that began under the Biden administration then doubled down on it with buybacks that call for issuing more short-term notes to retire longer-term debt. As more U.S. debt comes due in quicker timelines, rolling it over gets costlier when yields spike as they have in recent months. Meanwhile, price-sensitive hedge funds have become bigger players in the $32 trillion Treasury market, replacing foreign central banks that were more stable holders of U.S. debt and adding to market volatility. Further complicating the picture is the U.S. debt limit. Scope expects the current ceiling of $41.1 trillion to be reached by early 2027. The Treasury Department can use “extraordinary measures” to prevent the U.S. from defaulting for several months, but lawmakers must act at some point. “While Scope’s baseline assumes that policymakers will ultimately agree to raise or suspend the debt limit, the post-midterm political landscape could increase the scope for prolonged partisan standoffs,” Scope said. “Repeated debt-ceiling episodes continue to highlight weaknesses in fiscal governance and contribute to periodic market volatility.” The report coincided with the end of the federal government’s fiscal year on Wednesday and the start of fiscal 2027 on Thursday. According to a year-end tally by CRFB, fiscal 2026 closed with a budget deficit of $2 trillion (6.2% of GDP), publicly held debt of $32.3 trillion (100% of GDP), and debt-interest costs of $1.1 trillion—a record high 3.4% of GDP and the the second largest line item in the budget, topping defense and Medicare. “Based on evidence from the past year, we now expect much higher interest payments and lower tariff revenue going forward, which could send deficits and debt surging well beyond [CBO’s] projections,” CRFB said in a statement. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: ‘Really wealthy Americans will be embarrassed’ not to have an Argentine passport, program designer predicts
events.summary: A consultant who helped design Argentina’s new citizenship-by-investment program predicts it will become a status symbol for wealthy Americans. “I expect that the Argentina program will become so popular with the American [high-net-worth individuals] that really wealthy Americans will be embarrassed if they do not have an Argentina passport,” said Nuri Katz , founder of Apex Capital Partners , told Fortune on Friday. Economy Minister Luis Caputo announced the program in Paris, saying applications will open in the fourth quarter of 2026. It is billed as South America’s first. AP described it as the kind of “golden passport” scheme common in other markets, as Argentine President Javier Milei looks for ways to secure dollars for his debt-saddled country. The design The program has two routes. The first is a non-refundable $350,000 contribution for a single applicant, with a family of four expected to pay $500,000. The second is an $800,000 investment in a government security created for the program. The announcement gives no maturity, yield or repayment terms for the bond. The Agency for Citizenship by Investment Programs will assess each application, working with the State Intelligence Secretariat, the Financial Information Unit and the Ministry of Security. Checks cover identity, source of funds, criminal and reputational records, and immigration history. Funds must go through the formal financial system, and the National Directorate of Migration makes the final decision. Katz’s firm belongs to Argentina Mobility for Investment and Global Opportunity Limited, a group of five investment-migration firms that has advised the government on the program. Apex advises individual clients on second citizenship, and Katz helped create Antigua and Barbuda’s program in 2013 and draft Cyprus’s investor legislation in 2011. In June, he told Fortune that Argentina was developing South America’s first citizenship-by-investment program and that it would draw “significant American interest.” The pitch “Argentina, as the first G20 country, offers American HNWI the first opportunity to quickly and easily acquire a citizenship of a country that is both a safe haven and a huge business opportunity,” Katz told Fortune on Friday. He pointed to demand. “The desire for jurisdictional diversification amongst wealthy Americans, as can be seen by our survey, is overwhelming. The question is where to go, and until now the choices were not really that great.” Apex released a survey in June that polled 1,733 Americans with household incomes above $200,000, and 61% said they would consider leaving the U.S. within five years, Fortune reported . Cost of living and taxes ranked first, cited by 68%, ahead of political climate at 54%. Europe was the top destination at 42%, followed by Canada at 18% and the Caribbean at 16%. The survey measured intent, not actual moves. Katz, who was born in the U.S. and largely grew up in Montreal before moving to Moscow in 1990, has a wider argument about the U.S. itself, though he now lives in Antigua. He expects the national debt to force a choice between inflation and default, and that wealthy Americans are too concentrated in dollar assets. “I lived through hyperinflation,” he told Fortune in June. “I don’t think people understand how dangerous that is, once the lid comes off and they have to start printing money.” For this story,  Fortune  journalists used generative AI as a research tool. An editor verified the accuracy of the information before publishing. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: OpenAI safety employee resigns, claiming the company’s ‘culture is broken’
events.summary: Last day to exhibit your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders at Disrupt is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. By his own admission, David Robinson is “something of a cliché”: an employee at a leading AI company who issues a dire warning while resigning from their job. In an essay published in The Atlantic , Robinson said he led the writing of safety reports that accompanied OpenAI’s major product launches. He also said that with three-and-a-half years at OpenAI, he is “among the longest-tenured employees at the company.” Now he’s quitting, because in his view, the company’s “culture is broken.” In some ways, Robinson’s comments echo those of Jacob Coxon, who worked as a researcher at both OpenAI and Anthropic before quitting and declaring that these companies are “gambling with our lives.” Coxon’s comments led to a broader debate about AI safety, with Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei unveiling a plan for more cautious AI development ; AI executives met with President Donald Trump this week and signed what appeared to be hastily written, non-binding pledge to implement more safety controls . But in Robinson’s view, the debate needs to go beyond “specific rules or new laws,” addressing the overall culture at these companies. And while much of the reporting around OpenAI has focused on how the company’s CEO Sam Altman lost the trust of former colleagues , Robinson’s essay suggests that OpenAI’s culture issues are the same as those of Silicon Valley at large. “OpenAI has thrived by trial and error (which it calls ‘iterative deployment’), looking for problems and improving its guardrails in response,” he wrote. “But this approach, by its very nature, guarantees periodic failures — and the scale of those failures is growing as systems get more capable.” Pointing to the recent breach of Hugging Face systems by OpenAI agents, as well as continuing revelations of OpenAI discovering more rogue agents , Robinson argued, “An environment where things like this can happen is no place to grow artificial minds that could be smarter than we are and that might not do what we want them to.” Given the increased risk, Robinson argued that frontier AI companies need to start operating “like nuclear-power plants or busy airports, with layers of redundancy and careful, time-consuming planning, so that the occasional and inevitable human error does not open a door to disaster.” But Robinson said that in his time at OpenAI, he “never encountered a colleague who had experience making airplanes fly safely or nuclear reactors run without melting down, or helping the financial system grow without collapsing.” In response to Robinson’s essay, OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri said the company continues to improve its safety measures. “We’re making sure our models don’t become more capable than we can safely manage and secure, and we pause training or hold back models when we need to slow down,” Pusateri said in a statement. “We’re making significant changes to strengthen security in our research and testing environments, train models to not just complete tasks but do so responsibly, expand our work with third-party evaluators, and improve real-time monitoring so we can detect and respond to concerning behavior earlier in the training process .” Beyond calling for changes in OpenAI’s culture, Robinson also said it’s time to ask bigger questions about alignment — something that he admitted could sound “touchy-feely,” but he said it’s critical as companies’ current “measures of how well” AI systems “match human values are coarse.” “The smarter the industry lets models grow while these problems remain unsolved, the more dangerous our situation becomes,” he said. Robinson’s departure was first reported by Business Insider . In his essay, he also acknowledged that he’s following an apparently a common step in the AI whistleblower playbook: He’s hired a PR firm . But he insisted, “The decision to speak out is mine alone.” “Perhaps I should have stayed and fought for fundamental shifts in our staffing and culture, but in practice, my colleagues and I were so busy sprinting that we seldom had the chance to consider big changes, much less to actually make them,” Robinson said. “That’s why I concluded that stronger incentives for safety — coming from outside the company — are a big part of getting this right.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . events.title: Departure comes as the state investigates what went wrong during Pike's lethal injection.
events.summary: Tennessee's top prison official turned in his resignation days after the failed attempt to execute death row inmate Christa Pike , the state announced Saturday. Gov. Bill Lee said Department of Correction commissioner Frank Strada would step down this month. Strada, who had served as commissioner since 2023, said he would cooperate with the independent investigation of the failed execution attempt. Pike, 50, survived two doses of the lethal injection drug pentobarbital and was taken to a hospital for life-saving treatment. What they're saying: In a statement, Strada said he believed his department "carried out its responsibilities in accordance with the established protocol. "Even so, stepping aside is in the best interest of Tennesseans as the independent review moves forward." Lee said Strada "served with integrity," adding that he appreciated Strada's "willingness to put the interests of Tennesseans first during this difficult moment. … "I thank Commissioner Strada for his dedicated service to Tennessee and pray God's blessings over him in the days ahead." The big picture: Strada's department has faced bipartisan criticism following the unprecedented failures during the attempt to execute Pike on Wednesday night. Her attorneys said the execution team used at least seven needles in their attempts to find a vein for an IV. Pike's attorneys said she complained of intense pain during the injection and developed blisters and burns around the injection site. Between the lines: Medical experts have said those details suggest the IV wasn't properly connected and that the drug might not have gone directly into her bloodstream. Pike was unconscious and on a ventilator in a local hospital on Friday, her attorneys said.

events.title: OpenAI's Altman: Ascribing religion to models a "safety issue"
events.summary: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman on Saturday took a veiled shot at Anthropic and its work on the soul of AI, saying he was "very uncomfortable" with the idea of attributing some kind of religious power to models. Why it matters: It's yet another point of division between Altman and his former colleague Dario Amodei, whose company has reportedly pursued scholars across faiths to make the case for moral, conscious models. But some of the top voices in AI are starting to publicly line up against Anthropic's efforts to infuse consciousness into models. What they're saying: "I am very uncomfortable about people trying to ascribe religious force or a surrender of human judgment to AI models, and think it is a real safety issue," Altman said in a post to X. Context: Earlier this week, the New York Times reported that Anthropic co-founder Christopher Olah has been meeting with religious leaders to consider questions of model consciousness — but also to figure out how to infuse morals and moral behavior into AI. At one point, the Times reported, Olah considered the possibility of models engaging in Catholic-style confession, not just to admit their mistakes but to shape their future behavior. The big picture: Spirituality is suddenly becoming something of a flashpoint around AI's future. On Friday Pope Leo, an outspoken AI critic, called on the church to ally with artists to preserve human creativity, saying: "Algorithms lack the spark of humanity." Between the lines: The pope's stance put renewed focus on a fundamental question: Do models have souls and feelings? The Times reported that Olah, before a Vatican event in May, tried to persuade the pope's advisers that they should take the prospect of conscious models more seriously. So far, other top scientists seem to be lining up against the idea. "I am disturbed by how some of my fellow AI researchers keep trying to elevate the moral standing of checkpoints and harnesses," Google DeepMind principal research scientist Jon Barron posted to X. "I hope the rest of us on Team Meatbag reject this movement and stay focused on solving real problems and helping actual humans." For the record: Neither OpenAI nor Anthropic immediately responded to requests for comment on Altman's post. The bottom line: The AI safety debate largely focuses on things like cybersecurity and bioweapons. The real problem may be more spiritual than that.

events.title: I reviewed luxury hotels for nearly a decade. Becoming a mom changed what I look for.
events.summary: The author said she has reviewed luxury hotels for nearly a decade, but the amenities she looks for have changed since becoming a parent. Courtesy of Lara Kramer. I've traveled a lot for work and pleasure, so I have some high standards when it comes to hotels. Since having a child, my needs have shifted, and I now look for different things. Attention is my new favorite amenity. It means so much when traveling with kids. When my husband and I were planning our honeymoon along the Amalfi Coast, we had three criteria for every hotel we booked: superb dining, a dreamy wellness program, and a wow factor. We wanted something like a breathtaking view or spa-inspired bathroom , something that would keep us on our just-married high. Years later, having traded newlywed life for the life of new parents, we were adamant that we would continue traveling. At 2 months old, our daughter Mabel had a passport. Before her first birthday, she'd clocked two international trips — one to Paris and one to the Dominican Republic — along with a domestic jaunt to Asheville. With each new hotel check-in during this new phase of life, I found that what I needed from my hotel stays started to shift. The parent effect I've had a long career in the travel space, with a decade spent on staff at "Fodor's Travel" and "Condé Nast Traveler," and now as a freelance travel writer. Hotels have always been front and center in my career and personal life. In my early years, I built digital products and guided editorial strategy centered on hotel evaluation, and later in my career, I was boots-on-the-ground reporting on the guest experience at luxury hotels around the world. My reporting always focused on the details the industry celebrates: the architecture, the spa, the lobby bar, the Michelin-starred restaurant . The author said she wanted to continue traveling after having a child. Courtesy of Lara Kramer. But traveling with my daughter forced me to notice a different set of details, ones that most travelers, and many hotels, overlook. Suddenly, I cared less about the premium wine list and more about if the in-room blackout curtains actually worked. I found myself checking how flexible the dinner hours were, whether there were affordable laundry services with same-day turnaround, whether the mini fridge could fit several bottles of milk, and whether there was a park within walking distance. The things I rarely, if ever, considered had suddenly become the things that could make or break my stay. My new definition of five-star hospitality Parenthood isn't for the weak . It shifts priorities and redirects attention in a way that can feel merciless. But it also brings a unique perspective and reveals the world to you in completely new ways: the joy of wide sidewalks, chasing park butterflies, and picking ice cream solely based on what color moves you that day. When it came to enjoying my lifelong passion for travel, parenthood didn't lower my standards for hotels, it just gave me an entirely new set of them. And for hotels looking to build and maintain guest loyalty, widening the focus on which amenities matter most is crucial. Because if there's one thing humans have proven they won't stop doing, it's making more humans. The hospitality industry has certainly gotten better at welcoming those new arrivals. "Family-friendly" no longer only implies overly stimulating Disney vacations or an unsettlingly warm kiddie pool. The growing trend of on-site kids clubs and child-friendly programming has also made traveling with children easier and more enjoyable. But if hotels truly wish to earn the loyalty of traveling parents, the focus needs to shift slightly. I expect more now Those traditional family amenities are low-hanging fruit, and the properties paying the most attention to families know it. The author said that small details, like staff tucking her daughter's stuffy into the hotel bedding, matter more to her now. Courtesy of Lara Kramer. The details that have come to matter most to me are much smaller: a hotel that asks what my daughter's favorite snack is before we arrive, a staff member who remembers her name, or a housekeeper who tucks her favorite stuffy neatly into the made bed. These things aren't particularly glamorous. Nor do they require big budgets. Instead, they remind me that true hospitality is about personalization and customization, across ages, and that the smallest details often say more about a hotel's hospitality than its most expensive upgrades ever could. For this traveling mom, attention is my new favorite amenity. Because at the end of the day, I didn't stop caring about the palatial marble bathroom anchored by a vanity with his-and-hers sinks, I just also want there to be a step stool so my daughter can reach the faucet. events.title: Anthropic's super bug-hunting model Mythos is hardcore good at math, as latest vuln under attack shows
events.summary: Security All Security Cyber-crime Patches Research CSO Off-Prem All Off-Prem Edge and IoT Channel PaaS and IaaS SaaS On-Prem All On-Prem Systems Storage Networks HPC Personal Tech Cx0 Public Sector Software All Software AI and ML Applications Databases DevOps OS Platforms Virtualization Offbeat All Offbeat Columnists Science BOFH Legal Site News About Us Special Features All Special Features Cybersecurity Month 2026 VMware Explore 2026 Cloud Infrastructure Month 2026 HPE: AI Explainers Agentic AI The Future of the Datacenter AWS:Reinvent Nvidia GTC Supercomputing Month Computex 2026 AI Infrastructure Month 2026 The State of Storage 2026 RSA Conference Vendor Voice All Vendor Voice Modernizing Financial Services with FIS and AWS Barco Infinidat Everpure Rubrik Make it real with Capgemini and AWS Money Movement Hub ZTE Nutanix: Scale Kubernetes. Not Chaos. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Exploitation attempts came from China-hosted IP, VulnCheck researcher says arXiv imposes rate limit on paper submissions to stem the AI slop tide 1 day ago OpenAI alerts 100+ orgs that its 'misaligned models' attempted to break in - or worse 1 day ago Californian accused of shipping $300M worth of Nvidia chips to China without Uncle Sam’s approval 1 day ago OpenAI's wandering AI agents earn it a California subpoena 1 day ago Power approval set to delay Oracle's Wisconsin AI datacenter 1 day ago The second Anthropic-linked vulnerability known to have been exploited in the wild saw initial activity from an IP address in China targeting vulnerable hosts in the US and Japan. The vuln is a critical authentication-bypass bug in Rejetto HTTP File Server (HFS) that can lead to full admin access and remote code execution. HFS is an open source web file server that previously appeared on the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency’s catalog of Known Exploited Vulnerabilities in 2024. On Wednesday, researcher Zach Hanley at AI pen-testing company Horizon3 said he used Mythos to uncover a new flaw in the file server , now tracked as CVE-2026-61500. If you use Rejetto HFS, be sure to update to v3.2.1 or later, which fixes this and other security flaws. Hanley also published a video showing the steps to exploit HFS and remotely execute code on the server. By the next day, the CVE was under exploitation. “We started detecting exploitation of CVE-2026-61500 in Rejetto HFS this evening,” VulnCheck security researcher Patrick Garrity posted on LinkedIn on Thursday, adding that Hanley and team reported the bug to VulnCheck for CVE assignment. “Our canaries detected an actor in China targeting real vulnerable hosts in the US,” Garrity added. Garrity has been tracking CVEs attributed to Mythos and Project Glasswing, Anthropic’s initiative to give select partners access to the bug-hunting model, since shortly after the program was announced in April. Anthropic claims that Mythos is too powerful to release to the general public (insert evil laugh). As of Friday, Mythos and Project Glasswing have uncovered 286 CVEs , according to Garrity’s tracker, and up until Thursday only one of these bugs had been exploited in real-world attacks. The Thursday night activity originated from one IP address in China and targeted vulnerable servers in the US and Japan, Garrity told The Register . “Today we have seen four hits,” he told us on Friday. These originated from two different IP addresses in the US: 173.239.211[.]248 and 173.239.211[.]249. Both are in the same subnet, and “appear to be coming from a proxy,” Garrity added. China-linked digital intruders routinely use compromised devices as proxies to route malicious traffic and disguise the attackers’ true location, and in April a 10-country security advisory warned of China-nexus cyber operatives using proxy networks “strategically, and at scale.” In his write-up, Hanley said Horizon3 has used Mythos in its vulnerability research – and discovered “many critical vulnerabilities” – ever since the security company joined Project Glasswing in July. CVE-2026-61500 highlights a couple of Mythos capabilities that make it really good at uncovering vulnerabilities, according to Hanley. Namely, Mythos excels at mathematical distillations and scientific tasks, especially those relating to computer science and operating systems. Finding this CVE “speaks to Mythos’s capabilities in understanding of mathematics, how it identified an exploitable set of cryptographic missteps, and approached solving the constraints to achieve remote code execution,” Hanley wrote. The security issue stems from how HFS authenticates users. It generates a random value with Math.random() and then passes this value to Koa , the Node.js web framework foundation for HFS. Koa uses keygrip to sign all session cookies with that random value. This means that if an “attacker can derive what the session signing key is, they can forge valid session cookies,” Hanley said.

events.title: I ordered the same 3 items at Jersey Mike's and Subway. Neither sandwich chain was perfect, but one stood out.
events.summary: I headed to both Jersey Mike's and Subway to see which sandwich chain is my top pick. Savannah Born I ordered a cold sandwich, a hot sandwich, and a cookie at Jersey Mike's and Subway to compare. Jersey Mike's Club Sub blew me away, but I didn't love either chain's cheesesteak. Both chains had great chocolate-chip cookies, but, overall, I prefer Jersey Mike's to Subway. For years, Subway felt like the only relevant sandwich chain. Its 2008 "five, five dollar, five dollar footlong " jingle still lives in my head. The Connecticut-founded fast-food giant operates over 35,000 restaurants worldwide, with the most recent 2025 industry data estimating an annual $9.2 billion in United States system-wide sales. Subway remains the largest sandwich chain in the US, both in location count and estimated sales — but size isn't the whole picture. Its US footprint has fallen from more than 27,000 locations in 2015 to fewer than 19,000 today, with more than 700 closures in 2025 alone. Subway's domestic location count has declined every year since its 2015 peak (though it has seen international growth ). In April 2024, Subway was sold to Roark Capital — a private equity firm that also has a large stake in sandwich-chain competitor Jimmy John's — for a reported $9.6 billion. Meanwhile, Jersey Mike's made headlines in July 2026 after announcing plans to go public . It hit the New York Stock Exchange with a $1 billion IPO, one of the largest restaurant-sector debuts in recent years. The New Jersey-founded sandwich chain now operates more than 3,300 locations across the US and Canada. Earlier this year, the chain also announced plans to expand into Europe by opening hundreds of locations across the UK and Ireland. By comparison, in 2015, it had just over 1,000 total locations. Jersey Mike's financials track with its physical growth. In 2025, it posted more than $4 billion in US system-wide sales, a major feat for a chain that has far fewer locations than Subway yet has become one of its top competitors. With all the buzz, I wanted to see which chain actually had better-tasting sandwiches and offered more value to customers. To do so, I ordered a similar cold club sandwich, hot Philly cheesesteak, and chocolate-chip cookie at each, sticking to the chain's regular size and default preparations. Here's how they stacked up. I started at Jersey Mike's, a chain I'd never tried. Savannah Born Walking in, the first thing I noticed was a wall decal that read, "It's not a real Jersey Mike's Sub without 'the juice,'" which I learned is a blend of oil and red-wine vinegar. It's one of the chain's specialties. The "Mike's Way" preparation is another signature touch: finishing sandwiches with lettuce, onion, tomato, and "the juice." Fans of the chain also tout its hearty portions and freshly sliced meats and cheeses. Customers can watch staff slice cold cuts with the large metal tools right behind the counter. Then I went to Subway, where I'd eaten a handful of times. Savannah Born I hadn't been to Subway since college, so I forgot the chain is basically a design-your-own sandwich bar. The customization aspect is a major highlight, with rows of metal containers filled with veggies, meats, dressings, and cheeses. Subway is also known for its freshly baked bread and offers multiple varieties to choose from — hence why the stores always smell divine. Jersey Mike's menu seemed to cater to sandwich lovers. Savannah Born Don't get me wrong, Jersey Mike's menu had plenty of subs and cheesesteaks — especially the latter, with unique flavors like bacon ranch and Buffalo chicken. But for anything beyond a sandwich, or a sandwich-turned-bowl-or-wrap, you may want to look elsewhere. My total at Jersey Mike's came to $22.70 Savannah Born I ordered a 7-inch Club Sub prepared Mike's Way (the default for cold sandwiches), a 7-inch Mike's Famous Philly, and a chocolate-chip cookie for $10.80, $10.40, and $1.50, respectively. My total came to $22.70 before tax. Subway's menu seemed more extensive. Savannah Born In addition to subs and cheesesteaks, Subway offered pizza, nachos, and breakfast sandwiches , plus lighter and more health-forward options like salads, bowls, and protein pockets. Salads usually call my name, but this time, I was on a mission. My total at Subway came to $17.97. My Subway order seemed promising. Savannah Born To match my Jersey Mike's meal , I picked a 6-inch American Club Sub, a 6-inch Steak Philly, and a chocolate-chip cookie. Each sandwich cost $8.49 and the cookie $0.99, so I paid $17.97 total before tax. Mike's Club Sub looked incredible off the bat — and the taste followed suit. Savannah Born Unrolling the oil-and-vinegar-stained paper, I held a bulky sandwich loaded with provolone cheese, ham, turkey, onion, lettuce, tomato, and bacon. The bread, slathered in mayonnaise, oil, vinegar, and oregano, felt pillowy with a crusty edge. Beautiful, yes, but I was skeptical about a wet sandwich. After taking a bite, however, I officially understood the hype. "The juice" gave the bread some tang, and miraculously, it didn't make it soggy. Better yet, the cheese was creamy and the deli meat relatively moist. Slices seemed individually stacked, not stuck together, so I could tell they were freshly cut. Perhaps the best part was the equal proportions of ingredients, or the oregano that rounded out the flavors. Unfortunately, the lettuce hung limp from "the juice," but given all the pros, I could forgive it. Subway's All-American Club also impressed me, though it had a few drawbacks. Savannah Born Following Jersey Mike's heaping sandwich almost felt unfair, but Subway's All-American Club held its own — for the most part. It contained the same ingredients, minus the oil, vinegar, and spices; instead of provolone cheese, it had American. Subway's club sandwich had a smoky flavor, thanks to the ham and bacon. I appreciated the crunch from the bacon, onions, and lettuce, as well as the generous amount of American cheese. However, the bread wasn't as soft as I'd expected, given Subway's reputation. In fact, it almost felt stale. The turkey also missed the mark for me. I uncovered two thin slices, and they had little flavor and a dry texture. The ham had more taste, but it wasn't juicy, either. My other qualm: The chain went way overboard on the mayonnaise. Personally, I didn't understand the "famous" element of Mike's Famous Cheesesteak. Savannah Born I wrongly assumed the cheesesteak would be as hefty as the club. It wasn't nearly as substantial. To its credit, the hot sub contained sliced steak, grilled onions, grilled red peppers, and white American cheese, all with outstanding flavor. The steak had a nice tender bite. It also had a solid meat-to-bread ratio, but the sandwich lost points in my book for the bread itself, which was too crusty. Additionally, I felt it needed another slice of cheese. events.title: FlyDubai co-pilot used cockpit’s crash axe to try seizing control of flight and was barred from flying by Oman due to concerns over extremist views
events.summary: The co-pilot accused of  attacking the captain of an Israel-bound flight  with an axe and trying to seize the controls was an Omani national who had been barred from flying on his country’s airline because of concerns about extremist views, officials said Saturday. The co-pilot has been identified as Hamam al-Hammami, according to three people with knowledge of the situation, including a Gulf and a Western diplomat, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to the media. The United Arab Emirates, which is leading the investigation, said the co-pilot attacked with the cockpit’s crash axe and tried to take control of the  plummeting plane  in a “terrorist attack” Wednesday. His actions nearly crashed the flight with 182 people on board before  passengers and others rushed in  and subdued him. The new details raised questions about how thoroughly FlyDubai vets potential employees, and how the co-pilot’s presence on a flight filled with Israeli passengers got past Israel’s strict security protocols. Israel has said it has agreements with foreign carriers to keep pilots of nations without diplomatic ties from flying there. Israel and Oman don’t have formal diplomatic relations. The UAE government has earned a reputation for effective measures against extremist activities but has bristled in the past over criticism of  security lapses. The incident occurred at a sensitive time for Israel, a week before the anniversary of the Hamas-led attack on Oct. 7, 2023, that sparked the war in Gaza. It also came weeks before a highly contentious election in which security, and Oct. 7 security failures, have been central issues. FlyDubai hired the co-pilot after Oman Air barred him Separately, a regional official and a person familiar with the matter said the co-pilot had been barred from flying by Oman over concerns that he had adopted extremist views. The official said he was moved to an administrative job at Oman Air. Both spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss the ongoing investigation. They gave no details about the alleged extremist views. The co-pilot was later hired by UAE-based airline FlyDubai, the person said. It wasn’t immediately clear to what extent the co-pilot was vetted. The Gulf diplomat said he had undergone standard security checks before being hired, but it appears that the checks focused on whether he had been convicted of criminal charges and didn’t go deeper into examining his background for potential signs of radicalization. The regional official also said security agencies from four regional countries were working to establish the co-pilot’s motives, aided by the United States and other Western governments. The Gulf diplomat said investigations were trying to establish whether the co-pilot acted alone or “has any connection with any extremist groups.” The regional official said the co-pilot was born in the UAE and his mother is Syrian. He obtained Omani nationality from his father, also an Omani national. The regional official also said the co-pilot had traveled to Syria, with no details. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Friday said the co-pilot had undergone “Islamist radicalization,” but provided no evidence. There was no immediate comment Saturday from Israel’s government. A social media account was deleted the day of the flight A FlyDubai spokesperson said in an email that the airline could not comment beyond its official statements and acknowledged “there are many questions at this stage.” There was no immediate comment from Oman Air, and Oman’s government has said nothing publicly in response to repeated questions since the incident. In a statement to The Associated Press, Royal Air Maroc, Morocco’s national carrier, said the co-pilot “completed a three-month theoretical training period with the airline in 2025, as part of the pre-employment process. At the end of this training period, his application was not selected for employment.” There were no details. Keith Coles, a spokesperson for Buckinghamshire New University in England, told the AP that al-Hammami previously completed a distance-learning course in aviation management there but “did not undertake any pilot training.” There were no details on the timing. Little else was immediately known about the co-pilot’s background. His Instagram account was active until the day of the flight and then deleted. Captain and passengers have described drama on board Airlines are generally required to carry crash axes in the cockpit that could be used in an emergency to break open a window to escape or break open a panel to access a fire. The  captain , who was badly wounded, has said he used his remaining energy while being attacked to unlock the cockpit door, allowing people who had noticed alarming sounds to come in, tackle the co-pilot and stabilize the flight while passengers screamed. The plane made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia after a descent so extreme that part of the rudder was torn away, and aviation experts have marveled that it didn’t crash. FlyDubai has said crew traveling on the plane helped to stabilize it and land. They haven’t been publicly identified. Both the captain and co-pilot were later taken to the UAE. The passengers, most of them Israeli, flew home later Wednesday on a separate plane, to cheers. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Jack Dorsey’s Bitchat disappears from app stores in India after government order
events.summary: Last day to exhibit your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders at Disrupt is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Bitchat, Jack Dorsey’s decentralized messaging app designed to work without an internet connection, has disappeared from Apple and Google’s app stores in India, months after New Delhi first sought to restrict access to the open-source software. Dorsey said Saturday that the Indian government had ordered Apple to remove Bitchat from its App Store in the country. In a notice from Apple that Dorsey posted on X, India’s Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology issued the demand under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, the country’s primary legal provision for government-ordered online blocking. Apple’s notice said Bitchat would remain available on its App Store outside India. However, access to the app through its TestFlight beta-testing service would also be blocked in the country. Bitchat was also no longer available for download through Google Play in India when TechCrunch checked on Saturday. Bitchat’s website was also inaccessible across various internet service providers in the country. It was not immediately clear whether Google and internet service providers had also received directions from the federal government. Apple, Google, and India’s IT ministry did not respond to requests for comment. Launched in July last year, Bitchat uses Bluetooth mesh networking to allow nearby devices to exchange encrypted messages without relying on cellular networks, internet access, or centralized servers. In July 2026, Dorsey revealed that Indian authorities had ordered GitHub to take down repositories associated with the open-source messaging app, raising questions among digital rights advocates and legal experts about the legal basis for restricting software based on its functionality. The Indian government said in its order to GitHub at the time that Bitchat’s architecture made it hard for law enforcement agencies to intercept communications or trace users, and pointed to its ability to continue operating during internet shutdowns. The July order relied on a provision of India’s information technology law that deals with intermediaries and their liability for third-party content. That differs from Section 69A, cited in Apple’s latest notice. The Internet Freedom Foundation, a New Delhi-based digital rights advocacy group, called the latest order unconstitutional, arguing that Section 69A allows the government to block unlawful information but not a messaging app because of its ability to operate during internet shutdowns. It also said neither the blocking order nor the allegedly illegal content cited as the basis for the action had been made public. The latest restrictions on Bitchat come as India is seeing a fresh wave of ⁠youth-led protests over changes to the country’s voter rolls. Police detained several people during demonstrations in New Delhi on Saturday, as protesters demanded the resignation of India’s chief election commissioner over alleged manipulation of electoral rolls. Authorities suspended internet services around New Delhi’s Jantar Mantar for 12 hours on Friday during protests there. During July’s protests, demonstrators reportedly turned to Bitchat and rival app Briar after authorities suspended internet services. Interest in Bitchat surged in India around the same time. The country accounted for about 85% of the app’s global downloads between July 17 and July 23, up from roughly 1% in the previous 30 days, data from market intelligence firm Sensor Tower showed.
