events.title: America’s data center fight is a preview of what's to come for the rest of the world
events.summary: Public backlash against power-hungry data centers is spreading beyond the U.S. to Europe and Asia as communities raise concerns over electricity, water and land use. Opposition is increasingly translating into project delays, tighter regulation and financial risks for data center developers and investors. Despite the pushback, the AI boom shows little sign of slowing, creating growing tension between governments' AI ambitions and local resistance. As the AI boom becomes a major part of political debate, the public backlash against data centers in the U.S. is spreading to Europe and Asia — raising risks for investors. Across the Atlantic, negative sentiment is growing in Europe, which has more at stake due to its densely populated countries and higher electricity prices , experts told CNBC. Similar tensions are emerging in South Korea, with growing opposition to data centers near residential areas and proposals for tighter local restrictions, even as the national government pushes to accelerate development. Public opposition has already impacted around $42 billion of data center investments in Europe, in account delays and cancellations, according to research from STL Partners. That compares to around $77 billion in the U.S. The pushback could be the "straw that breaks the camel's back," Olivier Darmouni, associate professor at HEC Paris who specializes in the energy transition, told CNBC. Data center opposition is growing in Europe More than 70 data center projects in Europe were rejected or restricted between January and April — more than in all of 2025, according to the European Data Center Monitor. It found that pushback had snowballed from local town halls to courts, regulators and parliaments. Scotland has paused planning approvals for new hyperscale data centers after campaigners called on the government to avoid the "cautionary tale" of Ireland, where overwhelming power demand led to a moratorium. Constraints have been rising in the Nordics, where investors were drawn to large tracts of land and renewable energy. After a surge in power applications , Denmark passed an emergency law that could see data centers at the back of the queue for grid power applications. Spain also proposed new data center rules this summer, requiring data centers to source 80% of their electricity from renewables. Projects in the U.K. have stalled after pushback from locals. Much of the concern centers around water usage , power consumption , electricity prices, and the sheer amount of space that some centers require. There is also little agreement on how many permanent jobs the sector creates, and no precedent for projecting a center's economic value per megawatt. "The gains of AI are very diffused," Darmouni told CNBC. "There's definitely been more understanding of the scale of the potential AI build-out and its geographical spread, and perhaps ... more information about how much bigger these are, and that they're a little bit more like giant ghost warehouses that consume a lot of resources and can hurt local communities in some ways." Europe's denser population, and the fact that many data center operators are U.S. companies, might mean that the backlash hits harder, the professor added. South Korea, home to tech giants Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, sits at the heart of the AI supply chain. In June, its government named AI data centers as one of three major investment projects, alongside semiconductors and physical AI. But its push to build the infrastructure needed is running into resistance at the local level. In the Geumcheon district of southwestern Seoul, residents have called for authorities to revoke the building permit and halt construction of a data center near their homes, according to the local government. In July, officials announced plans to require consent from a majority of residents living within 200 meters of proposed data center sites and to introduce a three-stage system for reviewing projects and mediating disputes. Residents have also gathered outside the local government office on weekday mornings for months to protest against the project. The demonstrations had continued for 172 days as of mid-August, according to local media . In Gwacheon, a city just south of Seoul, a local council member proposed an ordinance aimed at protecting nearby residents from risks associated with data centers operating around the clock, including potential fires involving backup batteries. Should investors be worried about the backlash? Despite the pusback, the AI boom shows little sign of slowing down. But a community's ability "to derail a $10 billion [data center] plan is quite powerful," said Asya Walters, managing director at Alvarez & Marsal. She told CNBC the business-friendly environment in the U.S. has historically made it easier to overcome pushback. But in Europe and Asia, there's some "hot and coldness" at the country level about where demand is going, Walters said.

events.title: FlyDubai plane attack by co-pilot was an attempted 'terrorist' act, UAE says
events.summary: The co-pilot of a FlyDubai plane who attacked the flight's captain with an axe was attempting a terrorist attack, the United Arab Emirates said. "The co-pilot began executing his plan during the flight, attacking the captain inside the flight deck using a crash axe and attempting to take control of the aircraft," UAE AG Hamad Saif Al Shamsi said. Anwar Gargash, senior advisor to the UAE's president, said the region's "struggle with extremism persists, and justifying terrorism through hate speech is part of the danger, not its margins." The co-pilot of a FlyDubai plane who attacked the flight's captain with an axe this week was attempting a terrorist attack, the United Arab Emirates said Saturday. "The co-pilot began executing his plan during the flight, attacking the captain inside the flight deck using a crash axe and attempting to take control of the aircraft," UAE Attorney-General Hamad Saif Al Shamsi said in a post on X titled: "Planning and attempted terrorist act behind flydubai flight FZ1073 incident." "The latest terrorist operation is a new warning that the confrontation has not ended," Gargash said in a post on X. The flight on Sept. 30 from Dubai to Tel Aviv was carrying 172 passengers and crew, according to UAE-based FlyDubai. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said most of those aboard were Israeli citizens, adding that the attacker "tried to crash the plane." The aircraft landed safely at Tabuk airport in Saudi Arabia. Media reports and witness accounts say passengers and crew subdued the co-pilot after he attacked the captain. The UAE's attorney general's statement was the first time authorities have clarified the weapon the attacker used. Large aircraft are typically equipped with a so-called crash axe that flight crews can use to break out of their cockpit in emergencies, according to the UK Civil Aviation Authority and the Royal Air Force Museum. "Investigations are ongoing to establish the full circumstances, motives, and any links related to the incident, as well as to complete technical examinations and analysis of physical and digital evidence," the UAE's Al Shamsi said. The Associated Press identified the co-pilot as Omani national Hamam al-Hammami, citing three people with knowledge of the situation, including a Gulf and Western diplomat, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to the media. CNBC could not independently verify the co-pilot's identity. Netanyahu identified the injured pilot as Indian national Smit Machchhar. The Indian embassy in Riyadh said on X that Machchhar was in a hospital in Tabuk and reported to be in stable condition. FlyDubai later said the captain was returned to the UAE. The Israeli prime minister also identified the passenger who broke into the cockpit as Yaniv Hayun, calling him a "hero" and adding he deserved "a global medal of honor." Flight data from tracking site FlightRadar24 showed that the plane, a Boeing 737 Max 8, experienced extreme altitude fluctuations before broadcasting a "general emergency" squawk code. FZ1073 dropped from more than 14,000 feet in just 29 seconds, according to FlightRadar24. Transponder data showed vertical speeds ranging from about -30,000 to +10,000 feet per minute. Vertical speeds during normal operations rarely exceed plus or minus 4,000 feet per minute, FlightRadar24 said.

events.title: The Supreme Court will hear a major climate change case involving a devastating Colorado wildfire
events.summary: Colorado's Boulder County is one of dozens of governments around the United States suing oil and gas companies to help pay for damage caused by disasters linked to climate change LOUISVILLE, Colo. -- Less than an hour after the first warning that a wildfire was headed for her suburban street, Tawnya Somauroo's Colorado home was in ashes. She has worked tirelessly for nearly five years to rebuild her house and help ensure her neighborhood can withstand the next blaze. But as climate change contributes to more frequent wildfires, she worries that the careful landscaping, metal fencing and flame-resistant siding are not enough. “We lost our homes and they left us to figure out for ourselves how to make our neighborhoods safe again,” Somauroo said. “At the end of the day, it comes out of our pockets, you know? And it does feel like maybe the oil and gas industry should have a part in this.” She lives in Boulder County, one of dozens of jurisdictions across the United States suing oil and gas companies to help pay for damage from disasters linked to climate change. The case is part of a wave of climate change litigation across the country and the world, with billions of dollars at stake. On Monday, the first day of the Supreme Court's new term, the justices will hear the Boulder case that could decide the fate of others like it. The city and county of Boulder first sued two oil companies in 2018, years before the fire. They argued that Suncor Energy and ExxonMobil had violated state law by deceiving the public about their contributions to climate change and sought unspecified damages to help cover the cost of worsening disasters. The companies say that a flood of lawsuits in state courts is not the way to deal with the global issue. “The problem is that climate change is caused by pretty much everybody living on earth,” said Phil Goldberg, special counsel for the Manufacturers' Accountability Project, an industry group. “We need to figure out how to address that. We need to address it in a very meaningful way. This litigation doesn’t do that.” The companies have the backing of the Trump administration. Federal government attorneys say the lawsuits are a backdoor way to regulate heat-trapping greenhouse gas emissions and amount to an unconstitutional power grab. “No one state can superimpose its own regulatory preferences on the rest — least of all to address a global problem that exists almost entirely outside its borders and affects the world at large,” they wrote. The Clean Air Act, they say, allows the federal government, rather than states, to regulate emissions. The Republican administration has largely used that power to roll back environmental regulations. Christa Pike unconscious and on ventilator after botched execution: Attorneys Suspect in FlyDubai incident was previously identified as security risk: Officials District attorney reopens case of alleged Cornell University 'gang rape' Last month, the Environmental Protection Agency ceded some of its climate authority by repealing rules that limit planet-warming greenhouse gas emissions from power plants fueled by coal and natural gas. The move could complicate its argument. Boulder says it is not trying to regulate emissions beyond its borders, only holding companies accountable for local costs. “Boulder County and city aren’t trying to change what’s happening in Texas or New York, they’re trying to get compensation for things happening now in Colorado,” said Sam Sankar, senior vice president at Earthjustice, which filed an amicus brief in the case. Climate change was considered a factor in the 2021 Marshall Fire that destroyed Somauroo’s home, after the county's suit was originally filed. The total damage was estimated at $2 billion. It was the costliest wildfire in Colorado history. “Local county municipal governments play a very important role in helping front line communities adapt to climate change. This case could very well set a precedent,” said Chris Winter, executive director of the Getches-Wilkinson Center, an environmental research group in Colorado. The case will come before a conservative-majority Supreme Court where environmental regulations have not always fared well, including a 2022 decision that limited the EPA's authority to regulate carbon dioxide emissions from power plants. Only eight of the nine justices will be on the bench, though. Justice Samuel Alito recused himself just a week before arguments after facing calls to step aside because he owns stock in oil companies. That creates the possibility of a tie vote in the case, though it's unclear how likely that might be. The court is also weighing a question that experts say is a potential “off-ramp”: whether the justices have jurisdiction to hear the case at this stage. Whitehurst reported from Washington. events.title: 12 cities around the world where you can live comparably cheaply, from $400-a-month rents to $1 cappuccinos
events.summary: Tirana, Albania. Arpan Chakraborty/Getty Images Many Americans are moving abroad in search of cheaper housing, food, and a more laid-back lifestyle. In these 12 international cities, the cost of living is relatively low compared to the US. It includes a city that sits among the Andes and a Thai paradise with ancient temples. More and more Americans are looking overseas to reinvent their lives, whether in search of a lower cost of living , better healthcare , or a more affordable retirement . But with so many countries offering different lifestyles and costs, deciding where to put down roots can be difficult. Business Insider compiled a list of 12 cities with relatively low living costs compared with the US, using data from Numbeo , a crowdsourced cost-of-living comparison website. Numbeo's estimates include monthly costs for a single person and a family of four, as well as city-center rent and home prices. It also tracks typical spending on coffee, a meal for two, and a gym membership. Because its methodology relies in part on user-submitted data, the figures should be treated as a guide rather than definitive costs. Many of these cities also rank well on quality-of-life measures, but each comes with its own challenges. Lower costs can sometimes mean concerns about safety, healthcare access , or air quality, and, as such, people looking to relocate should research the latest travel advisories from the US State Department before moving. And even where dining and entertainment are inexpensive, buying a home may still be costly. All prices have been converted to US dollars, and city populations are sourced from United Nations data, unless otherwise noted. Because the UN uses a standardized definition of city boundaries, its 2025 estimates may differ from official city or metro-area population figures. Read on to learn more about these places, including India's "Pink City" and a Colombian city set against the dramatic landscape of the Andes. Accra, Ghana Accra Skyline. Cyrus Wireko Wiredu/Getty Images Population: 5.6 million (2025) Known for: Ghana is one of West Africa's fastest-growing countries, and its capital, Accra, has become a lively landing spot for expats from around the world. Many make their homes in central neighborhoods like East Legon, drawn by the city's coastal setting, beach culture, and growing business and creative scenes. Average monthly rent for a one-bedroom home in the city center: $679.15 Average cost to buy a 1,000-square-foot home in the city center: $264,920 Monthly costs for a single person (excluding housing): $762.10 Monthly costs for a family of four (excluding housing): $2,841.0 Cost of a cappuccino: $4.43 Cost of a three-course meal for two (excluding drinks): $51.14 Monthly cost of a gym membership : $71.43 Someone who lives there said: "Ghana is not a typical expat destination unless you get a well-paying job there or go as a volunteer. Based on my own experience, though, I would recommend it," Elin, the travel blogger behind A Taste of Slow, told Nomad Girl. Bogotá, Colombia Bogotá, Colombia. cesarrosphoto/Getty Images Population: 10.6 million (2025) Known for: Bogotá, Colombia's capital and largest city, is a vibrant, multicultural city set high in the Andes. It is especially known for La Candelaria, its historic district of cobblestone streets and 17th- and 18th-century Spanish colonial and republican-style architecture. While Bogotá is popular with digital nomads and expats, visitors should be aware of the US State Department's travel advisory for Colombia (Level 3 - Reconsider Travel) and take precautions against street crime. Average monthly rent for a one-bedroom home in the city center: $752.16 Average cost to buy a 1,000-square-foot home in the city center: $245,310 Monthly costs for a single person (excluding housing): $678.30 Monthly costs for a family of four (excluding housing): $2,449.90 Cost of a cappuccino: $2.44 Cost of a three-course meal for two (excluding drinks): $40.25 Monthly cost of a gym membership : $32.27 Someone who lives there said: "We're a lot more active," Jennifer Jamali, who moved to Bogotá from Texas in 2025, told Business Insider. "And because we're saving more, the pressure we put on ourselves has gone down, the quality of life is better, and we're having better experiences." Braga, Portugal Braga, Portugal BrasilNut1/Getty Images Population: 105,073 (2025) Known for: Braga is home to the University of Minho and has the feel of a small college town. With numerous churches and cathedrals, Braga is often called the "Portuguese Rome" and nicknamed the "City of Archbishops." Average monthly rent for a one-bedroom home in the city center: $925.43 Average cost to buy a 1,000-square-foot home in the city center: $233,670 Monthly costs for a single person (excluding housing): $713.70 Monthly costs for a family of four (excluding housing): $2,590.9 Cost of a cappuccino: $1.91 Cost of a three-course meal for two (excluding drinks): $48.04 Monthly cost of a gym membership : $45.48 Someone who lives there said: "I tell you what, I could not recreate this kind of life back in Napa. It's half the cost, and you can live well," Bob, a retired military lawyer from California, told International Living. Chiang Mai, Thailand Landmark pagoda in Doi Inthanon National Park at Chiang Mai, Thailand. tawatchaiprakobkit/Getty Images Population: 627,000 (2025) Known for: With temperatures between 59° and 97° Fahrenheit year-round, the largest city in northern Thailand is a tropical paradise. The city is renowned for its ornately decorated ancient temples and its sprawling night market, which features local crafts, street food, and other knick-knacks. events.title: I left my husband and 3 kids for the first time for a work conference. I added 2 days at the end for some solo travel.
events.summary: The author got to do some exploring after her work conference. Courtesy of Kris Ann Valdez At almost 38, I took my first solo trip and worried about navigating everything on my own. I learned that traveling alone made me more responsible, and I relished the time to myself. After years of planning family trips, following only my own interests felt freeing. I'm almost 38 years old, and I just took my first solo trip for a work conference in Dover, Delaware, this September. For a few months leading up to the trip, every time I thought about the logistics and emotions of leaving my kids , I felt a tight knot of anxiety. I was also nervous about traveling by myself to a large conference where the only person I knew was a work connection I'd only ever met via email. When I visualized taking this trip, it was odd how much less anxious I felt when I inserted one or more of my kids, my husband, or a friend into the narrative. The idea of taking care of another person, or simply having company, seemed easier and less intimidating than spending that time alone, thinking only about myself. I also thought about all the times I'd forgotten a phone charger or toothbrush and how often I'd relied on others when traveling. I feared I was just too codependent to take a trip by myself and enjoy it. While solo traveling, the author was able to think only about her own interests. Courtesy of Kris Ann Valdez Navigating without anyone else was better than I expected I flew a red-eye from Phoenix to Philadelphia, then summoned an Uber for the 1.5-hour drive to Dover. Before I left, I messaged two girlfriends and asked whether they always chose female Uber drivers to feel safer when traveling alone. They told me no, but they used some of Uber's other safety precautions, like sharing their location with someone. Before I left, I turned these features on. Thankfully, I felt comfortable in all of my rideshare scenarios and navigated to each place with relative ease. I will admit I'm often forgetful, prone to losing my room key, and I struggle with running late . I was especially concerned about keeping my electronics charged, as my husband or teen son often handles that. But I found I was surprisingly more responsible when it was all on me. Over the course of six days, I was never late to meetings, never lost anything important, and never let my phone die. She stayed in Wilmington, Delaware, called "chateau country," and got to explore several beautiful estates and gardens. Courtesy of Kris Ann Valdez I wasn't lonely like I expected to be Since I was going to a conference , I knew I'd be surrounded by people every day, but I might still feel alone since they were strangers to me. While there were definitely awkward moments when I stood on the outskirts of conversations, I'm relatively chatty and friendly and was able to connect with others. My prior work connection turned out to be lovely in person as well, which definitely helped. I also basked in the alone time in my hotel each evening. As a busy working mom , I hardly ever watch movies or have time to myself to do whatever I want, so I selected a long movie I'd wanted to see for a long time, caught up on work, and listened to an audiobook. I got to enjoy doing things I love without having to check in with anyone else Perhaps the best part of solo traveling came at the end, when I spent two additional days after the conference exploring nearby Wilmington and the surrounding area, nicknamed America's "Chateau Country." I felt like I'd woken up in Europe. In total, I toured three elaborate du Pont family mansions and sprawling gardens, visited an art museum, breakfasted at the iconic Hotel Du Pont, and returned to Longwood Gardens, which I remembered vividly from my childhood. No one whined at me that they were tired, bored, or hungry. I didn't have to chase a toddler through the gardens or change plans because someone decided they were fed up with all this American history. Getting to indulge in the things that interest me most made me realize I was pretty good company. I took my time ogling over presidential fine china and Tiffany glass and lingering over historians' stories of hand-painted murals and family trees. I discovered that I liked hanging out with myself and that it's much easier than family travel. Besides, I made friends as I went, so I was never really lonely. Would I solo travel again? Absolutely. events.title: Clever database, but can it run Doom?
events.summary: Security All Security Cyber-crime Patches Research CSO Off-Prem All Off-Prem Edge and IoT Channel PaaS and IaaS SaaS On-Prem All On-Prem Systems Storage Networks HPC Personal Tech Cx0 Public Sector Software All Software AI and ML Applications Databases DevOps OS Platforms Virtualization Offbeat All Offbeat Columnists Science BOFH Legal Site News About Us Special Features All Special Features Cybersecurity Month 2026 VMware Explore 2026 Cloud Infrastructure Month 2026 HPE: AI Explainers Agentic AI The Future of the Datacenter AWS:Reinvent Nvidia GTC Supercomputing Month Computex 2026 AI Infrastructure Month 2026 The State of Storage 2026 RSA Conference Vendor Voice All Vendor Voice Modernizing Financial Services with FIS and AWS Barco Infinidat Everpure Rubrik Make it real with Capgemini and AWS Money Movement Hub ZTE Nutanix: Scale Kubernetes. Not Chaos. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Reg hack learns the meaning of 'Be careful what you wish for' Spies, prime ministers, and balls: The BBC Domesday project @ 40 now Flight delayed? So are these codec updates 1 day ago Erase social media tomorrow? Brits say yes 3 days ago YouTube lunatic designed and 3D printed a working mechanical calculator 3 days ago Drunk Van Halen fan called Microsoft support and demanded to speak to Gates 3 days ago "Can it run Doom?" now applies to databases, as the author of DOOMQL has released a far more visually accurate port. There's a saying: "Be careful what you wish for." In 2025, we wrote a piece about a database boffin coming up with a version of Doom that was written in SQL. It was neat, but the visuals were nearer to 3D Monster Maze than to the 90s pixel blaster. We commented, "If persuading SQL to do the entire rendering pipeline is a 'bad idea,' we cannot wait for a terrible one." And so here we are. The author, Lukas Vogel, has been at it again and ported both Doom's game logic and renderer to SQL, running it in a database. Python handles timing, keyboard input, and bitmap display, but the rest comes from SQL queries and the CedarDB database. DOOMQL was an undeniably impressive thing. However, Vogel told The Register , "Someone on Hacker News complained last year when I did the first iteration that that one was more Wolfenstein-like because I used raycasting instead of BSP-tree traversal which was *the thing* that made Doom revolutionary. "So I obviously couldn't let that stand." Which brings us to SQLDoom. Doom, ported to SQL. In his blog , Vogel noted the ground rules for the port. Unlike DOOMQL, this had to look like real Doom. The rendering had to be purely SQL-based: "the only acceptable SQL output is a table or a bitmap encoding exact RGB values for every pixel," and the game loop also had to be purely SQL-based. Vogel told us, "I was very thrilled to find out that porting the real Doom was a) feasible and b) the performance was actually *better* than the much more barebones approach from last year! "Also, at some point I started actually playing it for fun in my free time, which is still a very strange feeling. I intended it as a tech demo, but it just feels like the real Doom, even though it doesn't share a single line of code with any existing Doom port. So I wanted to see how far I could take it. "In the end, I even got deathmatch to work." According to Vogel, the game is perfectly playable on his laptop (using a Ryzen 7 7840U ), and multiplayer games can be played online using EU and US servers. We found the server performance a little sluggish – likely more due to the servers than the port – although getting SQL to jump through these hoops is something that, only a few short years ago, would be unimaginable. It's worth keeping in mind that this is a thinly veiled demonstration of the capabilities of CedarDB. It's a compiling database system where complex queries are eventually compiled to machine code. Still, it's hard not to get swept up in Vogel's enthusiasm and the fact that this is Doom… running in a database. Certainly this is a lot more fun than recreating yet another online store for yet another interminable keynote.

events.title: Nitrite-free bacon sales boom in UK amid fears over curing chemicals
events.summary: Shoppers are switching from traditional product despite little evidence alternative is safer Bacon has long been a favourite of carnivores, but there is growing consumer concern about the health risks posed by nitrites, chemicals used to cure meats. While many experts argue there is no evidence processed meat made without nitrites is safer, retailers have responded to consumer concerns by offering “nitrite-free” products to meet demand. Denhay, the Devon hand- dry-cured bacon specialist, has launched two new back bacon lines in 570 Tesco stores from 21 September – Made Without Nitrites Smoked Back Bacon and Made Without Nitrites Unsmoked Back Bacon (both 200g), both priced at £4. Waitrose has doubled its Made Without Nitrites range in the past year, with sales up more than 34%. Sales of its British roast and honey roast hams have risen more than 70% since launching in May, and its unsmoked back bacon is up 22%. Data from Worldpanel by Numerator shows nitrite-free bacon growing steadily while conventional bacon declines, and its share of the fresh bacon category has risen steadily from a small base. In the 52 weeks to 6 September 2026, nitrite-free spend reached £34.8m (up 11.4% year on year) and volumes were up to 2.2m kg (up 8.0%), while spend and volume for conventional bacon was 9.2% and 4.9%, respectively. Emer Lowry, a nutritionist at Waitrose, said: “As our customers pay closer attention to on-pack ingredient lists, providing options without added nitrites gives shoppers more choice without compromising on flavour and taste.” Marlene Godwin, the managing director of Denhay, said the move was prompted by retailers and shoppers rather than the producer. “We definitely don’t want to be telling people what to eat. This is about giving bacon lovers choice, not replacement. Retailers were saying customers want this, can you provide it? She added: “I can’t speak for shoppers, but I think health consciousness is driving it, and consumers are more interested. One of the things people said to me was, why not convert everything? Our customers still love traditional cure, but we’re offering another choice.” Sodium and potassium nitrates and nitrites are chemicals that are often used to preserve or “cure” meat. Nitrates, which contain one nitrogen and three oxygens atoms, can be converted by bacteria into nitrites, which contain one nitrogen and two oxygen atoms. Nitrites help to prevent the growth of microbes, including harmful bacteria, and can enhance the flavour and pink colour of meat products. People do not consume these chemicals only through eating meat – nitrates are also provided by vegetables, in particular leafy greens. The Food Standards Agency (FSA) says the key difference is that when nitrates or nitrites are consumed as part of protein-rich foods such as meat, they are converted into chemicals known as nitrosamines, which are thought to be harmful to health. “Vegetables provide nitrates alongside beneficial nutrients such as vitamin C, polyphenols and fibre. These nutrients help to reduce the formation of harmful nitrosamines,” the FSA adds The World Health Organization’s cancer agency classes processed meat as a group 1 carcinogen , the same category as tobacco, though the known link between processed meat and cancer cannot be directly attributed to nitrites. Research suggests eating about 50g of processed meat a day , roughly two rashers of bacon, is linked to a 16% higher relative risk of colorectal cancer. The FSA says no single component of processed meat has been identified as the cause , and there is no definitive evidence that nitrites directly cause cancer. The FSA also says there is no evidence that processed meats made without nitrate or nitrite additives are safer . It adds that removing them can create food safety challenges, because they help prevent the growth of dangerous bacteria and must be replaced by other methods of preservation. Gabriela Peacock, a nutritionist and founder of GP Nutrition , said: “People are much more interested in what is actually in their food now. They are turning packets over, reading ingredient lists and looking for products that feel a little less processed. If someone enjoys bacon or ham but sees an option made without added nitrates, it can feel like a very easy, positive swap, without having to change the way they eat completely.” Peacock said nitrite-free products are often more expensive. “That may be because they are made by smaller producers, use different curing methods or have a shorter shelf life. They may also use higher-welfare meat or more expensive ingredients. Sometimes, of course, you are paying for the premium positioning and packaging too,” she said. She added: “The most expensive option is not automatically the healthiest, just as ‘nitrate-free’ does not give a product a magic health halo.

events.title: UAE may halt UK investments after Manchester City guilty verdict
events.summary: Premier League’s actions would ‘have an influence on the bilateral state relationship’, Emirati officials said The United Arab Emirates has reportedly warned the government it could cancel big investments in the UK after Manchester City were found guilty by an independent commission. Emirati officials said “the Premier League’s actions” would “have an influence on the bilateral state relationship”, according to Bloomberg. Elsewhere, the Telegraph said the UAE is threatening to withdraw a multibillion-pound investment in a Silicon Valley-style Oxbridge tech hub. The Premier League brought 115 charges against the club for breaches of financial rules between 2009 and 2018. Of those charges, 114 were upheld by an independent commission in September, which described City’s activities as a “sham” multiple times, adding that its witnesses used at the hearing were “dishonest.” The Telegraph also reports that the City chair, Khaldoon Al Mubarak, met Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary, in Downing Street two weeks before the Premier League announced its decision. On Thursday, Downing Street said the guilty verdict against City was “serious”, after Andy Burnham was accused of making a “frankly extraordinary” intervention in support of the football club’s owners. A No 10 spokesperson issued the statement after the prime minister said he would be “really concerned” to see the current owners sell up. The Conservative shadow sport minister, Louie French, had accused the prime minister of “publicly backing the owners” amid an investigation into the club’s funding over recent years, describing his comments as “frankly extraordinary”. Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters Asked by the BBC earlier this week if he was worried about the current owners selling the club, Burnham said: “I would be really concerned to lose them. “They’ve been such a huge partner in the building of modern Manchester, obviously, the building of Manchester City into the global force that it is.” Asked also if his dealings with the club would stand up to scrutiny, he said: “I do actually thank the City Football Group and the wider ownership for the money that they didn’t just put into the Etihad [Stadium] and the campus around it but also into the city – but yes, of course.” The Premier League said an independent commission found City arranged “sham” commercial deals with a number of its sponsors during the period, which were part of a disguised funding scheme whereby those companies were required to pay only a portion of the relevant sponsorship fees. The commission found that the remainder was funded by Abu Dhabi United Group Investment & Development Ltd (ADUG), which owned the club. City lodged an appeal along with a short statement, saying the commission’s ruling contained “clear material errors of law, principle and fact, and is unsafe”. Insisting on its innocence, the club reiterated it had filed “a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence [that] exists in support of all of its positions” on Thursday evening.

events.title: 'Bond King' Bill Gross shares his best investment ever — and the brutal bet that lost him 50% in a month
events.summary: Bill Gross founded bond giant Pimco. Mary Hurlbut/Stu News Laguna Bill Gross shared his best investment and worst investing error with Business Insider. The billionaire "Bond King" said his bet on pipeline stocks has paid off handsomely. The Pimco cofounder said he lost 50% of his savings in a month when he bet on Treasurys in 1969. Bill Gross says he made the best investment of his career only a few years ago, while his worst investing error dates back nearly six decades. The billionaire cofounder of bond giant Pimco told Business Insider by email this week that his shrewdest wager to date was the purchase of a portfolio of master limited partnership (MLP) pipeline stocks around three years ago. Pointing to Western Midstream Partners as an example, he trumpeted the "enormous" tax benefits of these types of stocks. Specifically, Gross said their distributions are largely treated as return of capital instead of dividends, so they're only taxed upon sale, and those deferred tax liabilities can be erased if the returns are passed down at death on a stepped-up basis . "Yields are twice similar corporate pipelines," Gross said. Western pays a dividend yield of over 8%, whereas Kinder Morgan pays around 4%. "Higher oil prices have been an extra boost," Gross added. The US-Iran conflict has fueled a roughly 60% rise in crude prices since the start of this year, generating higher storage and distribution fees for energy infrastructure companies. Biggest misfire As for his gravest investing mistake, Gross told Business Insider it was buying 30-year Treasurys after opening his personal account in 1969. "Lost 50% in 1 month," he wrote. Gross — whose nickname is the "Bond King" because he grew Pimco's flagship Total Return Fund from scratch to $270 billion over nearly 30 years — previously described the episode to Financial Advisor as an "expensive lesson about the dangers of leverage." He told the magazine that he bought Treasury bonds with 10-to-1 leverage just months before starting at Pimco, using $10,000 he'd made playing blackjack. Treasurys promptly tanked and "wiped out half of my savings," Gross said. He added that it was the biggest mistake in percentage terms of his career, and it taught him that "gambling belongs at the casino." A pipeline of returns Gross has been touting MLP pipeline stocks for several years . In October 2024, he underscored on his blog that deferred taxes on their dividends allow investors to fully reinvest them and juice their compounding, potentially boosting an 8% return to 9% or 10% over a five-to-10 year period. He's also highlighted that mutual funds are limited in how much they can invest in LP stocks, which helps to shore up their distribution yields and constrain their valuation multiples relative to peers. My latest in the Financial Times. For readers looking for specific recommendations, I continue to like MLP pipelines with their high tax-deferred dividends (7–9%) and future infrastructure prospects due to AI, AI information centers, electricity demand, and the natural gas needed… — Bill Gross (@real_bill_gross) July 16, 2025 Western's total return, with dividends reinvested, has exceeded 200% over the past five years. Energy Transfer LP, Plains All American Pipeline LP, and MPLX, an offshoot of Marathon Petroleum, have posted similar gains. Other peers, such as Hess Midstream LP and Enterprise Products Partners LP, have performed more modestly. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: High-tech vehicles are driving up auto repair costs for shops and consumers
events.summary: A tour of an auto repair shop in Brooklyn, New York, revealed the investments small shops have to make to keep up with increasingly sophisticated cars. Agreements between automakers and repair shops are meant to guarantee shops have access to needed parts, tools and software. But accessing those tools can require significant and repeated investments and upgrades. Motor repair bills have outpaced inflation since 2019, and mechanics said fast-changing technology is partly to blame. Increasingly sophisticated vehicles are forcing repair shops to spend more on computers, software and calibration equipment — costs that mechanics say are reaching consumers. Auto mechanic Ralph Czeisler in Brooklyn, New York, said the rapid pace of technological change is forcing him to invest more time and money just to perform even basic repairs, and he is having to pass those costs on to consumers. "Every year, I update all my computers," said Czeisler, who owns Emil's All-Tire in the Gravesend neighborhood. "I have multiple computers for domestic, Asian, European cars, and it's very costly. Every year they make changes, and it costs more money and more money. And it's getting very challenging." Many mechanics across the U.S. face the same problems, said Greg Brannon, director of automotive engineering at AAA. "The repairs of these vehicles are so sophisticated now and almost always require a laptop," he said. Sometimes it's a laptop dedicated to that brand of vehicle, he added. The shop also needs subscriptions to software and data services to perform repairs on the car, which can be purchased for varying degrees of time, ranging from a few hours to a year. Those recurring costs can be difficult for a smaller shop to absorb. "It has become increasingly financially difficult for independent shops to be able to service all makes and models," Brannon said. Czeisler said he is passing at least some of these costs on to consumers. "The consumer is getting the shaft at the end of the day because they're getting offset by the monetary cost as well," he said. Overall, repair costs have risen about 60% from January 2019 to August 2026, according to the St. Louis Federal Reserve . That is almost twice the 32% increase in overall inflation over the same period. The data doesn't indicate exactly why prices are rising. But research suggests technological progress is driving up costs in at least some cases. A 2023 AAA study found that calibrating advanced driver-assistance systems, or ADAS, can raise the cost of a collision repair by 37.6%. Replacing a cracked windshield, for example, used to be a matter of ordering a new windshield and installing it. Now, the camera behind the windshield needs to be calibrated, said Ariella Czeisler, Ralph's daughter who also works in the shop. The camera behind the windshield is one of at least a few on a vehicle, depending on the model. These cameras and sensors usually support the ADAS and active safety features that automakers have been adding. A single calibration machine costs about $28,000, according to an invoice the shop provided to CNBC. The necessary computer that comes with it is another $12,000. A total array can cost up to $90,000. On top of that, there are target boards mounted to the machine that are designed to calibrate specific cameras. Each of those boards can run hundreds or even thousands of dollars for more premium brands, Ariella Czeisler said. "God forbid we don't calibrate the windshield and that camera is malfunctioning," she said. "The car can brake unexpectedly and cause an incident from the rear. We don't want to be liable for that." As vehicles and other devices have become more technologically sophisticated, a "right to repair" movement has gained force. Broadly, the idea is that consumers and small shops should have access to the tools, parts and information needed to repair their own electronic devices, farm equipment and cars, among other things. Lawmakers at state and federal levels have proposed legislation meant to support these goals — to varying degrees of success. Since 2014, trade groups representing both automakers and auto mechanics have made agreements meant to ensure that repair shops have access to the same data, parts and tools as bigger dealerships. "Generally the information is available to repair shops, both dealer and independent necessary to repair vehicles," AAA's Brannon said, though he said there can be exceptions. There is a task force to which shops can report problems or concerns to automakers. Brannon said that the vast majority of claims revolve around costs and complexity around accessing data. Czeisler said his main problem is usually the cost and hassle of accessing information or upgrading computers to keep them current. Some of the repairs that are becoming more expensive are virtually as old as fuel-burning vehicles themselves.

events.title: Private capital is reshaping Hollywood moviemaking
events.summary: Private investors are financing independent films as Hollywood’s funding mix shifts. Private backers say they can make decisions faster than traditional studios and pursue different types of projects to capture new audiences. As the cost to make movies rises, studios and private investors alike are racing to snap up intellectual property and get new storylines to the big screen. At the Toronto International Film Festival last month, audiences saw "Wicked" star Cynthia Erivo return to the big screen for her newest movie, "Prima Facie." Behind the scenes, there was a notable difference. While "Wicked" was a massive Universal undertaking, Erivo's new movie was produced in part by Camelback Productions, a smaller Hollywood venture aiming to fund independent film, according to CEO Anita Verma-Lallian. She's one of many private investors who are betting big on Hollywood as the moviegoing landscape shifts and a handful of indie films catch fire. "It's a different point of view to invest in these projects," Verma-Lallian said. "It's been so hard for people that are not in Hollywood to get into the industry ... We've been able to fund stories that otherwise would have had a hard time getting greenlit by the traditional studio system." Camelback has also produced films "Doin' It" and "Runner," with stars such as Lilly Singh and Owen Wilson. Big blockbuster films such as this year's "The Odyssey" and "The Devil Wears Prada 2" are still the domain of legacy Hollywood studios. But with the number of annual releases dwindling, and with forthcoming consolidation among major players Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery , there's growing opportunity for smaller production companies to hit it big. And while the business of making movies is still generally capital-intensive, recent breakouts including "Backrooms" and "Obsession" have found success on lower budgets. To thread the needle, private capital is buying into production companies, acquiring the infrastructure and diving deeper into the financing structure of entertainment. For example, private equity firm Silver Lake backs talent agency WME, and Blackstone is behind content studio Candle Media. According to consulting firm AlixPartners' 2026 Media and Entertainment Industry Predictions report , private equity investors in media are growing with precision, especially as studios and audience aggregators increasingly become vertically integrated. While the cost of entry has increased, private investors are eager to own intellectual property and audiences, the report said. "Private equity can build scaled, defensible businesses that profit regardless of which large media player owns the next blockbuster, effectively ensuring a central role in the future media value chain," the report read. And while deep-pocketed companies such as Netflix and Amazon continue to raise the bar for content spend to make or acquire new media, traditional studios are finding new ways to keep pace. An attractive investment opportunity For Verma-Lallian, investing in independent film means that she can complete movies on a much faster timeline than traditional studios can. "A lot of times, if you go through the traditional Hollywood system, it could literally take five to 10 years from the time of inception," she said. "Whereas if you're doing it independently, we've made some movies in as quickly as a year." This can often mean lower production costs and a quicker return on investment. Verma-Lallian, whose background is in real estate investing, said Hollywood has proven to be a largely attractive market for herself and other nontypical private investors looking to diversify their portfolios. She said they're also jumping on the opportunity at a time when existing financing models are weakening. "I think the traditional sources [of financing] are starting to decline, and they're becoming a lot more risk-averse," she said. "I do also believe now with more independent films being funded and going to different pools of capital, you're able to do more." While Verma-Lallian said she doesn't believe private capital will become the primary source of financing in Hollywood, she said the agility of investors can potentially put pressure on the incumbents. "Hollywood is incredibly traditional, and it's very old-fashioned in the way it operates, which always I find so ironic, because ... Hollywood's so progressive, but the way that the studio systems work, it's just a very dated process from my experience," she said. Still, studios and private investors are racing to get new storylines to the big screen. For investors, that means capitalizing on the intellectual property that hasn't already been used, according to Alex Michael, senior managing director at investment firm LionTree. "What is clear to me is that IP has never been more valuable. It's never been harder to find," Michael said at the Financial Times' Business of Entertainment Summit last month.

events.title: I thought I was raising my daughter. Looking back, I think we raised each other.
events.summary: The author was 20 when she had her daughter, who is now 21. Courtesy of the author I became pregnant at 20 and had to leave college and give up my full scholarship. I returned to school while working and raising my daughter, graduating seven years later. My daughter is now 21, and I realize we grew into adulthood together. Growing up as a first-generation immigrant , I understood early how much my parents sacrificed to build a better future for our family. They left everything they knew behind so their children could have opportunities they never had. For me, that meant becoming the first in my family to graduate from college. I graduated from high school with a full college scholarship, and for a while, my life seemed to be unfolding exactly as my parents and I had imagined: college, a degree, a career, marriage, and children — the American dream as we understood it. Then, a month after my 20th birthday, everything changed. I found out I was pregnant. I lost my scholarship My second trimester was difficult, and I ultimately had to leave college in the middle of the semester, which meant losing my full scholarship. Not knowing if, or when, I would be able to return was heartbreaking. But what hurt most was seeing my parents' disappointment. I'll never forget telling my dad I was pregnant and would have to drop out of school . We didn't speak for months. He reminded me how unprepared I was and how quickly the future I had worked so hard to build seemed to be slipping away. My mom was disappointed, too, but remained supportive. The author felt bad about losing her scholarship after everything her parents had done. Courtesy of the author My parents had sacrificed so much to give me an education, and I had always seen graduating from college as a way to honor those sacrifices. I felt I had let them down — and was facing a future I wasn't ready for. I was technically an adult, but I was still learning how to become one. While my peers were navigating college and discovering themselves, I was learning to care for someone who depended on me completely. I was becoming a mother while still becoming myself, and every decision about my future now had to take Samantha into account. People asked if my daughter was my little sister I remember dropping her off at day care and having her classmates ask if I was her sister. The question reminded me just how young I was — and sometimes felt more embarrassing than flattering. I couldn't help but compare our lives to those of her classmates. We didn't have the house with the yard or white picket fence — the traditional symbols of success . For a while, I lived paycheck to paycheck, stretching every dollar to cover day care and make sure Samantha had what she needed, while my friends were enjoying the freedom of their 20s. Over time, I realized that providing for Samantha wasn't about giving her the life I had once imagined. It was about creating a life where she felt secure, supported, and loved. I had to redefine what success looked like — not as the house, career, or financial stability I had once envisioned, but as the ability to keep moving forward when life didn't go according to plan. It took me 7 years to graduate from college With the support of my partner and family, I eventually returned to school while working full time and taking night classes. I had gone from a full scholarship to taking out student loans and financing my education while supporting my daughter. I envisioned graduating in four years, but my path took longer than expected. It took seven years of balancing work, school, motherhood, and countless late nights to finally earn my degree. Having her daughter see her graduate from college was very meaningful for the author. Courtesy of the author Crossing that stage meant far more than finishing college . It was proof that motherhood hadn't erased my dreams or defined the limits of my future. I had kept going, built a career, and created more opportunities for Samantha. Seeing the pride on my parents' faces — and having Samantha there to witness it — made the moment even more meaningful. But I also knew the sacrifices hadn't been mine alone. My parents had sacrificed for me, and Samantha had sacrificed precious time with her mother. Moments we could have spent playing or simply being together were sometimes replaced by my late-night studying. She was too young to understand why I was always buried in books, but she knew I was working toward something. Years later, she told me she remembered how hard I worked and how proud she was of me. Hearing that stayed with me. I was her mom before being her friend Being a young mom sometimes made our age gap feel small enough that I wanted to be her friend. But I had to remind myself that before I could be her friend, I had to be her mother. That meant saying no when I knew she would be upset, setting curfews, making sure her schoolwork was done, and holding boundaries even when it would have been easier not to. Now, as Samantha celebrates her 21st birthday, I see the young woman she has become: independent, thoughtful, and full of dreams of her own. Our conversations have evolved from childhood questions to honest discussions about relationships, careers, friendships, and the challenges of navigating adulthood. Watching her grow has made me realize that, in many ways, we've grown up together. The author's daughter is now 21. Courtesy of the author Somewhere along the way, something unexpected happened: Samantha and I became friends — not because I stopped being her mother, but because I never did. Today, one of my favorite parts of our relationship is the life we share. We travel, explore new places, spend time in nature, and share a love of reading. Some of my favorite moments are the simplest — reading side by side, laughing, sharing TikToks, or calling just to catch up. She chooses to spend time with me, not because she has to, but because she wants to. That means more to me than I could have imagined. For years, I believed becoming a mother at 20 meant my life had gone off course and that I had failed the future my parents had sacrificed to give me. Eventually, I understood that their sacrifice was never about giving me a specific life — it was about giving me the freedom to build my own. Motherhood forced me to grow up while giving me the opportunity to grow alongside Samantha. I thought I was raising her, but in many ways, we were raising each other. events.title: The US Navy needs more ships. The workers building them are winning bigger paychecks.
events.summary: "I think overall, it'll bring the industry back to where it needs to be," one union official said of recent contract wins. US Navy photo by Mass Communication Specialist 2nd Class Kenneth Melseth Shipbuilding workers in California and Maine won big union contracts for more pay and better benefits. Union members said the gains would help attract and keep more skilled workers. Shipbuilders need experienced workers to meet the Navy's needs for more ships. The US Navy needs more from the American shipbuilding industry, which depends on skilled workers. Recent contract wins by shipbuilding unions in California and Maine are delivering better pay, better benefits, and more structured approaches to the introduction of new technologies into shipyards. Shipbuilders and union leaders told Business Insider the improvements would help attract and retain skilled workers as the Navy and industry race to rebuild and revive America's shipbuilding capacity. "I think overall, it'll bring the industry back to where it needs to be," International Association of Machinists and Aerospace Workers Eastern Territory Coordinator George Edwards said, adding that the new contracts between the workers' unions and shipbuilding companies have "set the trend for where you're going to see things going in the next couple years in shipbuilding." Last week, IAM union members at General Dynamics NASSCO in San Diego, which specializes in building auxiliary vessels for the Navy, ratified a three-year agreement that delivers  wage increases , improvements to retirement benefits, floating time off, and worker protections. Over 800 workers will receive a 10% wage increase in the first year, followed by 5% in the second and 4% in the third. More money helps workers grappling with the rising cost of living in San Diego, which is nearly 50% higher than the national average. "It's also helping the company minimize the turnover," IAM Western Territory General Vice President Robert Martinez explained, by reducing "losses of skilled workers to other shipyards because they weren't paying as competitively." The successful negotiation came on the heels of a similar contract win in Bath, Maine, last month. Over 4,500 workers at Bath Iron Works ratified a contract giving them a 17% wage increase in the first year and a 4% bump in the following four years, as well as stronger retirement benefits. Hiring and keeping skilled workers Skilled trade workers have left shipbuilding for competing industries. Staff photo by Brianna Soukup/Portland Press Herald via Getty Images Across the US, shipyards have lost employees due to pay and working conditions. The attrition rates have been especially high among workers early in their careers , as shipbuilders lose talent to competitors — both inside and outside the industry — that offer better pay or benefits or a less demanding environment. Senior Navy leaders have argued that shipbuilding wages need to be competitive with other sectors of the economy, quality-of-life improvements are essential to recruiting and retaining workers, and the workforce must be preserved. "I think this is really an issue of wages , to be honest," John Phelan, the Navy secretary until late April, said last year. He said that if a welder makes the same money they might earn at a Buc-ee's convenience store or at Amazon, but instead spends most of their day working inside tight, uncomfortable spaces, "it's hard to get that person to want to do that job." Hung Cao, the acting secretary of the Navy, said during a May congressional hearing that "we need to get this industrial base going," adding that "we need to build ships, and we need to do it yesterday, so we will make sure that we protect our workers." Work in shipbuilding? We'd like to hear from you. Business Insider is reporting on the challenges and opportunities facing America's shipyards, from hiring and pay to automation, production delays, and efforts to build the Navy's future fleet. Contact reporter Chris Panella at cpanella@businessinsider.com . Union members told Business Insider that to retain skilled talent, shipyards have to not only pay well but also demonstrate that the job can be a long-term career with applicable benefits, healthcare, flexibility, and retirement. Keeping those workers raises the overall experience level inside shipyards, which has declined significantly since the end of the Cold War as the industry has been hollowed out. Huntington Ingalls Industries, America's largest shipbuilder, said last fall that it had invested more heavily in wages and, in turn, seen "an increase in experienced hires." In March, the union-represented workers at HII's Ingalls Shipbuilding division negotiated an immediate base-wage increase of 18% or more, with total wage growth of 35% to 47% through 2031. Across the US shipbuilding industry, the average worker's experience level is a fraction of what it was in decades past. Within HII's shipbuilding division, the average electrical supervisor in the mid-1990s had more than 20 years on the job. As of February last year, that had dropped to about four and a half years. "That's a lot of lost experience," Tom Moore, HII's senior vice president of government relations, said at the time. At Bath Iron Works, "maybe three-quarters of the shipyard has got about six years or less of experience," IAM District 4 Assistant Directing Business Representative Chris Wiers told Business Insider. In a few years, with retention, they'll have greater seniority and be able to raise the baseline expertise of the workforce. In a statement, President of General Dynamics Bath Iron Works Charles F. Krugh said that the contract "demonstrates our commitment to retaining our experienced workforce and to our mission of building the highest-quality surface combatants that protect our country and our families." During contract negotiations, the union at NASSCO saw membership jump from 21% to 67% as more workers voiced concerns. "There has been a change of culture in the shop. It's becoming more of a union shop, and I think you feel the solidarity," IAM Western Territory Special Representative Luis Silvas said. "There's a certain youth and passion that comes from believing in themselves, understanding that they're skilled workers." The push to revitalize US shipbuilding Navy officials and shipbuilding experts have pointed to worker problems as the core issue to solve. DoD photo by US Air Force Staff Sgt. Jack Sanders Higher pay is only one part of a much broader effort to rebuild and strengthen the nation's shipbuilding workforce. Other actions include investments in infrastructure, targeted hiring campaigns, expanded training pipelines, and transportation solutions like gas and public transport cards. Transportation has been make-or-break for some workers, who may not live near the yards where they work. events.title: I used a fake Craigslist ad to test my business idea. The reaction gave me the proof I needed.
events.summary: Founder and CEO Alison Donnally says three family tragedies inspired her unique business idea. Photo courtesy of Alison Donnally Alison Donnally founded JoeyCo to connect aging adults and college students. She tested the idea by listing her parents' home on Craigslist. The results inspired a business blending student housing with elder care. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Alison Donnally , the founder and CEO of JoeyCo . It has been edited for length and clarity. Prior to starting JoeyCo , I worked in strategy and business development within healthcare. That started me down a path of ideating better solutions for elderly patients. But personal tragedies within my own family are what really confirmed for me that a business like JoeyCo was needed. Many older people want to retain their independence. I've had a lot of family history with this pattern of aging independently, living alone, and everything working out fine, until suddenly it doesn't. I've seen firsthand the safety of that situation changing very quickly. So, I started JoeyCo in 2024 and created a new category of business, one that blends housing and healthcare . Three of my family members experienced mental and physical health declines while living alone My husband's grandmother was isolated in a nursing home during COVID. Before this, she was social and deeply engaged in her community and civic life. Her mental and physical health declined rapidly while living alone. She felt isolated and lonely . This all really changed her health trajectory. She experienced several falls and didn't seem to have enough help. Then there was my uncle, a lifelong trucker. His dream of owning a rural plot of land in Tennessee eventually turned dangerous when he was found disoriented, driving down the wrong side of the road. Living that rural dream made it harder for our family to understand how his progression with what turned out to be dementia was really evolving. After that, my cousins moved him closer to where they were living in upstate New York, where he received memory care until he passed. Finally, my aunt, who once happily lived alone in a retirement community, fell in her shower, and there was no one there to help her for several hours. With all these elderly family members living alone and independently, their safety became an issue, and not a good situation for them. JoeyCo emerged as an answer to a question We wondered how we could keep older people independent and in their own homes as long as possible. Our solution is to help connect students, whom we call joeys, with older adults (hosts), creating a symbiotic relationship where both parties benefit. Students find affordable housing and employment that fit their college schedules, while older adults get the support they need to live their best years at home. This increases what I call their 'joyspan,' their ability to live vibrant and happy lives. However, housing regulations have been one of the biggest challenges we've had to help our hosts navigate. Launching this business took a lot of research, legal assistance, and AI The hosts' role blends landlord and employer into one, and so, understanding how to do this safely matters. I spent a long time initially trying to find the expert on this intersection between housing and employment, but after much research into how we could make the business work, we became the experts. We work closely with a law firm, so everything we do is attorney-reviewed. We also work strategically with AI , helping us reduce our costs by creating templates for different regions, showing hosts what the regulations are in their area that they should be aware of. We don't offer legal advice, and we are not insurance agents. However, we can point you in the right direction on all these fronts. We are not profitable yet, but we will be We're funding and financing the business unprofitably right now, but once we get a bit bigger, we will be able to finance our operations and turn a profit. We are a small but growing team of seven. We're creating rental income for the host, enabling the household to get affordable help, making sure the student gets an affordable home, and running the business. I earn a salary, but it's not comparable to what I've earned in the past. I take a salary mostly to afford childcare , so I can focus on the business and bring my best self to running it. I want to support every vulnerable older person wanting to live independently, but our services aren't for everyone. For example, we might not be the right fit for cases where the host has severe dementia. So, as much as we care and want to support that person, the depth and complexity of that person have to be balanced with real care and a real safety infrastructure. My advice to others wanting to start a unique business is to figure out if there's a demand Ask yourself, would others want this business? The first step I took was figuring out if there was a proof of concept. I made a Craigslist listing for my parents' house to see if someone would want to live in their extra bedroom. I got so many bites. I had to tell everyone, no, this isn't a real opportunity yet, but I appreciate your interest because you are validating this business idea I have. It's really challenging to be an American right now. There's the cost of living, the housing crisis, and the isolation we all experience because we're all looking at screens and disconnected from life a bit. With this business, we've seen hosts and joeys cultivate true friendships that dive into their humanness and the complexities of our world so seamlessly across generations. events.title: ‘I was making no money’: Travel agent side hustle promoted by influencers criticised over fees
events.summary: Would-be marketers enticed by online talk of entering a world of travel and easy cash find that the reality is rather different M onths before she entered the Love Island villa, the content creator Yasmin Hadlow promised viewers of her online videos that they could “catch flights and get paid mid-air”. All they had to do, she said, was send her a direct message with the word “freedom”. The 23-year-old is among several influencers and celebrities, including the former Geordie Shore star Vicky Pattison, working for PlanNet Marketing, which recruits people to work as independent travel agents with a separate US business, InteleTravel. Pattison’s Instagram page, Vickys Vacays, says it helps women “build confidence, income and freedom through a supportive online travel business”. It sounds like a great way to make money. But the Guardian has spoken to seven people who were recruited as InteleTravel agents by PlanNet Marketing reps, not the influencers mentioned above, who said they struggled to make money once sign-up costs and monthly fees were taken into account. Some of them said the people who recruited them encouraged them to sign up as PlanNet Marketing reps and recruit others, and that became their main focus rather than selling holidays. Mark* always wanted to be a travel agent. He was recruited by a PlanNet rep to work with InteleTravel in 2021 when he was 28. He had just been furloughed during Covid, wanted a career change and was looking at different routes to his dream job. He paid InteleTravel a sign-up fee of about £150, plus £30 to £40 a month for access to its booking system and training. Agents earn about 70% of the roughly 10% commission suppliers pay on bookings. So, if they sell £10,000 worth of holidays, the supplier pays out £1,000 in commission and the agent gets £700. After about 18 months working long days, Mark had only made a handful of sales. “I was making no money on the travel side,” he says, adding that the PlanNet rep who recruited him told him “to try recruitment instead, by signing up with PlanNet Marketing”. If you are an InteleTravel agent, joining PlanNet Marketing is optional. Those who do so pay PlanNet Marketing a separate monthly fee of about £14. They then get roughly $4, or about £3, for every new person they recruit as an active travel agent, plus referral bonuses and rank-based payouts as their “downline” (number of recruits) grows. “I ended up with a team of 10 people, but it never felt like me,” Mark says. “The whole point of joining was to be a travel agent, not a recruiter.” PlanNet Marketing’s annual income disclosure statement suggests earnings from recruitment are typically very low. Its most recent figures show average annual earnings across its general base of representatives are about $40. Mark was with InteleTravel and PlanNet Marketing for about two years. “I made about three bookings and maybe £1,000 in commission, but I was paying £32 a month in fees, plus about £100 to sign up,” he says. “That wasn’t because I was bad at it. It’s not set up for people to succeed.” A spokesperson for InteleTravel said: “As with any self-employed business owner, there can be no guarantee of continuous profit and success when starting a business … An unwavering guarantee of significant profit is not a foregone conclusion and cannot be guaranteed, as is the case with any form of self-employment.” The spokesperson said joining fees covered regulatory licensing and memberships, operational insurance, mandatory training and booking systems, to enable travel advisers to make bookings in accordance with the UK’s travel regulatory requirements. InteleTravel offers a 30-day money-back guarantee so agents can cancel for a refund. Any travel commissions earned during that first month are deducted from the returned amount. The company also offers a “first-year profit guarantee”, which pledges to refund the difference if an agent doesn’t earn back their fees in their first 12 months, as long as they meet certain contractual conditions. For example, according to its website, the agent must have “completed one full year of valid adviser status”, purchase branded business cards, create a website, successfully book one completed hotel stay every quarter, and submit their written refund claim within a 30-day window after their one-year anniversary. Shelley, 52, a nurse from Suffolk, signed up to InteleTravel during the pandemic in 2021 after seeing a Facebook advert. She says: “I’d always loved travelling, and with everything shut down during Covid, I thought: ‘Why not build up some knowledge and training for when things reopened?’” She says that after filling out a form, she was approached online by a local PlanNet recruiter advertising support, training and “excellent commission”, before being introduced to the recruiter’s manager (also a PlanNet person) on social media. “It was sold really well – the impression given was that you really couldn’t lose anything,” she says.

events.title: David Ellison just brought in a co-CEO to run his new empire: Meet Ynon Kreiz
events.summary: David Ellison's appointment of Ynon Kreiz as co-CEO of the soon-to-be-merged Paramount Skydance and Warner Bros. Discovery answers a key governance question for the new media empire. Kreiz has earned a reputation as a turnaround man during his time at Mattel and has roots in entertainment. The co-CEOs will be faced with a complex task of merging two behemoth media companies, realizing $6 billion in cost savings and managing $79 billion in debt. David Ellison has spent two years fighting to build his media empire. Now, he's bringing in a heavyweight to help him run it. Ynon Kreiz, outgoing CEO of Mattel , will serve as co-CEO of the combined Paramount Skydance and Warner Bros. Discovery , to be named simply Skydance , when the merger closes on Tuesday. The new entity will unite the storied film studios of Paramount and Warner Bros.; the CBS broadcast network; a sprawling portfolio of pay-TV networks that include CNN, TNT, MTV and BET; and streaming services Paramount+ and HBO Max, all under one roof. The appointment of Kreiz to a top executive position alongside Ellison speaks to a governance question that has surrounded Ellison's aggressive pursuit of the legacy media assets: The tech executive and son of billionaire Larry Ellison can buy it, but can he lead it? Not even 18 months ago, Ellison was the CEO of film production company Skydance with a limited portfolio of hits , namely the Tom Cruise-led Mission: Impossible franchise and "Top Gun: Maverick." By August 2025, he was successfully closing an acquisition of Paramount, a deal worth around $8 billion . Roughly a month later, he started his campaign for WBD, spurring a back-and-forth bidding war that would ultimately result in a deal worth roughly $110 billion on an enterprise basis to merge two of Hollywood's biggest media companies. Kreiz is a 30-year veteran of the media space, arguably best known for ushering "Barbie" to the big screen in 2023. He's earned a reputation as a turnaround man, with roots in entertainment despite his more recent stint in consumer goods. He joins Paramount Skydance on Monday , and becomes co-CEO on Tuesday upon closing. Many on Wall Street have lauded Kreiz for reviving toymaker Mattel through various cost-cutting measures, though others question if his previous entertainment experience is enough to help navigate Skydance through this merger — and how successfully he and Ellison will share the duties. "We view the appointment of Ynon Kreiz positively, as his operating experience and brand/IP focus uniquely position him to help lead the integration of Paramount Skydance and WBD and build the combined business into a best-in-class content and IP platform," said Matthew Condon, analyst at Citizens Bank, in a research note published this week. Ellison's focus will be on the company's long-term strategy, creative vision, technology and capital allocation, and Kreiz will be responsible for the company's day-to-day management and the integration of the combined businesses, the company said in announcing his role. "Kreiz has extensive experience in media and entertainment from before his time at Mattel," Matthew Dolgin, senior equity analyst at Morningstar, wrote in a research note this week. However, "We don't necessarily think he is the best conceivable choice to handle this task." "He undoubtedly is an experienced hand who fills a void that had been present, leaving the firm better positioned with him, in our view, than it was without him," Dolgin wrote. "Though his title is co-CEO, we view Kreiz as a chief operating officer." Prior to his eight-year stint as Mattel CEO, Kreiz was chief executive and chairman of Maker Studios, which was sold to The Walt Disney Co. in 2014. Before that he was the chairman and CEO of Endemol Group, one of the world's largest independent television production companies. Earlier in his career, Kreiz co-founded Fox Kids Group Europe, a children's entertainment company, which was also acquired by Disney in 2002. "It's an excellent choice for Paramount," Eric Handler, managing director and senior media and entertainment analyst at Roth Capital Partners, told CNBC. When Kreiz took the helm at Mattel in 2018, he was the fourth CEO in four years to take control of the toy company. At that time, the company's Fisher-Price, Barbie and American Girl brands were struggling to connect with changing consumer tastes and Mattel was reeling from the recent bankruptcy of Toys R Us. "Mattel had like a four-year revenue downturn, gone from being quite profitable to losing money, and he turned that around in like two years," Handler said. Wall Street analysts told CNBC that Kreiz's experience righting the ship at Mattel will help Skydance navigate a sprawling and complex merger. "He got off to a really great start [at Mattel] because he did some structural improvements," said Gerrick Johnson, equity research analyst at Seaport Research Partners.
