events.title: Rising energy costs add to cost of living for Northern Ireland's consumers
events.summary: Households across Northern Ireland face increasing pressure on the cost of living as energy price hikes have come into effect. Northern Ireland's largest provider of natural gas, SSE Airtricity, increased its prices by almost 19% on Thursday for its 200,000 domestic and small business customers. That means the annual gas bill of a typical household in the greater Belfast and west gas network areas will increase by almost £172. The company said "unprecedented levels of volatility in global energy markets and higher wholesale gas prices" had led to the price rise. Wholesale gas prices in the UK have effectively doubled since the US and Israel began their attack on Iran. Keeping the house warm is particularly important for parents with young children and babies. Lucy Kells is a mum of two in east Belfast on maternity leave. She said she expects the winter months to be difficult because "most people are going to have to have the heating on, especially if you've young kids in the house". "There's no escaping it - everything feels more expensive and it is more expensive." Lucy Kells is a mum of two in east Belfast on maternity leave She added that, despite "budgeting proactively" and "being as careful as you can with savings and credit cards", rising bills mean people's financial situations are out of their control. "You have to cut somewhere else and I already feel we are doing that," she said. Nuala Hyde said she has noticed more people using her branch's free activities to combat the rising cost of living Lucy is one of the parents who attend a weekly baby class at Woodstock Library in east Belfast. Branch manager Nuala Hyde said she has noticed more people using their free activities to combat the rising cost of living. She said: "As well as families, we have lots of older people coming in now to keep warm." "We have people coming in who will stay all day, use the computer, have a chat and stay until closing time sometimes, so it is quite evident that we are providing an essential service at the minute when people are struggling," she added. Ryan McStay said he was "shocked" by the energy price increases Ryan McStay is a final year student at St Mary's University College Belfast, where he is studying to become a primary school teacher. He said he and his flatmates were "shocked" when they received a letter explaining their Firmus energy bills would be rising by 12.5%. "It shouldn't be normalised," he told BBC News NI. Ryan said increases like this exacerbate an already serious cost of living crisis for students like him. "The price of everything is rocketing. You're always second guessing and thinking about how much money have I got." The 21-year-old, who is from Newry, said the cost of living in Northern Ireland means he plans to move abroad after university. "I personally believe the best option for me right now would be to leave the country." Naomi Campbell is an urgent hospice care nurse for Marie Curie Naomi Campbell is an urgent hospice care nurse for Marie Curie. She provides palliative nursing care to patients in their homes. "Many of them are affected by fuel poverty," Naomi said. "I think it is getting worse. People are struggling more, and the problem is that your energy needs increase hugely when you're dying at home. "Somebody is already struggling with the fact that they're dying. To then know that they can't keep their house warm." Naomi said a number of factors contribute to the increased energy needs, including the need to stay warm, different sleeping patterns, and essential medical devices. She said some patients have turned down services that could help improve their quality of life because they can't pay their electricity bills. Terminal illness adds further costs for patients, such as the cost of transport to and from hospital appointments, Naomi added. "The support is limited, there is very little out there. There is no reduction in costs of their electricity, even though their needs are so much higher and essential for their care." Naomi added that Marie Curie have called for the implementation of a "social tariff" for people with terminal illnesses, to ease their financial burden. "It would make such a huge difference to have that bit of extra money in your last months of life, so you're comfortable and you can spend it with your family," she said. She said some people spend the end of their life working because they "don't have any other access to money". "You end up dying not being able to keep your house warm. That to me is just devastating." Households across Northern Ireland will get a one-off £63 reduction in electricity bills from this month It comes as Share Energy announced electricity prices will also rise by 12.6% from today. This will add an extra £129 per year onto the typical household bill of their 41,000 customers.

events.title: Verity is the latest Colleen Hoover novel to get a film adaptation
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Verity Crawford (Anne Hathaway) is a renowned author who seeks help in the film Verity. ( Supplied: Amazon MGM Studios ) Hollywood loves a Colleen Hoover adaptation. The latest is psychological thriller Verity. In the film, struggling writer Lowen Ashleigh (Dakota Johnson) is hired as a ghostwriter for renowned author Verity Crawford (Oscar winner Anne Hathaway). It starts out as an assignment taken under mysterious circumstances, with Lowen recruited by Verity's husband, Jeremy (Josh Hartnett). Lowen Ashleigh (Dakota Johnson) is a struggling author hired as a ghostwriter. ( Supplied: Amazon MGM Studios ) But when Lowen uncovers what appears to be chilling autobiographical confessions in Verity's notes, she wrestles with these disturbing and twisted revelations. Verity is a glossy thriller punctuated by its beautiful people and slick presentation. It's a fun watch that ends on a tantalising cliffhanger, which is almost as scandalous as it is unexpectedly satisfying. Verity is married to Jeremy Crawford (Josh Hartnett). ( Supplied: Amazon MGM Studios ) But critics have both emphatically praised the film and have had scathing reactions. The Sydney Morning Herald called Verity "perfect for these post-truth times". Mamamia referred to it as a "delicious" thriller. But The Nightly called it "diabolical", saying it was "embarrassing" for its A-list stars to be "dragged" into the film. Who, meanwhile, has categorised it as a "straight to DVD territory" type of movie. One of Hoover's biggest outings since It Ends with Us As far as Hoover adaptations go, Verity comes after Reminders of Him (2026) and Regretting You (2025), but the internet is still talking about 2024's It Ends with Us. Justin Baldoni and Blake Lively settle legal battle over It Ends With Us scandal The pair settle their civil case two weeks before a trial had been set to begin in New York. That movie was overshadowed by the off-screen drama between its two stars, Blake Lively and Justin Baldoni. They have settled their legal battles in a civil case. Lively had alleged Baldoni conspired with publicists to pre-emptively destroy her reputation after she privately accused him of sexually harassing her on the movie set. From Misery to Yellowface, books about writers are favourites among the authors who pen them, and audiences also love a behind-the-scenes look at the literary world. It's fertile ground for novelists writing about a world they're familiar with, setting the stakes high in an imagined narrative. The authentic details an author can bring to such a story are what make them so spicy and alluring as they blend reality and fiction. Verity is based on the worldwide best-selling novel of the same name by Hoover. Colleen Hoover is a trailblazer. ( Eric Charbonneau/Getty Images for Sony Pictures ) In 2012, Hoover was the first self-published author to top The New York Times bestseller list, which she did again with Verity in 2018, and is a pioneer of modern indie publishing. She has since had a great deal of mainstream success. Verity was Hoover's first thriller. She had already authored 16 romance books prior to that and amassed millions of fans. In adapting the novel, director Michael Showalter aimed to produce a film as closely aligned with the book as possible. "The book is a big hit, people love it, so let's make a movie out of the book," Showalter said. "My approach was to do it the way it was in the book wherever possible. "Let people see what a true adaptation would look and feel like and honour that." events.title: UAE Property: 'Who pays to install an EV charger at a rented villa?'
events.summary: Question: I rent a villa in Dubai and recently bought an electric car. There is no charging point at the property, so I asked my landlord whether I could have one installed at my own expense. He initially agreed, but is now saying that because the charger will remain with the villa when I eventually leave, I should also pay for any approvals, electrical upgrades and reinstatement, if required. The community management told me I cannot simply appoint an electrician and install one myself. With more people buying electric cars in Dubai, I imagine this is going to become a common issue. Who is responsible for getting permission, and if I pay for something that ultimately improves the landlord's property , can I take the charger with me when I leave? James, Dubai Answer: This is an interesting issue and one I suspect we'll see much more frequently as electric vehicle ownership increases. I would not install anything without written approval. An EV charger isn't simply an appliance you plug into the wall; it can involve alterations to the property's electrical infrastructure and, potentially, the community's systems, so the landlord and relevant community or building management may need to approve the installation. The question of who pays is largely something for you and the landlord to agree on. If you're requesting the charger for your personal use, it's reasonable that the landlord may expect you to meet the installation cost. Equally, you're correct that a professionally installed charging point potentially becomes an improvement to his property and could make it more attractive to future tenants. I'd therefore negotiate before spending anything. Agree in writing who pays for the equipment, installation, approvals and electricity consumption, and importantly, what happens when your tenancy ends . If the charger can be removed without damaging the property, you may want the agreement to allow you to take it. Alternatively, if the landlord wants it left behind, perhaps he contributes towards the installation. This is ultimately less about who is “right” and more about documenting the arrangement properly. The mistake would be spending thousands of dirhams improving somebody else's property and only discussing ownership of the equipment when you're moving out. Q: My wife and I bought an off-plan apartment in Dubai largely because of the view shown to us when we purchased. The sales presentation, brochure and agent all made a big point of the open waterfront view and we paid considerably more for that particular unit. Construction is now well advanced, but we've discovered another building is planned on the plot directly in front of ours. The developer says master plans evolve and that our sales and purchase agreement (SPA) doesn't guarantee a permanent view. I appreciate Dubai is constantly developing , but if somebody pays a premium specifically because a property is marketed with a particular view, surely the developer cannot simply change it afterwards? Do buyers have any protection in this situation? Jonathan, London A: This is a very good example of why buyers need to distinguish between what is shown in the marketing material and what is actually contractually guaranteed. A beautiful rendering showing uninterrupted water, golf-course or skyline views doesn't necessarily amount to a contractual promise that those views will remain forever. The starting point should therefore be your SPA, together with the approved plans and any documents incorporated into the sale. Look particularly for provisions allowing the developer to modify the master plan, surrounding plots, building configuration or overall development programme. I would also retain the original brochure, emails, WhatsApp conversations and anything else demonstrating how the apartment was represented when you purchased it. If you were specifically charged a premium for a particular view and this can be evidenced, that information could become important. I would also ask the developer for details of the proposed building and establish whether it was already part of an approved master plan when you purchased or represents a subsequent change. Those are potentially quite different circumstances. The fact that the view influenced your decision doesn't automatically establish that you're entitled to compensation, but if something material was expressly represented and the eventual product differs substantially, it's certainly worth obtaining independent legal advice. There's also an important lesson here for anyone buying off-plan . Don't simply ask the agent what your apartment overlooks today. Ask who owns the land in front of it, what that plot is designated for and what could legally be built there in the future. In a rapidly developing city like Dubai, today's empty plot isn't necessarily tomorrow's view. The opinions expressed do not constitute legal advice and are provided for information only. "Now I have to make a decision: either Iran signs the deal, or it won't exist any longer," he said on Thursday. At the same time, Trump is being asked to join Saudi Arabia's planned offensive against the Houthis in Yemen. The Saudis are urging the president to conduct airstrikes against the Houthis. Trump has been leaning against it, but U.S. officials say he could change his mind. What he's saying: On Friday afternoon, while his advisers were at Camp David, Trump was asked by reporters what his next move on Iran will be. "If I told you, you would have a major story," he said. Meta’s Muse, a personal AI agent that books travel, fills out forms, and shops on a user’s behalf, has already proven popular with the masses, but a new side project could be particularly alluring to tinkerers and hackers. On Friday, the company introduced Muse Gadgets , an open-source project that lets developers build their own hardware that connects to Muse. Meta is providing open-source firmware (the low-level software that runs a device), and a Linux software development kit (SDK), along with a few project ideas to get users started. These include giving Muse a color e-ink display or loading it onto a stick that plugs into a TV’s HDMI port. There don’t appear to be many limits, either. Users can set up a low-cost hobbyist computer like a Raspberry Pi or an off-the-shelf ESP32 board, and then connect Muse “to your displays, buttons, sensors, actuators, and whatever else you’ve got lying on your workbench,” Meta notes. The company has also set up a Discord channel to support users. Meta has already tried the code itself, naturally. Nat Friedman, head of product at Meta’s Superintelligence Labs, said in a post on X that the company built a gadget called Muse Home Link. The USB-C-powered device lets Muse connect to a home network and talk to the smart devices on it, including speakers and smart TVs. Meta made 5,000 of these Home Links, in fact, and is giving them away for free to Muse subscribers while supplies last, according to Friedman. Considering Friedman’s post about Home Link received nearly 30,000 views in a few hours, we’re guessing those freebies have been claimed. Friedman said Home Link would be ready to ship a few weeks. Muse Gadgets may not have wide appeal, but it fits nicely into Meta’s all-in strategy to make Muse more than a standalone chatbot. Meta isn’t content to push Muse on everyday consumers; it’s also trying to woo small businesses and enterprises. The company earlier this week introduced Muse for Small Business, which is free with usage limits and connects Muse to tools such as Shopify, Dropbox, and Slack. It has also launched a new business unit, Meta Enterprise Platform, to help it push its AI offerings to businesses and corporate customers. events.title: Sanders introduces bill to ban the federal government from using Flock
events.summary: Last day to exhibit your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders at Disrupt is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Flock Safety, whose cameras scan license plates across the country, continues to draw public anger, and now Senator Bernie Sanders wants the federal government out of the business altogether. Sanders on Friday introduced the Ban Flock Act , which would bar federal agencies from using automatic license plate readers (ALPRs) or tapping into data collected by readers run by local police and private companies. Despite its title, the bill doesn’t call out nine-year-old Flock in the text but rather covers any and all ALPR systems. The bill allows exceptions only for toll collection and for uses that Congress approves in future legislation, which would have to limit data retention to 48 hours. State and local governments would be dinged financially for not complying if the bill became law. (Like most bills, this one faces long odds.) Starting the first fiscal year after enactment, they would lose grants from five federal departments, including the Justice Department and the Department of Homeland Security, unless they ban the tech. Americans could also sue the federal government over violations, and state attorneys general could enforce the law. Flock is the largest ALPR vendor in the U.S., according to Sanders, with more than 120,000 cameras. In a blog post back in February, the company — currently valued by its venture backers at north of $8 billion — said its network processes more than 20 billion vehicle reads each month. Under increasing pressure from communities that are protesting the product, suspending their use , and, at an escalating rate, canceling their contracts, Flock has tightened its rules. In August, CEO Garrett Langley, who’d previously said that how police use the cameras is up to local agencies, announced a new default data retention period of seven days, down from 30. Customers must also now use an audit tool that locks officers out pending review when it flags unusual searches. In one of the highest-profile cases of an officer abusing Flock’s platform, a former Milwaukee officer pleaded guilty to misconduct after searching for his then-partner and her ex 179 times, listing the reason as “investigation.” (During a recent podcast interview, investor Jason Calacanis suggested a “double-key” system in which two people must approve a search, and Langley said the idea is “on the whiteboard.”) Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) and Senator Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.) are co-sponsors. events.title: Saudis plan major offensive against the Houthis, but U.S. won't join for now
events.summary: Saudi Arabia and Yemeni government forces are planning a major counteroffensive against Iran-backed Houthis in the coming days — an effort to push them away from areas on the Red Sea coast that control the Strait of Bab al-Mandeb, two U.S. officials say. Why it matters: For the second time in recent weeks, the U.S. rebuffed Saudi pleas to join the operation and conduct airstrikes. But U.S. officials say that could change if the operation runs into problems. The Bab al-Mandeb Strait is a vital artery for global trade and Saudi oil exports. Control over it gives the Houthis and their Iranian backer a powerful new point of leverage over the U.S., its Gulf allies and the world economy. Driving the news: In recent weeks, the Houthis took over key areas of the southern Red Sea coast that control the strait. They also increased missile and drone attacks against Saudi Arabia. The Saudis retaliated with airstrikes against Houthi targets. Behind the scenes: A U.S. official said the Saudis have been planning the operation for weeks and that plans were approved by Saudi leadership several days ago. The operation will include ground forces loyal to the internationally recognized government in Yemen with Saudi air cover. On Thursday, Saudi Defense Minister Prince Khalid Bin Salman called Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to brief him on the planned operation and ask again for U.S. airstrikes against Houthi targets, the U.S. official said. A U.S. official said that the U.S. "is not going to take kinetic action for now." Last week, President Trump was close to ordering a strike on the Houthis after a request from Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman (MBS), but eventually decided to hold off . Between the lines: Trump is caught between wanting to help his friend and ally MBS, and avoiding getting entangled in a new front in the Middle East. The U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) also had serious reservations about launching strikes in Yemen and saw it as a distraction from its focus on Iran, a U.S. official said. Zoom in: U.S. officials say the U.S. military is helping the Saudis with everything short of direct combat, mainly intelligence and targeting data. One U.S. official said that in the last two weeks, the U.S. military provided the Saudis with more than 200 Houthi targets to strike. The official said the strikes significantly increased pressure on the Houthis.

events.title: Apple changes full-disk access permissions to curb abuse from AI agents
events.summary: Apple says it is changing its macOS privacy settings to stop third-party app developers from misusing them to access message histories. Friday's announcement comes two weeks after tech columnist Jason Aten said that Meta’s new general-purpose AI agent Muse sent him an unsolicited notification referencing a thread between him and a co-worker over Apple Messages. Aten said he never granted Muse permissions to read his messages and had assumed they were off-limits. Social media last week blew up with masses of people who agreed and said the incident showed that AI assistants given access to calendars, emails, messages, shopping accounts, and other resources are akin to a skill saw or other power tool. While potentially useful, they can do real damage if not used carefully. He said/she said Meta CTO David Singleton joined the fray with a rebuttal that appeared solid. For Muse to access Apple Messages, a user must manually give it two privileges. One is full-disk access, a macOS system-level permission. The other is to enable a Messages connector setting in Muse. events.title: Complaint over senior NT public servant who ran private NDIS provider
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Senior NT public servant was sole director of private NDIS company in Alice Springs for years Kudzai Mutsunge ran the NDIS business Life Aspects while holding senior roles in the NT Department of Children and Families. ( ABC News Graphics: Jess Henderson ) A senior public servant responsible for child and family support in Central Australia was simultaneously running a National Disability Insurance Scheme (NDIS) provider company in Alice Springs. The Department of Children and Families has confirmed it forwarded a complaint about her involvement in the NDIS provider Life Aspects to an integrity process. The status of the process remains unclear. Documents obtained by the ABC show the department has recently strengthened its internal conflict of interest procedures, especially for staff with the power to influence NDIS referrals. A senior Northern Territory public servant responsible for child and family services in Central Australia spent nearly three years as the sole director of a private National Disability Insurance Scheme (NDIS) provider in Alice Springs, and for 15 months also owned a 50 per cent stake in the business's parent company. The Department of Children and Families plays a significant role in the NDIS system in the NT, with the most recent figures from 2024 showing more than 300 children in its care had active NDIS plans. An ABC investigation has confirmed public servant Kudzai Mutsunge ran the NDIS business Life Aspects while holding senior roles in the Department of Children and Families, and held shares in the business's parent company, Japhin The Teacher Pty Ltd, from December 2024 to February 2026. Life Aspects is registered to provide a range of disability services, including assistance with independent living and support coordination, an area that involves arranging other providers for people with disability. Kudzai Mutsunge was the sole director of Life Aspects for almost three years. ( Supplied ) The ABC has seen no evidence that any child in the care of the department was a Life Aspects client. The department has referred a complaint about a potential conflict of interest to an internal integrity process. Ms Mutsunge wound up her directorship and shareholding in Life Aspects earlier this year, one week before an anonymous complaint was sent to the NDIS Quality and Safeguards Commission in March. A separate complaint went to the Department of Children and Families in August, from the Alice Springs-based Disability Advocacy Service (DAS). On August 21, the department told the service it had referred the information "through the appropriate internal integrity processes" and was coordinating with the National Disability Insurance Agency (NDIA) "where relevant". The outcome of that process, if any, is unknown. In response to questions from the ABC, the department declined to say whether Ms Mutsunge had declared a potential conflict of interest or sought approval for outside work, saying it could not comment on individual employment or conduct matters. Kudzai Mutsunge ran the NDIS business Life Aspects while holding senior roles in the Department of Children and Families. ( ABC News: James Elton ) The ABC understands Ms Mutsunge quit the department on September 11. Ms Mutsunge said she did not "endorse or agree to the allegations or characterisations" put to her by the ABC about whether her roles presented a potential conflict of interest, and said she could not respond to further questions within the timeframe provided. Under the NT public service code of conduct, employees must declare any perceived, potential or actual conflicts of interest in writing to their chief executive. The department's acting chief executive Karen Broadfoot said it had "zero tolerance" for a failure to declare a conflict. Ms Broadfoot said that where integrity matters involved the NDIS, the department would also coordinate with the Australian Federal Police when relevant. The NDIA said it could not comment on ongoing investigations. DAS chief executive Scott Richardson said government officials needed to be held to a higher standard on potential NDIS conflicts, to ensure they "don't have access to participant information that they could then benefit from, or family could benefit from". DAS chief executive Scott Richardson says government officials should be held to a higher standard on potential NDIS conflicts. ( ABC News: Pete Garnish ) In a meeting in March, Ms Mutsunge reportedly told DAS staff that she was "operationally removed" from placement decisions, and denied any role in referring children to NDIS providers.

events.summary: Manufacturing, Packaging & Materials Technical Papers Home '; AI/ML/DL Architectures Automotive/ Aerospace Communication/Data Movement Design & Verification Lithography Manufacturing Materials Memory Optoelectronics / Photonics Packaging Power & Performance Quantum Security Test, Measurement, Analytics tech papers Transistors Z-End Applications Videos & Research Videos Industry Research Newsletters & Store Newsletters Store MENU Home Special Reports Systems & Design Low Power-High Performance Manufacturing, Packaging & Materials Test, Measurement & Analytics Auto, Security and AI Knowledge Center Videos Startup Corner Business & Startups Jobs Technical Papers Events Webinars Industry Research Newsletters Store Special Reports Researchers at Infineon Technologies and Technical University of Munich published a technical paper titled “From Physical Devices to RTL Models: Abstraction and Validation in Hardware Engineering.” “This paper introduces the foundational principles underlying hardware engineering models and argues that abstraction is their defining characteristic. Because abstraction necessarily omits detail and constrains what engineers can build, models are inherently incomplete in specific respects – or, as George Box famously observed, “All models are wrong, but some are useful”. At the same time, abstraction is essential for simplification, which is key to managing complexity. More abstract models also tend to simulate faster because fewer details must be considered. This paper subsequently examines a range of abstraction methods in digital design – sometimes referred to as design disciplines – including lumped models, value-discrete models, and time-discrete models. Together with constraints that define the validity of the abstraction and design guidelines, these abstraction methods establish design disciplines. This paper further relates these forms of abstraction to pre-clustered design elements such as transistors, gates, registers, and transfer functions. These pre-clustered elements define abstraction levels, such as the gate level, and are presented as a key enabler of increased design productivity.” Find the technical paper here . October 2026. events.title: Cerebras stock hits post-IPO low, tumbling 20% for the week on Nvidia pressure and lockup expiration
events.summary: Cerebras is down about 50% from its opening price that followed its market debut in May. The company lost a key inference workload for OpenAI's "Ultrafast" mode for the GPT-6.1 Sol AI model to chip giant Nvidia. Executives are also selling shares as the company's lockup period expires, putting more downward pressure on the stock price. Cerebras stock plummeted nearly 20% this week to its lowest price since the company's monster IPO in May, after a report that chip giant Nvidia will power a crucial piece of OpenAI's latest model. Research firm SemiAnalysis posted on X on Wednesday that OpenAI will power its "Ultrafast" mode for GPT-6.1 Sol with Nvidia graphics processing units instead of Cerebras hardware. Cerebras shares are now down by more than half since their initial pop that followed the company's debut on the Nasdaq. The stock, which closed on Friday at $166.43, was also under pressure this week due to the expiration of post-IPO restrictions on some insider shares. However, it rose almost 3% in extended trading on Friday after OpenAI CEO Sam Altman responded to the "speculation about our partnership with Cerebras." "Cerebras is a close partner, and we have a deep engagement pushing on the frontiers of speed," Altman wrote in a post on X . Still, it's been a brutal stretch for Cerebras, which closed at a $95 billion market cap on the first day of trading, just shy of joining the ranks of Meta , Alibaba and now SpaceX , which closed their initial day with valuations over $100 billion. Cerebras' market cap now sits at just over $39 billion. Investors were excited by the prospect of an alternative to Nvidia to power AI. Cerebras makes dinner plate-sized ASICs, or a custom microchip built for inference workloads, and leases them from inside its own data centers as a cloud service. In January, Cerebras struck a deal worth over $10 billion with OpenAI to supply it with 750 megawatts of computing power through 2028. Losing OpenAI inference to Nvidia has put a damper on that exuberance. According to McKinsey , inference is set to surpass training as the most dominant workload in AI data centers by the end of the decade. Meanwhile, as more time passes from the IPO, additional shares will hit the market. According to the company's prospectus, up to 19.4 million shares held by directors, officers, non-executive employees, and non-employee holders unlocked on Wednesday. That's equal to 8% of total shares outstanding. Prior to that, up to 14.6 million shares have been unlocked for sale every two weeks since Aug. 19. CEO Andrew Feldman and CTO Sean Lie, both minted billionaires by the IPO process, sold over $240 million of Class A shares between Aug. 20 and Sept. 25 under trading plans adopted shortly after the IPO. Other executives have also sold shares valued in the millions. WATCH: CNBC’s full interview with Cerebras Systems CEO Andrew Feldman

events.title: Golf club spends $30k on water changes, only for policy to change
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Mowbray Golf Club spends $30k on water changes, only for TasWater to change policy General manager Hayden Roberts says the club has taken a financial hit for no reason. ( ABC News: Morgan Timms ) Businesses and sporting clubs faced significant bill increases from July 1 after a TasWater policy change on sewerage charges. Some decided to change their water connections, on the advice of TasWater, only for the billing system to then be changed again. One golf club is calling for compensation after spending $30,000 on changes that have now been made void following the policy change. A golf club in Launceston is calling for compensation from TasWater after spending an estimated $30,000 on water infrastructure works in response to billing changes, which were then essentially reversed. Mowbray Golf Club saw its water bill double from $20,000 to about $40,000 due to a TasWater policy change to charge based on the size of a water pipe connection, rather than sewerage usage, from July 1. The charge was based on the club's 100-millimetre connection, which it says it only uses in drought conditions and instead relies on its own storage for irrigation. In response, the club decided to sever the 100mm connection and connect its clubhouse and other services to its 50mm connection at significant cost. The club says it decided to sever its 100mm connection on the advice of TasWater. ( ABC News: Morgan Timms ) It increased fees for its members by 10 per cent to help pay for the works. Club general manager Hayden Roberts said they chose to go ahead with the works after being told by TasWater that reducing connection size was the easiest method. "I know we're not the only ones that have done such," he said. On Friday, TasWater announced a change in response to concerns from businesses and sporting clubs. It would take fixed sewerage charges from $20,000 to under $1,000 and charge 100mm connections as 20mm connections, with refunds offered for bills paid since July 1. The change came too late for Mowbray Golf Club, however. "I think it's only reasonable at this point that TasWater remediates these situations, whether it be credit or an outright refund of works completed. "We've actually lost an asset in the process of this removal of connection." TasWater says changes had 'unintended consequences' TasWater contacted the club in response to the policy change but had not made assurances regarding compensation. Callan Paske from TasWater says the changes had unintended consequences. ( ABC News ) TasWater general manager of customers and community Callan Paske said the water authority was aware of other clubs and businesses that had made changes to their connections based on TasWater advice. "We're working with those impacted clubs to ensure that we can work through what the final solution is for them," he said. The change in sewerage charging followed an inquiry by the Tasmanian Economic Regulator, which required TasWater to move from an equivalent charging method to a fixed and variable method. This is similar to methods used in other states. Mr Paske said it had disproportionately impacted sporting clubs and businesses, which was addressed by the change announced on Friday. "What this shows is that in any tariff reform there is nuance and we need to fix those outlier impacts that are in unintended consequences of major change," he said. Water infrastructure challenges remain TasWater again faces a challenge in how to fund upgrades to its aging infrastructure. The changes have hit its bottom line by between $7 million and $14 million, according to Mr Paske. "We've got aging infrastructure, failing pipes, we've got growth that we need to cater for, and we've got environmental impacts that we're having that are not what Tasmanians want to see," he said. The change came following discussions between TasWater, the economic regulator, councils and the state government. Premier Jeremy Rockliff said it was a "significant and lasing outcome" for businesses and sporting clubs. Shadow treasurer Dean Winter said the government had the power to veto TasWater's corporate plan, and questioned why this had not occurred following successive significant price increases.

events.title: DOJ says it will not reopen criminal probe into former Fed Chair Powell
events.summary: The Department of Justice will not reopen its criminal investigation into former Fed Chair Jerome Powell over the renovation to its headquarters building. The Fed inspector general found no basis for a criminal referral but faulted major oversight failures as renovation costs more than doubled. Powell stepped down as chair when Kevin Warsh took over in May but remains a Fed governor through January 2028, as Trump continues pressing him to leave the board. The Department of Justice will not reopen its criminal investigation into former Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell over the central bank's overbudget multibillion-dollar headquarters renovation a department spokesperson told CNBC. "We're not reopening a criminal investigation into him," Attorney General Todd Blanche told Bloomberg in an interview Friday. Blanche did not rule out separate Justice Department action related to the renovation in his interview. He told the outlet the independent audit of the renovation could prompt an investigation if it uncovers evidence of criminal wrongdoing. His comments come days after the Federal Reserve's inspector general found no reasonable grounds to believe that a federal crime had occurred requiring a referral to the attorney general, even as the watchdog faulted the central bank for major management and oversight failures that contributed to the project's soaring costs. President Donald Trump slammed the decision, said in a Truth Social post Wednesday after the news, saying that Powell should be "forced to resign" from the central bank's Board of Governors "at a minimum." "He can't manage a Building, and he certainly shouldn't be allowed to manage his High Interest Rate Policy (only on 'TRUMP!')," Trump said. The Justice Department opened its investigation into the renovation in January. Prosecutors issued grand jury subpoenas seeking related records but a federal judge quashed those subpoenas in March, finding they had been issued for an improper purpose and that the government had produced essentially no evidence that Powell committed a crime. The DOJ disputed the ruling but later closed its investigation rather than appeal. Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh , who succeeded Powell in May, said the central bank would bring in an independent auditor and strengthen oversight of the project. Powell remains on the Fed's Board of Governors, where his separate term runs through Jan. 31, 2028. Trump has repeatedly pushed Powell to leave the board altogether after years of clashes over interest-rate policy. CNBC's Ryan Ruggiero contributed to this report.

events.title: How employees forced OpenAI’s president to back down
events.summary: The Scoop On June 1, OpenAI chief strategy officer Jason Kwon gave employees a preview of a blog post denying the company had any connection to Leading the Future, a super PAC established to defend AI from regulation. OpenAI president Greg Brockman’s support for the super PAC “has been in a personal capacity, not on behalf of the company,” Kwon wrote in an internal Slack message. Not everyone on his staff bought it. One OpenAI employee took to Slack to warn of a dangerous trade-off: The company’s aggressive political activity threatened to drive researchers to Anthropic, and hamstring OpenAI in the all-out race to recursively self-improving AI. The post earned 24 “agree” reactions and a solitary eyes emoji. The next day, Kwon gave ground to a different internal critic: The company, he said on Slack, was “taking reputational hits.” They had drawn “some clear public lines,” but “I wish we’d done it even sooner.” Ten days after Kwon’s post, Brockman backed out of the second half of his public $50 million commitment, saying he felt “terrible about the fact that LTF keeps reflecting on the company” in a post first reported by The New York Times. Brockman’s message received 40 hearts, five checkmarks, and three thank-you emojis. The episode, part of a set of Slack messages shared with Semafor, offers a window into the complex internal politics of the handful of companies shaping the global future of artificial intelligence. Outsiders observing the tribal world of San Francisco frontier labs often see OpenAI as the “accelerationist” cousin to the safety-oriented Anthropic. The rare glimpse inside the company’s Slack illustrates a more complex reality: Many of OpenAI’s developers, engineers, and researchers — whom the company is fighting to keep in intense talent wars whose bidders also include Meta, Google, and an array of startups — aren’t sanguine about unregulated AI. And they dislike being associated with the political group’s aggressive tactics. A spokeswoman for OpenAI declined to comment. One employee initially placated by Kwon’s post followed up two days later flagging that Brockman’s money would be used to fund an X account the employee described as “an LTF sockpuppet ( confirmed here ) that posts stuff like “ [sam altman is] a caterpillar that murders insects and stitches their dismembered body parts onto its back as armor .” (Twenty-two other employees responded, “WTF.“) A source familiar with the situation told Semafor that employee pushback was definitely part of Brockman’s decision, but that he had his own qualms that began with LTF targeting New York Assemblymember Alex Bores, an AI safety advocate running for Congress in New York. The person said that Brockman had expected the PAC to focus more on supporting allied candidates. The people running LTF appeared not to understand the complex internal dynamics of frontier safety policy — and how the whole industry would react to attacking someone running on that platform. At different points, the person added, Brockman gave pointed feedback to LTF; the source noted they hadn’t heard of the PAC attacking candidates since Bores. Since then, the PAC has overwhelmingly donated to front-runners in congressional races. And candidates LTF has endorsed or implicitly supported have come out in favor of a bill from Sen. Bernie Sanders and Rep. Greg Casar that would pause frontier AI development and criminalize attempting to build superintelligence, OpenAI’s stated goal . Leading the Future LTF launched in August 2025, well before AI became a major public issue. The group boasted more than $100 million in commitments, with $50 million to come from Brockman and his wife Anna. OpenAI’s global affairs chief Chris Lehane had helped set up the PAC, which followed a model he pioneered for the crypto industry. OpenAI sought to characterize the PAC as a totally independent entity, but employees — encouraged by critics on X — were skeptical. Staff were complaining about the connection in February, Wired reported, and Transformer reported that employees confronted Lehane in a meeting in May, pushing the company to explain its relationship with LTF. Kwon’s June 1 Slack message sought to defuse the controversy. “Many have posted questions,” he wrote, about the nature of the relationship between OpenAI and LTF. At the end of the multi-paragraph message, he concluded, “Thank you to everyone who has given feedback on this topic and pushed for a stronger company statement, in particular” before tagging three employees. It worked — for about an hour. More than 80 employees reacted with approving emojis, and the first reply was excited and appreciative. But then others questioned the group’s independence, highlighted LTF’s controversial and backfiring track record, and worried about the super PAC’s toxic effect on OpenAI’s brand and retention of senior researchers. The messages were shared with Semafor on the condition that they not be quoted directly out of concern that employees would feel uncomfortable seeing their messages reproduced verbatim, potentially chilling future Slacktivism. The dispute flared up again on June 11. One worker posted a Transformer article in which the director of LTF’s sister lobbying group, Build American AI (BAAI), which does not disclose its donors, texted journalist Veronica Irwin, “For this project I’m funded by four separate entities … OpenAI is just one of them” (OpenAI told Irwin and other journalists that the company had not provided funding to the groups). Just over an hour later, Brockman weighed in for the first time, denying the story’s claim that OpenAI backed BAAI and assuring staff that he’d given nothing to the organization (though as employees noted later in the thread, LTF gives money to BAAI). He then apologized for how LTF reflected on the company and abandoned his additional $25 million donation. Initially, responses in the thread under Kwon’s post ping-ponged between appreciation and recrimination, with approving Slack reactions hovering in the 20s and 30s for each variety. But skepticism and pointed questions mounted. A day later, Kwon weighed in again, addressing a disappointed employee. “I generally agree with what you’re saying, including the part about taking reputational hits for their activities. This is one of the reasons it made sense for us to draw some clear public lines about what we don’t condone. I wish we’d done it even sooner,” he wrote. “I don’t think we are asking people to believe that separation of scope and control means no accountability. I can’t speak for Greg but it does seem like LTF is in the process of adjusting. events.title: Fishers warn snapper, kingfish prices could soar under proposed catch limits
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Snapper, yellowtail kingfish price could soar under proposed catch limits Topic: Fishing and Aquaculture Industry Fishers say stricter limits would see snapper and kingfish prices rise. ( ABC Coffs Coast: Claire Simmonds ) Stricter limits have been proposed for snapper and yellowtail kingfish to help rebuild stocks in NSW fisheries. Commercial and recreational fishers are opposed to the changes. The NSW government has extended the consultation period for the proposed changes until February 15. Seafood shops and fishers are warning snapper and yellowtail kingfish could become unaffordable if catch limits are tightened. Both species are popular menu items, but stocks of kingfish in particular were described as "dangerously low" in a recent statement from the NSW Agriculture Minister Tara Moriarty. The state government has proposed reducing the annual kingfish catch from 250 tonnes to 120 tonnes a year. The snapper take would remain at 300 tonnes a year, but the proposal would include commercial monthly catch limits and a bag limit of three, with only one over 70 centimetres for recreational fishers. Naeco Blue Seafood's Adam Hambley says he cannot see people willing to pay any more for snapper and kingfish. ( Supplied: Adam Hambley ) Adam Hambley, who owns a seafood shop in South Grafton in northern NSW, said stricter limits would lead to higher prices. "If we see a $5 increase on the whole fish, we're going to see a $20 increase in the fillet, so you're going to near $80-90 a kilo for snapper fillets… I don't believe that anyone here will pay that much," he said. On a regular day, Noel Gogerly would pull in up to 40 kilograms of snapper while commercially fishing at Tuncurry on the NSW mid north coast. Under the proposed reforms, he would be allowed 10 kilograms, which he estimated would cost him up to $300 a day. Fisherman Noel Gogerly says the changes could cost him hundreds of dollars a day. ( ABC News: Lauren Bohane ) Mr Gogerly said any fish thrown back were unlikely to survive due to internal damage caused by the pressure change when pulled from the deep ocean. "You're going to have snapper just laying on top of the water," he said. Charter operators and recreational fishers are also worried. Under the changes yellowtail kingfish limits would drop from five per person to one per boat. Charter fishing operator Craig McGill said the proposed changes would ruin his business. Craig McGill says if the proposed changes to catch limits for yellowtail kingfish are implemented it could destroy his business. ( ABC News: Supplied ) "That would probably be the end of me," he said. "I get four guys on board; for me to have to tell them that they've got to share one kingfish, or that one guy gets to take one kingfish and the others can't catch one … they all pay a premium to come charter fishing with me." Michael Mashado estimated the proposed changes would cost his tackle store in Eden, on the NSW far south coast, up to $200,000 in sales per year. "Nobody's going to come and buy the quantity of gear to go and catch one kingfish or three snapper," he said. Mr Mashado said fishing was one of the south coast's biggest tourism industries. Michael Mashado says the proposed changes could have a broader impact on local towns where fishing is a major tourist attraction. ( Supplied ) "If you look at a family that comes here with a big boat, they spend [money] in the tackle shop, they spend it at the pub, they spend it at the supermarket," he said. The DPIRD said the proposal aimed to allow historically depleted fish stocks to recover, while still allowing some commercial and recreational catch. "We know approximately recreational fishers take about 50 per cent of the catch, as do commercial fishers, for both of these species," DPIRD director of fisheries management Heath Folpp said. Public consultation on the proposed changes was extended until mid-February in response to industry concerns. Fishers have warned any snapper thrown back would likely not survive.

events.title: One Nation makes election promise to revive Victoria's timber sector
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts One Nation promises to revive Victoria's native timber industry but cannot cite the cost Topic: Forestry, Logging and Timber Industry One Nation has pledged to let loggers back into native forests in Victoria if it wins the state election. ( Supplied: Victorian National Parks Association ) One Nation has promised to resume native timber logging in Victoria if it wins the state election, but has not said how the policy would be funded or achieved. The party says its policy also includes provisions to protect old-growth forest and native habitat. The Victorian Coalition is finalising its timber policy ahead of the election. Two years after sawmills fell silent in Victoria's native forests, the logging industry could be revived if there is a change in government at the November election. While the Coalition and One Nation have committed to restarting native forest logging, which was shut down by the Labor government in January 2024 , it is unclear what it would take to get the industry back on its feet. One Nation's Narracan candidate Ben Lucas said the policy supported country-of-origin labelling laws on timber and wood products, and a self-funding model in which harvest revenue supported forest improvement and fire prevention. He said the party would consult industry leaders and audit the millions of dollars Labor spent on the logging industry transition fund before settling on a new approach. He said the party would incentivise the use of Australian timber in construction through a "local wood first" policy in government procurement and would ensure timber was extracted using a selective harvesting model. "You can't take away the forestry industry from a town like Noojee and replace the economy with a truffle festival once a year," Mr Lucas said. Pauline Hanson with Ben Lucas during a visit to Gippsland in August. ( ABC News: Madeleine Stuchbery ) But when pressed for details, Mr Lucas would not clarify how much it could cost or what would be involved in reopening native forests to logging. "This is a broad policy and it's very open-ended, but with clear guidelines on how we want to do it and why we want to do it," Mr Lucas said. "We've got the words on paper and if we get in, we can have some influence on how that happens." The Liberal-National Coalition is still working through the details of its policy, but Nationals leader Danny O'Brien previously vowed to restore native forest logging. Nationals MP Melina Bath, whose portfolio includes timber, said the coalition was finalising its policy but also backed a return to logging. "We will be announcing a suite of packages and policies in relation to this," Ms Bath said. "They're still going through a parliamentary process and we make sure … that we've done our costings correctly." Victoria's Regional Development Minister Michaela Settle said restarting native forestry under a Coalition or One Nation government would cost Victorians. "Labor is backing forestry workers into new jobs, growing local plantation timber and keeping forestry skills and experience in our forests to reduce bushfire risk and support better forest management," she said. According to a 2026 Victorian Auditor-General's report, the Victorian government's decision to shut down the industry affected 1,000 workers and 200 businesses. It found the Victorian government spent $1.5 billion on transition arrangements and 87 per cent of workers had retired or found new jobs. But it found many had moved into part-time, casual or contract roles and it was "not clear if workers' new jobs meet their needs or are sustainable". Ms Bath said a revived industry would "look different to what the Labor government shut down in 2024" and would need to overcome challenges, such as rebuilding the workforce. Orbost District Chamber of Commerce and Industry secretary Garry Squires said any move to revive the forestry sector would be well received in the regions. Garry Squires says rural towns like Orbost would love to see a return of native forest logging. ( ABC Gippsland: Natasha Schapova ) "The reality is you can't just start big harvesting operations right across Victoria in a hurry, but start off slowly with thinning operations," he said. "We've got this great resource of eucalypt forests across Victoria. Victoria has more than 380,000 hectares of plantation forest, totalling more than 20 per cent of Australia's plantations. Victoria also produces about one-quarter of Australia's plantation-grown wood, at a gross value of about $550 million each year.

events.title: Qld government rejects petition to change stop signs to give way
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Queensland government rejects petition to change all stop signs to give-way signs Topic: State and Territory Government The petitioner argued stop signs offer "no safety significance". ( ABC News: Luke Bowden ) The Queensland government has rejected a petition to swap all stop signs with give-way signs in the state. A petition signed by 391 Queenslanders argued that stop signs provide "no safety significance" and cost drivers more in fuel. Transport Minister Brent Mickelberg said the safety benefits outweigh any operational impacts associated with stopping. The Queensland government has rejected a petition to change every stop sign in Queensland into a give-way sign. The petition was signed by 391 Queensland residents and was tabled to the government late August. It argued "requiring vehicles to come to a complete stop is almost always of no safety significance". "Collectively, it wastes a significant amount of fuel or electrical energy," the petitioner said. Minister for Transport and Main Roads, Brent Mickelberg, responded to the petition confirming the Crisafulli government would not be making the change. The petition was signed by 391 Queenslanders. ( ABC News: Luke Bowden ) The petitioner said petrol, diesel and LPG powered vehicles use more fuel to come to a complete stop. They also stated stop signs could create more traffic accidents by drivers rear ending cars that have come to a complete halt. "It is important to note up front that stop and give-way signs are not interchangeable traffic controls," Mr Mickelberg wrote in his response. "They serve different road safety and traffic management functions and are installed in accordance with nationally recognised engineering standards and traffic control guidelines." He said stop signs are more often used on intersections where visibility is restricted, in an attempt to limit crashes. The minister admitted bringing vehicles to a complete stop "may result in some additional fuel or energy consumption compared with giving way". Brent Mickelberg said the signs are not interchangeable traffic controls. ( ABC News: Mark Leonardi ) But he wrote that despite that, the safety benefits outweigh any operational impacts associated with stopping. "I recognise that unnecessary traffic controls can impose costs on road users and that traffic control devices should be proportionate to the level of risk. "Installation of stop signs is based on an assessment of site-specific conditions, including sight distance, intersection geometry, traffic volumes and safety performance. He finished his response by reminding any Queenslander that if they feel an intersection may be incorrectly signed, to contact the relevant council. events.title: Anthropic to invest $100 million to train AI engineer talent
events.summary: Anthropic will invest $100 million in a program to train AI engineers. The program aims train 10,000 "frontier deployed engineers." by the end of 2027. As Anthropic pushes toward what's expected to be a historic IPO, the company is seeking to address a gap in available AI talent across industries. Anthropic will invest $100 million into an academy for training AI talent, working with companies to integrate artificial intelligence into their operations. The investment will fund a program called the Claude Frontier Academy, which aims to train 10,000 "frontier deployed engineers" drawn from companies that are part of Anthropic's Claude Partner Network by the end of 2027, the company said in a press release on Friday. Engineers from Accenture , Morgan Stanley , Novo Nordisk and a number of top consulting firms are included in the first groups. The program was borne out of Anthropic's work partnering with businesses in implementing Claude, according to Anthropic. "We hear our customers and partner organizations say, we need more people who can bring together familiarity and — with the enterprise tech and business context — and combine that with the highest level of AI fluency to solve the problems that need solving," Shambhavi Shambhavi, Anthropic's head of strategy and operations for partnerships, told CNBC. Anthropic is in the midst of massive expansion as companies across the globe race to infuse its AI tools across their business units. The company is expected to hit the public market later this year, and could reportedly seek a $2 trillion market cap. Reuters reported earlier this week, citing a leaked copy of the IPO prospectus, that Anthropic generated almost $4.6 billion in revenue last year while racking up an operating loss of over $8 billion. The training program will begin with an intensive "simulated enterprise deployment" with a graded assessment. Those who pass will enter a residency that follows a medical teaching model, with software engineers learning from instructors and practicing with casework before being assessed and credentialed. The first engineers are expected to be certified in early 2027. "Claude Frontier Academy trains people the way our own engineers learn, and we want those who graduate to set the standard for how AI gets built inside a business," Steve Corfield, Anthropic's global head of business development and partnerships, said in the release. The launch comes amid soaring demand for AI engineering expertise across multiple industries. Job postings for forward deployed engineers and other AI-related roles have surged in the finance world this year , according to data from Draup provided exclusively to CNBC. — CNBC's Ashley Capoot contributed reporting. events.title: I used AI to tailor my work wardrobe. Here’s how you can too
events.summary: Shopping online was far more efficient, but the writer needed every purchase to hit the mark to save time, effort and money on returns. The author used AI as a personal stylist to tailor a wardrobe that fits her post-pregnancy body shape, saving time and money compared to traditional shopping or hiring a stylist. AI provided detailed outfit suggestions, fabric recommendations, and size advice based on precise body measurements and preferences, helping her shop confidently online. While AI guidance was useful, the author cross-checked with a human tailor to adjust for personal nuances, highlighting AI’s value but also its limitations in fashion advice. SINGAPORE – Recently, my husband has been dressing up rather snazzily for work . So much so that his new look has caught the attention of his colleagues, prompting them to ask if he is going for a job interview. Gone are the casual printed T-shirts, light blue jeans and chunky grey Hoka sneakers. He now rotates between plain, heavy cotton tees, knit polo shirts and tailored shirts , paired with high-waisted tailored pants and leather loafers. Little do his colleagues know that his style transformation isn’t the work of a personal stylist or fashion influencer – but AI-generated advice . He was inspired to try it after I did the same and told him how pleased I was with my new wardrobe and new-found confidence. It all started around March, when I returned to work after maternity leave. Getting dressed for the office – or anywhere else, for that matter – had become an uninspired and frustrating chore. About 90% of my wardrobe no longer fitted after my third pregnancy, as my ribs and hips had permanently widened by a full dress size. At the same time, I had grown to favour a wardrobe system where I could stick my hand in with my eyes closed and pull out an outfit that looked completely cohesive. I needed comfortable clothes not only to run after cheeky toddlers escaping diaper changes, but also to wear in smart-casual business settings. I could have done it the “regular” way: heading down to stores individually, browsing the racks hoping to find something that might work, trying it on to confirm, and mentally mapping out whether it would match at least three other pieces in my wardrobe. The time and energy required for that would be infinite – and I had a strictly finite supply of both. Shopping online was far more efficient, but I needed every purchase to hit the mark to save time, effort and money on returns. I could have consulted a personal stylist, but I wanted to save some money. Personal styling services typically start at around $1,000 for a consultation that includes a body-shape analysis. Some stylists offer a package deal which includes other services such as colour analysis, wardrobe edit and personal shopping that can take the total above $3,000. So I enlisted AI as my personal stylist – and shot a barrage of questions and prompts at it to help me figure out a functional head-to-toe uniform featuring silhouettes and colours specifically tailored to flatter me. Here’s how I did it in one afternoon. I started by putting in the hard data of my body measurements in centimetres or inches, and let AI spit out the facts. The basics: Total height; shoulder width; circumference of bust, waist and hips; and length of legs from natural bend in waist to heel. Additional inputs if you want: Whether you are fine- or heavy-boned (usually determined by whether your middle finger and thumb meet around your wrist), your weight and your exact foundation shade, which the artificial intelligence uses to determine your skin tone and suggest the most flattering colours. From my measurements, the AI-generated response declared my frame to be a “proportional masterpiece” and an “haute couture silhouette”. That’s flattering, but talk to me in straight terms, I prompted. It clarified to say that it meant I have a balanced hourglass shape, with broad shoulders, and that because of my measurements, “standard off-the-rack styling logic does not apply”. That meant buying clothes in bigger sizes and then getting them altered to fit perfectly. The prompt I used here was: What outfit silhouette will best flatter my body shape? I received three suggestions for a signature everyday look, a dressy evening event and a casual off-duty outfit. Each came with detailed suggestions for tops, bottoms and outerwear, plus the reasoning behind them. From here, it is a matter of following up with prompts to find tailored solutions for myriad conditions, such as the event setting, the climate and personal style preferences. You can even prompt AI to suggest actual products you can buy. There were times when a suggested outfit combination was too glamorous for the office or for a colder climate. So I prompted the AI to suggest minimalist or “quiet luxury” styles that would work in both an air-conditioned office and humid weather.

events.title: Christa Pike survived lethal injection. How your state carries out executions
events.summary: Data: Death Penalty Information Center ; Note: New Hampshire abolished the death penalty but retains one prisoner on death row; Map: Erin Davis/Axios Christa Pike 's survival after two lethal injection doses has put state execution protocols nationwide under new scrutiny. The big picture: How prisoners are executed varies by state , with lethal injection, electrocution, lethal gas and firing squads among the methods authorized. Lethal injections are the most common U.S. execution method , accounting for roughly 89% of the 1,683 executions carried out since 1976, per the Death Penalty Information Center . By the numbers: More than two dozen states have lethal injection as a primary method. Lethal gas is authorized in Alabama, Arizona, Arkansas, California, Louisiana, Mississippi, Missouri, Oklahoma and Wyoming. Electrocution is allowed in Alabama, Arkansas, Florida, Kentucky, Louisiana, Mississippi, Oklahoma, South Carolina and Tennessee. Firing squad is allowed in Idaho, Mississippi, Oklahoma, South Carolina and Utah. Idaho is the only state where it is the primary method. Context: Some states let prisoners choose among the different execution methods. Zoom out: The Supreme Court requires states to keep the death penalty only for the most heinous murders. Pike , convicted of killing a classmate three decades ago, survived two rounds of lethal injection drugs earlier this week in what would have been the first execution of a woman in Tennessee in 200 years. Pike was still alive as of Friday, remaining on a ventilator and unconscious, AP reports.

events.title: HBF for High-Throughput LLM Serving (UC Berkeley, FuriosaAI)
events.summary: Manufacturing, Packaging & Materials Technical Papers Home '; AI/ML/DL Architectures Automotive/ Aerospace Communication/Data Movement Design & Verification Lithography Manufacturing Materials Memory Optoelectronics / Photonics Packaging Power & Performance Quantum Security Test, Measurement, Analytics tech papers Transistors Z-End Applications Videos & Research Videos Industry Research Newsletters & Store Newsletters Store MENU Home Special Reports Systems & Design Low Power-High Performance Manufacturing, Packaging & Materials Test, Measurement & Analytics Auto, Security and AI Knowledge Center Videos Startup Corner Business & Startups Jobs Technical Papers Events Webinars Industry Research Newsletters Store Special Reports Researchers at the UC Berkeley and FuriosaAI published a technical paper titled “Characterizing High Bandwidth Flash for LLM Serving.” “Large language model (LLM) serving requires substantial memory to store model weights and KV caches. As models grow larger and contexts become longer, memory capacity and bandwidth increasingly become bottlenecks for serving performance. Agentic workloads compound this pressure through repeated interactions over growing contexts, making it increasingly important to retain KV state for reuse. High-bandwidth flash (HBF) offers a way to expand accelerator memory capacity for large language model (LLM) serving, but its access costs and limited write endurance complicate its use. We evaluate HBF for high-throughput agentic serving across system design and scheduling choices to understand when additional capacity improves serving performance and energy efficiency. We introduce an HBM-HBF-host hierarchical storage system and buffered cache-aware scheduling, and use trace-driven simulations to analyze their effects on performance, energy consumption, and HBF write lifetime. Across the evaluated workloads, the fastest HBF-augmented systems reduce completion time by 36.1-87.0% relative to HBM-only systems. Modeled energy savings reach 55.8%, although HBF increases energy consumption on some light workloads. Buffered cache-aware scheduling extends estimated HBF write lifetime from 4.77 to 14.82 years in the evaluated configuration. These results demonstrate the importance of coordinating data placement and scheduling to improve serving efficiency while sustaining a practical HBF write lifetime.” Find the technical paper here . events.title: Oil prices lower as G7 nations to release diesel stocks, Saudis reportedly plan attack on Houthis
events.summary: The Group of Seven nations agreed to a "substantial diesel release" as fuel prices surge, its leaders said in a joint statement. As Western nations prepare to release more stockpiles, tensions are simmering in the Middle East. Crude oil prices edged lower Friday, after the Group of Seven nations announced the release of diesel and crude stocks to ease surging fuel prices. Brent crude futures, the international benchmark, lost 6 cents to close at $102.25 per barrel, while U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude shed $1.76 to settle at $91.11 per barrel. The G7 will deploy 100 million barrels of reserves over the next four months "with a frontloaded substantial diesel release within the first 20 days," the group's leaders said in a joint statement. The G7 are France, Canada, Germany, Italy, Japan, the United Kingdom and the United States. As Western nations prepare to release more stocks, tensions are simmering in the Middle East. Saudi Arabia is planning an offensive against Iran-backed Houthi militants in Yemen, regional and Western officials told Reuters . Oil prices settled higher in the previous session following a report that the U.S. is sending a third aircraft carrier strike group to the Middle East. The Trump administration has called on Europe to release diesel stocks as the world faces a fuel supply shortfall due to the wars in Eastern Europe and the Middle East. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Thursday that "American farmers, truckers, and businesses should not be left carrying the burden of a global diesel shortage." U.S. President Donald Trump has indicated the U.S. could impose a diesel export ban, but he appeared to cool on the idea earlier this week due to its potential impact on gasoline prices. The U.S. supplied around half of the EU's diesel imports in August, according to the International Energy Agency, underscoring the 27-nation bloc's exposure to a potential export ban.

events.title: 10-year Treasury yield ticks higher despite weaker-than-expected jobs report
events.summary: Treasury yields rose on Friday, after initially falling following an unexpectedly weak September jobs report likely put the brakes on a Federal Reserve rate hike in October. The benchmark 10-year Treasury yield rose almost 5 basis points to 5.281%. Earlier this week, the yield reached its highest levels since 2002. The 30-year Treasury yield added 2 basis points at 5.629%. The 2-year Treasury yield, which is the most sensitive to Fed moves, was higher by 5 basis points at 4.839%. One basis point is equal to 0.01%, and yields and prices move in opposite directions. Nonfarm payrolls increased by just 29,000 for the month while the unemployment rate increased to 4.2% from 4.1%, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Friday. Economists surveyed by Dow Jones had been predicting an 84,000 increase and unemployment to remain steady. The August jobs count was revised lower to a gain of 133,000. Yields initially fell in reaction to the report, but throughout the trading session they moved back into positive territory. "I think that's the right move because I don't think this report necessarily changes the story for the Fed," said Timothy Chubb, chief investment officer at Girard Advisory Services. "I still think the trajectory from here is higher for longer." Traders now see a 77% chance that the Federal Reserve will hold rates steady at its October meeting, according to the CME Group's FedWatch tool , though traders still see a high likelihood for a hike at its meeting in December. Lindsay Rosner, head of multi-sector fixed income investing at Goldman Sachs Asset Management, agrees that a rate increase is unlikely this month, but that it's likely the Fed's hiking cycle isn't over. "Today's soft print argues against the idea that the labor market is retightening," she said. "One follow-up hike in December remains our base case; however, continued pressure by markets and moves higher in energy prices could force the Fed's hand this month as well." Pressure on global government bonds eased elsewhere after a sharp sell-off this week, with 10-year yields down by around 3 basis points across major European economies. The recent rise in yields reflects concerns about stubborn inflation and hawkish central bank commentary, fueling expectations that interest rates could remain elevated for longer.
