events.title: Democrats’ hopes rise in Texas
events.summary: Democrats are feeling newly optimistic about Texas, even in deep-red seats. Polls shared with Semafor show Democratic candidates running surprisingly competitively in the 9th and the 10th Congressional Districts. In the 10th, Democrat Caitlin Rourk is polling at 41% to Republican Chris Gober’s 48%, with Trump’s favorability underwater at 50% unfavorable and 47% favorable. Democratic Senate nominee James Talarico is also statistically tied with Republican Ken Paxton in the district, which Trump won by 22 points in 2024. And in the 9th District (also handily carried by Trump), Democrat Leticia Gutierrez is trailing Republican Alex Mealer by six points, with Trump’s favorability negative and the Senate race statistically tied. Still, both Democratic candidates trail the Republicans in fundraising and are looking for more resources. Gober, the former lawyer of Elon Musk’s America PAC, might be able to call for substantial backup. “We have been doing the path-breaking foundational work and are ready to go exponential in the final stretch. Now, we just need the investment to go execute and win this race,” Rourk said in a statement. The polling, shared by Democratic campaigns, could nevertheless be a warning sign for Paxton and Republican Gov. Greg Abbott. — Nicholas Wu

Both rally sites — Durant, Oklahoma, and Mobile, Alabama — “hit multiple states and media markets” because of their proximity to neighboring states, a Republican official familiar with the strategy said. Trump officials hope to turn out low-propensity voters, particularly in close races that Republicans need to win to keep control of Congress. The Republican official also emphasized that Trump will travel to actual battleground states like Florida, Texas, Ohio, Iowa, and Michigan. Not everyone in Trump’s orbit is convinced. “I don’t really buy it, but it’s a well-thought-out explanation,” one person close to the White House told Semafor. “I think they want big rallies.” — Shelby Talcott

events.title: 'The No. 1 thing': Republicans agonize over their economic inaction
events.summary: The News Senate Republicans are departing Washington to defend their majority — and many are carrying with them real fear that the party didn’t do enough to address constituents’ economic concerns ahead of the impending election. Despite passing a huge tax cut law last year, Republicans are fretting they have not demonstrated to voters that they are tackling high gas prices, stubborn inflation, and sky-high interest rates that threaten their House and Senate majorities come November. “If you’re not worried, you’re living in a cave,” Sen. Jim Justice, R-W.Va., told Semafor. “There’s no question that there’s people out there that are hurting.” Justice said West Virginians love President Donald Trump but people in the Mountain State “really probably feel like Congress deserves what they get — a 14 percent approval rate.” And if that’s the case in a conservative state like West Virginia, it explains why Republicans are praying Trump can help turn out his voters to support the congressional GOP in the midterms. “If you’re sitting home without a job and you can’t make ends meet … at some point in time, what do you decide? You decide, ‘Well, I can’t stand to vote for those Democrats because they got us all in this mess. But I’m just not going to vote,’” Justice said. “If you lose your base, you’re in trouble, and then you’re going to have a bad outcome.” The unease with the economy — and voters’ perception of it — is widespread across the Republican Party. Some House members desperately want the body to return to Washington to address fuel prices. And many GOP senators think the party made a mistake by not staying and working on cost-of-living issues deeper into the fall. Battleground campaigns are largely being fought on cost-of-living and economic issues — the same challenges that cost Democrats the 2024 election just two years ago. “If we had done enough, our constituents wouldn’t be continuing to raise it, and it wouldn’t be the No. 1 thing that everyone’s campaign is talking about,” Sen. Lisa Murkowski, R-Alaska, told Semafor. Her colleague, Sen. Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska, is in the fight of his political life, as are Republican Sens. Susan Collins of Maine and Jon Husted of Ohio and GOP candidates in open seats in Iowa, North Carolina, and Texas. Democrats are also targeting Sens. Roger Marshall of Kansas, Darline Graham of South Carolina, and Cindy Hyde-Smith of Mississippi — all of whom are red state incumbents. Republican leadership tried to address concerns about utility costs with a data center bill from Husted, but Democrats blocked it because its requirements were voluntary. And Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., prevented Marshall’s medical price transparency bill from getting a vote. “Ending Joe Biden’s inflation crisis has been a Day One priority for President Trump,” White House spokesperson Olivia Wales told Semafor, pointing to the tax bill as well as progress on private-sector jobs, manufacturing investments, and beef, drug, and insurance prices. He “remains laser-focused on delivering even more economic relief for American families,” she added. But both Marshall and Husted told Semafor that they wanted Republicans to do more. Husted said voters “rightly always want us to do all we can to make their lives more affordable and that’s exactly what we should do.” Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., said that he wanted the Senate to stay longer, “but there are a lot of folks that are in tight campaigns and want to go back home and campaign, and I understand that.” And while there is broad recognition of the economic challenges facing the country, there isn’t exactly agreement on what to do about them. “Everyone’s looking for the magic bullet. There’s no one magic bullet here. I mean, yes, the war in Iran is not helping at all. And in my view, that’s the first piece. But there is so much more to this,” Murkowski said. Republicans are increasingly calling for an end to the war, a break with Trump that underscores the conflict’s unpopularity. Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, who was defeated in his primary by Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, said the “national mood is not great for us.” Paxton is struggling to defeat his Democratic opponent James Talarico in a state that rarely votes for Democrats. “Foreign wars don’t typically motivate people to want to go vote. And kitchen table issues do,” Cornyn said. “And I certainly think the president hasn’t been focused on that and has kind of deprecated the suggestion that we spent more time and effort to focus on it. So, that’s not going to help.” Know More Trump signed Republicans’ signature legislation last summer, which preserved many tax cuts and enacted some new ones on things like overtime pay, tipped wages, and car interest. “Just think what we did to put money in the pockets of working men and women,” said Senate Finance Committee Chair Chuck Grassley of Iowa, home of another tough race. Nonetheless, Grassley is leaning on Trump to help lower fuel prices, the most visible sign of high prices. Consumer confidence in September sank to its lowest level since 2014, The Conference Board said Tuesday, as higher oil and gas prices eclipsed more positive economic indicators. The AI buildout, higher tariffs, and the Iran war together “had the effect of raising the prices that consumers and businesses face,” Federal Reserve Gov. Michael Barr told the Detroit Economic Club Tuesday. “While the effects of tariffs may have diminished, high energy prices are still with us — and there is considerable uncertainty about when the conflict driving them may be resolved.” The House left town two weeks before the Senate after passing bills like the data center legislation, giving lawmakers more time to campaign in their districts. Since then, some lawmakers in tight races like Rep. Ashley Hinson, R-Iowa, who’s running for Senate, said the House needs to come back to suspend the gas tax and act on diesel prices, among other legislation. Most Republicans are doubtful they’ll return before the midterms, however. Meanwhile, the White House is pulling out all the stops it can. Trump will travel to battleground states in coming weeks, chief of staff Susie Wiles recently told GOP senators , in an eleventh-hour bid to bolster the party’s most vulnerable incumbents. He also announced plans this week to spend billions on a steel mill in Iowa and a natural gas facility in Alaska — both states where Republicans are facing tough races for House and Senate. “I’ve done a very bad job of explaining how good the country is doing,” Trump said Wednesday. events.title: Erase social media tomorrow? Brits say yes
events.summary: Just 7 percent of Brits think social media is a force for good and around one in three suspect that life would get better if all these sites were erased from the internet tomorrow. Or so claims Opinium Research, which describes itself as a “strategic insight agency.” It polled 2,000 adults and 1,100 parents in September and The Register’s major surprise is that more people of Britland didn’t want to see social media rubbed out. Some 42 percent surveyed said these networks are addictive, and half think they are worse for society now than they were in 2010 as they contain false or misleading information and the algorithms dictate what they see, making public debate more divisive. More than half reckon the rot set in due to commercialization, yet one in ten admitted buying products every day via the platforms in the last year with around a fifth doing so every week and 12 percent claiming they discover new brands via their feeds daily. Irrespective of the negative sentiments, 49 percent use social media more now than they did 16 years ago, and a third use it a lot more. 31 percent are more using it to view content than post themselves. When there’s so much bot slop and political propaganda to chew through, who has time to upload pictures of, er, cats or the meals they made for themselves? More emphatically, seven in ten people surveyed support fines for social media businesses whose platforms expose under-16s to harmful content. Britain has tried to tackle this and a social media ban for that age group is in the offing. The research was not commissioned by any commercial or government entity, Opinium told The Register it was designed as a “thought leadership piece.” It lands a week before The Social Reckoning hits the cinemas, Aaron Sorkin’s sequel to his critically acclaimed The Social Network, a film that cast Mark Zuckerberg in a less than favorable light. The digital ditch has widened in the past five years since Elon Musk bought Twitter - a tool used by a tool to sow seeds of discontent. Some of the glorious leaders of social media empires have also kowtowed to US President Donald Trump, emboldening those with opinions some may consider racist or sexist. Trump threatened to send Zuck to prison if he was re-elected, branding him a so-called “election fraudster.” Trump lost the 2020 election and there is no evidence he lost it due to fraud. The depressing fact is that more Brits are shovelling social media up their nose than ever before. According to Statista, 55.5 million are signed up, compared to 29.4 million in 2010. This is despite people knowing it is addictive, has ruined the quality of public discourse, and wrecked privacy - we all know none of these platforms are truly free; users pay with their data. This vulture’s account on X is mostly unused, though he is testing out Bluesky, which seems to be a gentler and kinder version of the artist formerly known as Twitter. He deleted Facebook years ago and never looked back (yes, including the data it held in its datacenter). And you can’t find him on Instagram or Snapchat or anything else used to “socialize” or argue with other humans. The UK’s latest Prime Minister – the seventh in ten years – last week announced a center to fight misinformation. If that had been in place around the time leading up to the Brexit vote in 2016, maybe the country could have countered alleged Russian interference. Perhaps other divisive forces in British politics would have crawled back under a rock. Then again, Trump did enjoy a second coming. So what to do? Apart from Reg readers and the quality of the comments they add to our articles, should the internet should become a read-only medium? Terminating social media might be a first step in the right direction. ®
